item.title: Queens-Style Pizza Screens: Project Plan
item.description:
A plan to buy, size, season and bake on a fine stainless mesh pizza screen like the ones used by a few Queens, NY pizzerias (Margherita Pizza in Jamaica, Gaby’s in Hollis). The pie is dressed on the screen, then usually finished directly on the oven deck, which gives the underside a fine mesh pattern and a bagel-like chew. The notes come from the pizzamaking.com thread on these screens and the videos linked from it.

Source caveat. The forum blocks automated fetching, so everything below is from forum posts I read as screenshots (2017 through September 2026) plus one video title. Facts are tagged (stated) where a poster said it. Anything else is (plan), my own proposal. See Open questions.

What the Queens pizzerias do (stated)

From hammettjr’s 2017 visit to a Long Island pizzeria that uses the same screens:

  • The screens are “custom made” and arrive in a shipment every 2 to 3 months. The owner then “makes” each one by folding over the edges.
  • They bake in Baker’s Pride deck ovens.
  • Pies are dressed on the screen, and the poster was fairly certain they finish baking directly on the deck.
  • The crust has a bagel-like chew and the sauce is sweet and complex. Parmesan is probably in the sauce.
  • The hand-folded screen he took home was 18.5″, and his largest stone was 16″.

From a 2026 post in the thread: a poster who called a pizzeria that uses the fine-mesh screens was told they are aluminum and turn black with use. Another poster said Gaby’s opens its dough with oil, as Frank Giaquinto did.

Videos

  • How to make a pizza at Gaby’s Queens, NY (posted by “Mike”, mikeman0341) — the Gaby’s screen-and-oil technique. I could not load the page, so I have only the title.
  • A second YouTube link in post msg826338 — still to be added.

Choosing a screen

Choice Notes from the thread
Material 304 stainless was used by one builder (stated). The pizzeria screens are reportedly aluminum that blackens with use (stated). Stainless is my pick: it does not darken or flake.
Mesh Target spec: 304 stainless steel, 20 mesh, 0.30 mm wire. That is about 0.012″ wire with roughly 0.97 mm (0.038″) openings. A thread poster compared two 20-mesh listings: one is 0.15 mm wire, and the same 20 mesh at 0.3 mm is twice as thick. They judged the mesh in a closeup photo of a working screen to be “much thicker than 0.15 mm”, and wondered whether the weight of the pie or repeated high heat would tear thin mesh. So buy the 0.30 mm wire, not the 0.15 mm. (I have not checked that listing’s stated alloy; confirm it says 304.) A Sept. 2026 poster used 60 mesh and found it “simple to shape” (stated). Another poster’s 40-mesh screen is 0.0085″ wire (stated). Ask sellers for mesh count and wire diameter.
Size Buy at least 1 to 2 inches over the target size. The goal here is a 16″ pie to fit a 16″ stone. A Sept. 2026 poster ordered one cut to about 17″.

Ordered (Nov. 2026)

  • Lianart 304 stainless wire mesh, 20 mesh, 23.6 × 47.2 in. The listing gives a 1 mm hole and 0.3 mm wire, so it matches the target above. One sheet is large enough for several 16″ rounds with room for the folded rim.
  • HURRICANE 3-inch sheet metal hand seamer, so no need to hunt for one I might already own.

Sizing and folding the edge

A hand-folded rim is what makes the screen rigid and keeps raw wire ends away from you.

  1. Cut off the existing folded edge with aviation snips (vtsteve, stated).
  2. Mark the new diameter with a compass or a 16″ stone as a template (plan).
  3. Refold to the new diameter with a hand seamer (vtsteve, stated). A round tool to smooth the folds also worked (stated).
  4. File any cut ends and check that nothing snags (plan). Wear cut-resistant gloves.

Tool. A hand seamer is required (see Ordered, above). A poster confirmed the edges are simply folded over with a hand seamer, and showed a resized screen with a flat double fold along the rim (2018 photo).

Seasoning

One builder seasoned a screen with grape seed oil at 450°F for about 30 minutes (stated). Results were still pending. I plan to do the same, wiping the oil on very thinly so it does not pool in the mesh.

Baking plan

  1. Preheat the oven with the stone on the lowest rack for at least 45 minutes at its highest setting (plan).
  2. Open the dough with oil, as at Gaby’s (stated), onto a seasoned screen.
  3. Dress it on the screen. Slide the screen onto the preheated stone.
  4. After the crust sets (about a third of the bake, plan), slide the pie off the screen to finish directly on the stone, as the pizzerias do.
  5. Rest the pie on a rack, not on the screen.

Why a mesh screen helps: TXCraig1’s 16″ screen (Sept. 3, 2025, stated)

TXCraig1 bakes in a built-in wood-fired oven and reported these results with a 16″ folded-edge mesh screen:

  • A regular screen forced him to pull the pie early, or it picked up screen marks and a screen-baked texture. The mesh screen lets him leave the pie on as long as he wants without either.
  • With a regular screen his deck was effectively limited to about 675°F. With the mesh he runs 750°F and prefers the result: a delicate, crisp crust with a very light crumb.
  • Pizzas release from the mesh almost on their own.
  • A minor downside: the rolled edge makes the center bake slightly differently from the rim.
  • His next change is about 10 more seconds on the screen at 750°F. He pulled his first pie too soon and struggled to get top color.

His dough: 62.5% hydration Caputo Pizzeria flour, 2.8% salt, 2.0% lightly melted beef tallow, 0.032% IDY, mixed by hand, 450 g per 16″ pie, 12 hours at 78°F all in balls. His oven is far hotter than a home oven, so treat the timings as a guide, not targets.

Expectations, quoting hammettjr: a home oven will not give you a copy of the pizzeria pizza. Treat the first bakes as experiments.

Experiment log

Bake Screen Dough / hydration Oven temp Time on screen Result
1

Open questions

  • What is in the second YouTube video, and what do both videos show about oiling and when the pie leaves the screen?
  • How much extra diameter does the fold take? Cut the disc 1 to 1.5 inches oversize and test on scrap mesh first.
  • Does the pie finish on the screen or directly on the deck? One account says deck, and it is not confirmed for Gaby’s.
  • Does the mesh pattern on the crust underside survive a home oven’s heat?

item.title: The Tower: Parts, Pot, and Pump
item.description:
Notes from the Vertical Garden: Large Hydroponic Vegetable Tower (archive) page on MakerWorld, designed by Structales (released 2025-04-21). Summarized from a PDF printout of the page; the filament list at the page break and the video were not captured. Check the model page for anything you are about to buy or print.

At a glance

Type Pump-fed “rain” tower: pump in a sealed pot, 20 mm center pipe, sprinkler at the top
Height Up to 180 cm with all three pot sizes stacked
Footprint Pot 38 × 38 cm (printed lid 36.8 cm square)
Pot sizes GrowBig4 (large crops), Grow8 (radishes, small salad), GrowSmall4 (head lettuce, herbs, flowers); each big pot is about 18 × 18 × 20 cm
Print time Main tower profile: 72 h over 14 plates (P1S shown). Optional support rings: 15 h, 6 plates. Alternatives and options: 41.5 h, 4 plates
Filament Lots of it. Designer: use PETG, smooth plate recommended
Track record Tested outdoors for 5 months, wind-resistant per the designer

What to buy besides the printed parts

From the designer’s list:

  • A large plant pot, at least 40 L / 10 gal, square, thick upper rim, no drainage holes, plastic (preferably polyethylene), with a drillable rim. The model is sized for a 38 × 38 × 40 cm pot; the page lists several European planters and notes the lid’s STEP files can be adapted. A commenter points out you can screw the lid to a board and cut it to fit any pot. The designer says a 5-gallon bucket is too small. See Tower Sourcing in the USA for pots that worked.
  • A submersible pump. The designer uses a Sicce Syncra Silent 2.0 (the 1.5 should also work). Another commenter designed a connector for a cheaper Amazon pump (MakerWorld model 1625658).
  • 20 mm outer-diameter sturdy pipe, 2 m, cut to length (designer used aluminum; one commenter used stainless). In the US see Tower Sourcing in the USA for 3/4" OD options.
  • About 28 × M4 countersunk screws, 16 mm, with nuts; 2 × shorter M4 countersunk, 8 mm, for the filter flap.
  • 12 × M5 screws and nuts for the base lid. Nuts go into the grow pots too: 4 per big pot and 2 per small pot.
  • 3 cm aquarium foam, cut into a filter pad for the lid.
  • Net pots for the plants. One commenter notes that nuts can get stuck, and suggests embedded nuts instead.

The designer’s growing setup: Terra Aquatica TriPart fertilizers, a pH meter and EC meter, filtered or rain water, rockwool cubes with vermiculite on top, then clay pebbles in the net pot after the roots develop.

Assembly order, in short

The designer says don’t use an electric screwdriver or overtighten: it cracks the printed and plastic parts.

  1. Base — screw together the base lid parts (12 M5 screws and nuts), put the pump in the pot, and make sure the pump output sits dead center in the pot (measure it).
  2. Lid and filter — route the cable through the square hole; drill two holes on each side of the pot to line up with the lid (they hold the rods); nuts in the small holes; foam filter with a center hole and a slit facing away from the filter flap.
  3. Structure — the 2 m pipe goes in the center and must line up with the pump outlet; two rods go through pot and base; fill remaining lid holes with the cover parts; put the GrowBig4 on top.
  4. Final — stack the pots, then the black sprinkler on top.
  5. Test — fill the pot halfway. If no water comes out the top, the pump is too weak or the pump-to-pipe connection leaks (add a sealing ring). Screw the grow pots to each other, then fit the lids. If the water gets too warm, use the white cap on the top; take it off on colder days to warm the water.

To clean the pot, remove the top lids, pull the two base rods, and lift the whole tower aside so the pipe slides out; the plants stay in place.

What commenters found

  • Algae at seams. Each level snaps together, and one commenter got algae from water seeping at the seams, so they printed a cover that snaps inside to hide it. The designer says their own tower ran two months indoors on parquet without a spill.
  • Leak at the pump diaphragm. One builder found the diaphragm isn’t airtight and sealed it with gaffer tape.
  • Print problems. A builder had trouble at the grow pot’s connector; the designer says to use the “BigTower with connector supports” print profile.
  • Water temperature. A commenter running two towers reports the high flow rate keeps the water temperature stable even in high ambient heat.
  • Add-ons. A TPU cover cap for the plant holes (MakerWorld model 1526313) and a “Hydroponic tower light kit” from another designer.

Implications for the garage

  • Pump: the 180 cm tower needs a pump with enough head to push water 2 m up. Pick by max lift, and don’t assume a cheap pump has it; see the shopping list.
  • Reservoir heat: the sealed pot is a good place for a 50 W aquarium heater, and the white cap stays off in winter per the designer.
  • Freeze risk: the pot’s water is insulated by the lid, but the 20 mm pipe, pots, and net cups are full of water in cold air. Drain the pipe before a hard freeze.
  • Light: 180 cm of tower needs lights along its whole height; see Garage Grow Setup.

item.title: E-ink Poem Frames: Gift Build
item.description:
A little battery-powered e-paper frame to give as a gift. Twice a day it wakes, shows a one-line weather forecast at the top (icon, high/low, rain chance) and a short poem underneath, or a personal message if I’ve scheduled one for that day, then goes back to sleep. E-paper keeps its picture with no power, so the frame stays readable around the clock and a charge should last months.

There are three parts: a 3D-printed case (P1S, parametric), ESP32 firmware, and a small Cloudflare Worker that picks the poem, fetches the weather and lets me queue messages from my phone.

Status (2026-11-22): designed, not yet built. The case passes its own fit checks, the firmware compiles, and the worker is tested locally, but nothing has been on real hardware yet. See Verify before building a batch.

How it works

  • Frame: wakes at the refresh times (default 6:00 am and 5:00 pm local), joins Wi-Fi, fetches one JSON payload, redraws, and deep-sleeps until the next slot. After 3 pm the weather line shows tomorrow.
  • Worker: one poem per day for everyone, 4–14 lines long, filtered so it always fits the screen. A message dated for that day replaces it, and a pinned message replaces it every day until removed. The admin page at /api/eink/admin adds frames (type a town; it looks up the coordinates and time zone), queues messages, previews what a frame will show, and lists each frame’s last check-in and battery voltage.
  • Recipient setup: on first power-up the frame shows instructions and opens a Wi-Fi hotspot called Poem-Frame-XXXX. They join it on their phone, pick their home network and type its password, and the frame does the rest. If their Wi-Fi ever changes, the frame notices after two failed wakes and opens the hotspot again on its own.

Code: firmware/eink-frame/ (PlatformIO) and workers/eink-frame/, each with a README covering wiring, flashing, deployment and the API.

Bill of materials (per frame)

Part Qty Example Notes
7.5″ e-paper raw panel, 800×480 black/white (V2) 1 Waveshare 7.5inch e-Paper raw panel (archive) 170.2 × 111.2 × 1.18 mm outline; 163.2 × 97.92 mm active area (about 6.4 × 3.9″). Buy the bare panel, not the HAT kit. Glass: handle by the edges.
ESP32 board with LiPo charger and USB-C 1 DFRobot FireBeetle 2 ESP32-E (DFR0654) (archive) 60 × 25.4 mm. Charges the LiPo at up to 500 mA over USB-C and has a PH2.0 battery socket. Get the version without soldered headers.
E-paper FPC adapter 1 Good Display DESPI-C02 (archive) Takes the panel’s 24-pin ribbon and does the panel’s high-voltage boost. Set its RESE switch for the 7.5″ panel. The larger Waveshare Universal Driver HAT also works electrically, but the case’s adapter pad is sized for the DESPI-C02.
LiPo pouch cell, 3.7 V, about 7 × 50 × 60 mm 1 “705060” 2000–2500 mAh, with protection circuit and a PH2.0 (2.0 mm JST-PH) lead Check lead polarity against the FireBeetle’s socket before plugging in; sellers aren’t consistent. Any cell up to 60 × 52 × 7.5 mm fits the cradle.
Hookup wire, 26–28 AWG silicone, 8 colors ~1.5 m Adapter to FireBeetle: eight short runs, about 12 cm each.
M3 brass heat-set inserts, short (4.0 mm hole, ≤ 6 mm long) 4 CNC Kitchen-style “M3 short” Press into the front frame’s corner bosses with a soldering iron.
M3 × 8 countersunk screws 4 Back cover to frame.
Foam tape, 0.5 mm, about 6 mm wide ~0.6 m One strip around the panel’s border between glass and bezel.
Foam pads, about 1 mm thick, 6 mm round 7 One on each press post behind the panel.
Double-sided foam tape, about 1 mm small piece Holds the FireBeetle, the adapter and the battery to the back cover.
Thin card or Kapton sheet, about 165 × 105 mm 1 Optional. Sits behind the panel so nothing scratches the back of the glass.
Felt or rubber feet, 10 mm round 4 In the recesses under the desk stand.
Filament (PLA or PETG) about 300 g Frame about 45 cm³, back cover about 72 cm³, stand about 172 cm³ (it’s solid; print it at 15% infill).
USB-C cable + 5 V charger 1 For the gift box. Any phone charger works.

Shared across all frames: a USB data cable to flash firmware, a soldering iron (for the wiring and to set the inserts), and a Cloudflare account with the extra-ransom.net zone (free tier is plenty).

The case

  • Size: 194.8 × 145.8 × 15.7 mm (7.7 × 5.7 × 0.6″), landscape.
  • Front frame: 12 mm bezel on the sides and top and a 22 mm chin at the bottom that hides the ribbon bend and sits in the stand. The window has a 1 mm chamfer. Four M3 insert bosses, and a USB-C slot in the right-hand wall lined up with the FireBeetle’s port.
  • Back cover: screws on with four countersunk M3s. A skirt locates it inside the walls. On the inside it carries the battery cradle, rails for the FireBeetle (USB end against the right wall), a low outline for the adapter, and seven posts that press the panel forward through foam pads.
  • Desk stand: a separate cradle the case drops into, leaning back 15°. Its front lip covers only the bottom 10 mm of the chin.

Downloads: front_frame.stl · back_cover.stl · desk_stand.stl · generator script

The STLs come from generate_eink_frame_stls.py. Edit its parameter block (panel and board sizes, bezels, battery size, stand tilt) and re-run python3 generate_eink_frame_stls.py (needs pip install manifold3d trimesh numpy matplotlib). Every run checks that each part is watertight and that the panel, board, battery, adapter, back cover and frame don’t collide, and it prints the case size.

Printing on the P1S

Part Orientation Notes
Front frame face down The textured PEI plate gives the bezel a nice finish. 0.2 mm layers, 3 walls. No supports: the USB slot and window chamfer print as bridges and 45° overhangs.
Back cover outside face down 0.2 mm, 3 walls, 15–20% infill. No supports.
Desk stand as exported (base down) 15% infill. The felt recesses on the base bridge fine.

PLA is fine indoors. Use PETG if a frame might sit on a sunny windowsill or in a hot car on the way to someone.

Assembly

  1. Print all three parts. Press the four inserts into the frame bosses (soldering iron at about 220 °C, push straight down, let it set flush).
  2. Wire the DESPI-C02 to the FireBeetle: 3V3, GND, SDI → GPIO23, SCK → GPIO18, CS → GPIO14, D/C → GPIO13, RES → GPIO26, BUSY → GPIO25 (GPIO numbers; check the FireBeetle pinout for the pad labels). Keep the wires just long enough to reach across the bottom of the back cover. Cut the FireBeetle’s low-power pad to switch off its power LED (DFRobot’s wiki shows where).
  3. Flash and test on the bench before anything goes in the case (see Setting up each gift).
  4. Lay the frame face down on a soft cloth. Run the 0.5 mm foam strip around the bezel’s inner ledge, then drop the panel in face down with the ribbon at the bottom, passing through the notch in the locating lip. Add the card sheet behind it if you’re using one.
  5. Stick the FireBeetle between its rails with its USB-C end against the right wall, the adapter on its outline, and the battery in its cradle, all with foam tape. Stick the foam pads on the seven press posts.
  6. Fold the ribbon back and plug it into the adapter’s connector (contacts toward the latch). Plug in the battery last.
  7. Set the cover on, check the USB-C plug goes in through the side slot, and screw it down. Snug is enough: the posts only need to hold the panel against its foam.

Setting up each gift

  1. Deploy the worker once (workers/eink-frame/README.md).
  2. Open https://www.extra-ransom.net/api/eink/admin, add the frame with who it’s for and their town, choose °F or °C, and keep the default refresh times or change them.
  3. Flash it with that frame’s token: cd firmware/eink-frame && EINK_TOKEN=<token> pio run -t upload.
  4. Bench test: it shows the Wi-Fi setup screen. Join Poem-Frame-XXXX and enter your own Wi-Fi. It should draw the poem within a minute, and the admin page should show the check-in with a battery voltage.
  5. Before wrapping it, queue a message dated for the day they’ll open it. The frame will forget your Wi-Fi when it can’t find it at their house and show the setup screen; a one-line card in the box (“join the Poem-Frame Wi-Fi on your phone”) covers the rest.

Verify before building a batch

These are estimates or unconfirmed. Fix the parameter in the script or firmware if they’re wrong.

  • Where the active area sits inside the panel outline (ACTIVE_Y0 = 9.0 mm from the bottom edge, est.). The vertical border isn’t split evenly. Check against the mechanical drawing in the Waveshare 7.5″ V2 spec (archive) before printing.
  • Ribbon position: assumed to leave the bottom long edge at the centre.
  • DESPI-C02 size: the pad outline is 36 × 32 mm (est.). Measure the board.
  • USB-C height in the wall: assumes the FireBeetle is stuck to the cover with 1 mm tape, component side toward the panel.
  • Battery sense pin: GPIO34 through a 2× 1 MΩ divider according to most sources. Measure with a meter once.
  • Sleep current and battery life: “months per charge” is arithmetic, not a measurement. Put a meter on the battery lead of the first frame.
  • Poem selection: PoetryDB leans heavily on 19th-century English poets and Shakespeare sonnets (most 14-line poems are sonnets). If the mix gets repetitive, the worker’s src/poems.js can hold a hand-picked list instead.
  • Cloudflare certificate authority: the firmware trusts Google Trust Services, GlobalSign, Let’s Encrypt and SSL.com roots. If Cloudflare ever switches the site to a CA outside that list, the frames will stop updating until re-flashed.

Sources

  • Panel dimensions: Waveshare 7.5″ e-Paper V2 specification (archive) and the 7.5inch e-Paper HAT manual (archive).
  • Why not Waveshare’s own ESP32 driver board: it has no LiPo charger, and like most development boards its regulator and USB chip keep drawing current in deep sleep. See the e-Paper ESP32 Driver Board wiki (archive) and JLCPCB’s ESP32 power write-up (archive).
  • FireBeetle 2 ESP32-E: DFRobot wiki (archive).
  • Weather: Open-Meteo (archive), free for non-commercial use (terms, archive). Poems: PoetryDB (archive).

item.title: Tower Sourcing in the USA: Pot and Center Pipe
item.description:
The tower is designed around European parts: a 38 × 38 × 40 cm square planter and a 20 mm OD center pipe. Neither is easy to find in the US. This page collects what builders in the MakerWorld comments (about 1,200 ratings; read through 2026-11-12) actually used, plus my own sizing checks. Claims are marked (commenter) where a builder reported them, and (calc) where I worked them out from standard sizes. Nothing here has been built or tested by me yet.

Center pipe (20 mm OD)

The pipe carries water up the middle and, per the designer, also adds stability. It runs through a 20 mm bore in every module, so anything that sticks out past the OD will not pass: no welds, rivets, or external couplers.

What commenters used

Pipe Fit Source
20 mm aluminum Designer’s choice; third season, still looks fine Designer
20 mm stainless Works Commenter
3/4" OD vinyl tubing 19.05 mm, “worked perfectly” Commenter
1/2" PEX Used as the center pipe once; mostly used for the 16 mm ring uprights (see below) Commenters
16 mm aluminum plus a printed 20→16 reducer at the pump Works but is “a snug fit”; how the 16 mm pipe is centered in a 20 mm bore is not explained Commenter
16/22 aquarium tubing One builder says it fits; another says it does not (22 mm OD in a 20 mm hole). Treat as not working Commenters

Standard US sizes against the 20 mm bore (calc)

Stock OD vs 20 mm
3/4" OD tube (aluminum, stainless, vinyl) 19.05 mm 0.95 mm under; slides through, a little play
1/2" PEX 15.9 mm 4 mm under; needs a shim or sleeve
1/2" PVC / CPVC 21.3 mm 1.3 mm over; needs shaving (a commenter did not want to)
3/4" PEX 22.2 mm Over

So 3/4" OD tube is the closest US match. A metric 20 mm tube from a supplier such as McMaster-Carr is another route, but I have not checked stock.

The aluminum tubes I am considering

Two 3/4" OD, 6 ft candidates. The Everbilt tube is the better fit: its thinner wall leaves a 16.6 mm ID, about 70% more flow area than the Grainger tube’s 12.7 mm ID (calc), and it is close to the roughly 17 mm ID of a 20 × 1.5 mm tube.

Everbilt (Home Depot) Grainger 795AP1
OD 0.750 in (19.05 mm) 0.750 in (19.05 mm)
Wall 0.0489 in (1.24 mm) 0.125 in (3.2 mm)
ID 0.652 in (16.6 mm) (calc) 0.500 in (12.7 mm)
Alloy Not stated on the listing 6061-T6, extruded
Length 6 ft (3 ft and 4 ft also sold) 6 ft

Everbilt 3/4 in x 6 ft aluminum round tube (archive): specs from a screenshot of the listing (retail page, in stock for store pickup on 2026-11-12). Measure the real OD with calipers; the thinner wall is more flexible, so handle it carefully.

Grainger 6061 aluminum round tube, item 795AP1 (archive):
Material 6061-T6, extruded
OD 3/4 in (19.05 mm)
Wall 0.125 in (3.2 mm)
ID 0.5 in (12.7 mm)
Length 6 ft (183 cm)

Spec as shown on the listing; check the current page before ordering.

  • Length: a single 6 ft piece means no joint. The designer’s 180 cm tower includes the pot and the pipe stops 1 cm above the Rainbase, so 183 cm should just do it. Add up your module heights first; a taller build will not fit.
  • OD: 0.95 mm under the bore. Take up the slack at the pump connector with PTFE tape or heat shrink, or print a connector with a 19.05 mm bore. A loose connector is where leaks start (the designer’s fix for leaks there is a sealing ring).
  • ID: the Grainger tube’s 12.7 mm gives roughly 45% less flow area than a 20 × 1.5 mm tube (about 17 mm ID; the designer’s wall thickness is not stated) (calc); the Everbilt’s 16.6 mm is nearly the same as that tube. It matters because the pump has to lift water about 1.8 m. Check the pump’s maximum head against the finished tower height before relying on it; I have not verified the Syncra’s head rating.

If you have to join shorter lengths

Use an internal sleeve: a tube that slides inside both ends, 4 to 6 in long, scuffed, degreased, and bonded with two-part epoxy, with the sections butted tight. Welding thin aluminum tube needs TIG and leaves a bead that must be ground flush. Rivets and screws leave heads that snag in the modules. With the Everbilt tube (16.6 mm ID) a 5/8" OD (15.9 mm) sleeve leaves about 0.7 mm of clearance for epoxy. The Grainger tube’s 12.7 mm ID is too small for that, so with it just buy the 6 ft length.

Epoxy and food safety

Cured epoxy is generally inert, but look for NSF/ANSI 61 (drinking-water components) or FDA 21 CFR 175.300 compliance on the datasheet for the exact product. Avoid metal-filled putties. Wipe out squeeze-out so no bead is exposed to flowing water, mix at the stated ratio, cure fully (often 24 h or more), and flush the system with plain water before planting. An epoxy-free alternative is a tight press-fit sleeve sealed with 100% silicone sold as aquarium-safe (bathroom silicone often contains mildewcide).

Aluminum in nutrient solution

One commenter worried aluminum reacts with fertilizer salts at pH 5 to 6.5 and suggested PVC-U or polyethylene. The designer found no evidence against aluminum online and is in their third season with it. Someone else planned a polyethylene pipe (cheap, easy to cut, 10 m coil). If it bothers you, choose stainless or plastic.

Ring uprights (optional support structure)

The “Rings V4” print profile needs four 1 m uprights of 16 mm OD pipe. In the US, 1/2" PEX works (15.9 mm). One builder put a 7/16" wooden dowel inside the PEX to stiffen it. Copper also fits but is expensive. In Europe the part is sold as “rigid M16 installation pipe”.

Pump

Commenters used the Sicce Syncra Silent 2.0 (designer’s pick), a 700 GPH “WUCIOOO” pump, and a 40 W, 3000 L/h pump. The pump I plan to use:

VIVOSUN 660GPH submersible pump, size 6"×4"-660 (archive), from a screenshot of the listing on 2026-11-12:
Flow 660 GPH (2500 L/h), at zero lift
Max lift 8.2 ft (2.5 m)
Power 35 W
Price $19.99
Extras Adjustable flow, three barbed adapters, suction-cup feet, detachable body
  • Lift margin: the tower needs about 1.8 m of lift, 72% of the pump’s max head, so about 0.7 m of margin at shutoff (calc). Actual flow at 1.8 m will be well below 660 GPH, and the pipe’s friction takes more. Test it half full as the designer advises and use the flow adjuster if it sprays too hard.
  • Outlet adapters: three threaded barbs come in the box, 0.5", 0.62" and 0.75". None fits inside the 16.6 mm ID pipe, because barb ridges are wider than the nominal size. Use the 0.75" barb with a 2 to 3 in piece of 3/4" ID flexible tube, clamped on the barb, with the pipe pushed into the other end. The tube’s OD (about 1 in) does not matter because the joint sits below the lid. Do not clamp the pipe end: the pipe has to slide out for cleaning. The flexible tube also forgives a pump that is slightly off-center, but the outlet should still be near dead center under the pipe. Use the 0.62" or 0.5" barbs only to throttle flow; their bore sizes are not stated.
  • Cord: it has a molded plug. Check it fits through the lid’s square cable hole before assembly.

Pot (reservoir)

The designer’s requirements: at least 40 L (10 gal), square, thick upper rim, no drain holes, plastic (polyethylene preferred), drillable rim. The footprint is about 38 × 38 cm.

Option Reported by Notes
27-gal storage tote, cut a hole in the lid Commenter (BJ’s tote) “Works perfectly.” Wider base. Two builders used it.
Two 27-gal totes under a plywood top Commenter (4 towers, 2 reservoirs) Spray-painted the black totes white against heat. Got leaks between layers and at the board; plans silicone between each layer. Plants got crowded at two towers per 4 ft.
Plywood board between base and any pot Designer-endorsed (highest-liked tip, 39) Screw the round or square base to a board, then adapt the board to the pot. One builder clamped it with a gasket.
Step2 Lakewood planter box Three commenters Needs a modified base (STEP and STL shared by commenters in Google Drive). It is a self-watering planter; the inner basin cannot be removed, so usable volume is less. One builder refills about every 2 weeks at two 15-minute waterings a day. Hold the base plates carefully; they are tight against the rings.
Allen + Roth 14 in self-watering planter (Lowe’s) Commenter Extended the base edges by a few mm; no leaks.
Tusco MSQT23BK square planter (Amazon) Commenter Reported only as purchased.
IKEA Sortera 60 L Several EU builders Needs printed adapter parts (MakerWorld model 1594718). A high-tensile pipe was added to carry weight. I have not confirmed the US IKEA sells it.

Avoid:

  • 5-gallon buckets. The designer says that is too small for a tower this size, and one builder who adapted a thin square pot said the sides bulged when it filled.
  • Galvanized steel cans. Suggested once in the thread; they would rust in nutrient solution.
  • Thin-walled planters. One builder found a planter weak where the tower mounts.

Reservoir size matters. One builder says a 40+ L pot lasts about 4 days in summer if filled to the top; another lost track of pH and had to change the water repeatedly.

Build and print gotchas from the comments

  • Weak tabs. The joiner tabs on the main body break during printing or later (several builders). Printing with the BigTower with connector supports profile helps. Updated V5 profile moves the seam to the middle and slows the speed.
  • Feet failing on GrowSmall4 and Grow8. The bottom right foot fails on some printers (P2S reports). Changing the seam to random fixed one; adding hand-placed supports fixed another.
  • Wet PETG. Dry PETG first, even new rolls. Several builders say that fixed their failures.
  • Print bed. The rings do not fit on a 220 × 220 mm bed (K1C); the rest does.
  • Filter flap leaks. Too thick a foam pad caused it for one builder (thinner pad fixed it). Others used sealing tape, or a U-shaped TPU gasket (a flat 0.6 mm gasket made it worse). A “no flap” base option exists in the print profiles.
  • Missing a Big4 pot. The Grow8 pot with four top connectors has no offset, so with one fewer Big4 pot the rings will not attach (one builder hit this at 2 m tall).
  • Nuts stuck. An M5 nut jammed and blocked disassembly; embedded or heat-set nuts are suggested.
  • Layer leaks. Silicone or a seal at each seam if you mount the base to a board (see the four-tower build above).
  • Top rain module arms failed repeatedly for one P1S owner; the designer asks about brims and infill (use grid, crosshatch or gyroid, not something sparse).

Growing notes from the comments

  • A builder grew 72 strawberries in one tower; high flow also kept water temperature stable in heat.
  • Another runs EC at 1800 to 2200 for fruiting crops. Lettuce and herbs need much lower.
  • Rockwool starts, with clay pebbles in the net pot, per the designer. Clay can skew EC and pH readings, and one builder asked for printed inserts instead.
  • Several people added lights: LEDs built into the support rings, or a taller lid. Files are on other MakerWorld pages (one linked at the designer’s invitation).
  • PETG is fine in water, and white PETG reflects sun but encourages algae; the top parts are black for that reason.
  • Existing commercial towers: one builder scaled the model to 86% so their mesh pots and clips fit.

Shopping check before you buy

  • Pot is square, 10+ gal, no drain holes, drillable rim, or you have a board to adapt it
  • Pump max head is above tower height plus the extra loss from a narrower pipe
  • Center pipe OD is within about 1 mm under 20 mm and has a way to seal at the pump
  • Pump connector matches the pipe OD (printed connector in the print profiles)
  • Epoxy, if used, has an NSF 61 or FDA 21 CFR 175.300 datasheet
  • PETG is dry before printing

Open questions

  • Real flow of the VIVOSUN 660 at 1.8 m lift through the 16.6 mm ID Everbilt pipe (or 12.7 mm ID Grainger), and whether the lift is enough to reach the sprinkler.
  • Whether the 3/4" ID tube grips the 19.05 mm pipe snugly enough to seal without a clamp; pot depth minus pump height sets the pipe length and the joint length, so dry fit first.
  • Whether the VIVOSUN plug fits the lid’s cable hole.
  • Alloy of the Everbilt tube (not stated on the listing).
  • Whether the printed pump connector can be re-sized for a 19.05 mm pipe, or whether tape is enough.
  • Which US pot to use. The 27-gal tote and a plywood adapter is the most reported without custom CAD.

item.title: Water Filtration: Brevard and Black Mountain, NC
item.description:
Whole-house and kitchen-sink filters for two homes (two people each), one on city water in Brevard and one in Black Mountain. The goal is a practical balance of price and value, so this page starts from what the utilities actually report and only buys what that data justifies.

Status (2026-11-23): research only, nothing bought or installed. Prices are retail snapshots from late 2026 and move often, so re-check before ordering. Black Mountain has no PFAS data and no hardness figure for its wells, so test the tap there before spending much (see Open questions).

What’s in the water

From each town’s 2025 Consumer Confidence Report (CCR), the annual water quality report every utility must publish.

Brevard Black Mountain
Source Cathey’s Creek (surface water) About 49% Asheville surface water, about 51% town wells (10 wells, one entry point)
Disinfectant Chlorine, avg 1.34 ppm (0.8–1.7) Chlorine, avg 1.36 ppm (0.7–1.9); Asheville portion avg 1.21
Hardness ~4 ppm (third-party site, not in the CCR) Asheville portion 5.5 ppm; wells not reported
pH Not in the CCR 7.4 (wells), 7.6 (Asheville)
TTHM (limit 80 ppb) Avg 51, range <1–81 Avg 27, range 0–43
HAA5 (limit 60 ppb) Avg 50, range 27–75 Avg 36
Lead None detected At or under 14 ppb at the highest tap (action level 15)
Sodium Not in the CCR 150 ppm (wells, Dec 2023 sample)
PFAS None detected in the 2023 EPA screening round (third-party site) Not found
Violations None in 2025 Chlorine and E. coli monitoring lapses after Hurricane Helene, back in compliance early 2025

What that means:

  • Both towns use plain chlorine, not chloramine. Ordinary carbon removes chlorine, so a basic carbon filter does well in both.
  • Both waters are very soft. A softener would do nothing useful; skip it.
  • Brevard’s disinfection byproducts run high. The annual averages comply, but the HAA5 peak of 75 ppb is above the 60 ppb limit and TTHM peaked at 81. Carbon filtration reduces both.
  • Black Mountain’s wells are the unknown. The 150 ppm sodium reading is unusually high (it could be an outlier), and iron, manganese and hardness for the well side are not in the report.

Recommended setup

Brevard Black Mountain
Whole house Sediment + carbon (DIY Big Blue) Sediment + carbon (DIY Big Blue)
Kitchen sink Under-sink carbon block (Aquasana AQ-5200) Under-sink reverse osmosis (iSpring RCC7AK)
Rough total $400–$550 $500–$700

Why the split: Brevard’s problem is chlorine and byproducts, which carbon handles. Black Mountain’s is the unknown well water and the sodium, and reverse osmosis (RO) is the only affordable under-sink option that removes sodium and gives margin on anything the missing PFAS data might hide.

Whole house

For two people the flow demand is low, so a 20″ Big Blue two-stage setup is enough and is the best value. A packaged system is the low-effort alternative.

Option Price (late 2026) Notes
Big Blue 20″ housing, 1″ ports (Home Depot) ~$72 each; two needed 1st housing sediment, 2nd carbon
Pentair 20″ 5-micron sediment system (Home Depot) ~$159 Single-stage system, add a second housing for carbon
APEC 3-stage 20″ Big Blue housing set, model FH-3BB-20 Check the product page Three housings; the third is not needed here
Sediment + carbon cartridge sets, 4.5″ × 20″ ~$79–$230 Cheapest is a 5-micron sediment, charcoal and carbon set; APEC’s sediment, carbon and iron set is ~$230
SpringWell CF1 (packaged system) ~$1,105–$1,160 (MSRP $1,365) Install is extra; replacement pre-filters ~$20 each every 6–9 months

Estimate for the DIY route: two housings ($144), a starter cartridge set ($80–$160), plus shutoff valves, a pressure gauge and fittings (~$50–$100), so roughly $300–$400 per house, plus cartridges each 6–12 months. The CF1 costs about three times as much for less fuss; I’d only buy it if I didn’t want to touch plumbing.

Kitchen sink

Option Price (late 2026) Pick for
Aquasana AQ-5200 2-stage carbon ~$106–$125 (Walmart from $106, Aquasana direct $125) Brevard
iSpring RCC7AK 6-stage RO with remineralization ~$202–$341 depending on retailer and faucet (Amazon deal $202, Walmart black faucet $250, Lowe’s nickel faucet $341) Black Mountain

Notes:

  • The AQ-5200 is the cheapest option that addresses lead and chlorine byproducts. Check its current certification sheet for the specific claims you care about (lead, VOC, PFAS) before buying, since cartridge certifications change.
  • The RCC7AK is NSF certified and adds a remineralizing stage, which helps because RO water from already-soft water is very low in minerals. Expect a drain line and a storage tank under the sink.

Open questions

  • PFAS in Black Mountain. Not found in the Town’s report. Ask the town (828-419-9300) for its well and Asheville PFAS results, or test the tap with a lab.
  • Black Mountain well hardness, iron and manganese. If iron or manganese is present, the sediment-only stage is not enough and an iron cartridge (APEC sells a sediment, carbon and iron set) is worth adding.
  • The 150 ppm sodium. One sample from Dec 2023; confirm with the next report or a tap test before treating it as normal.
  • Brevard hardness and pH. Not in the CCR; the ~4 ppm hardness figure is from a third-party aggregator.
  • Installation details. Whole-house placement (before the water heater, shutoff and bypass locations) has not been planned for either house.

Sources

Utility reports:

  • Brevard 2025 Consumer Confidence Report (archive)
  • Town of Black Mountain 2025 water quality report, combined with Asheville (archive)
  • TapWaterData: Brevard (archive): PFAS screening and hardness (secondary source)
  • TapWaterData: Black Mountain (archive): confirms no PFAS on file

Shopping list (product links, unpaired):

  • iSpring RCC7AK at Lowe’s
  • Aquasana AQ-5200 at Walmart
  • SpringWell whole-house filters
  • APEC 3-stage 20″ Big Blue housing set at Home Depot
  • Pentair 20″ whole-house sediment system at Home Depot

item.title: Barn Lamp Shade: 3D-Printed, 12″ for a UNO Fitter
item.description:
A barn-style outdoor lamp shade for a UNO-fitter socket, printed on a Bambu P1S and modeled on the shade of the IKEA LÄGERVALL outdoor wall lamp (matte black, gooseneck arm). It has a stepped fitter cap, a bell dome and a short rim skirt. The top is a flat clamp plate with a 44.8 mm hole (1.75″ plus a little slip clearance). The shape and the STLs come from a parametric script, so any diameter or fitter size can be regenerated.

Status (2026-11-23): designed, not yet printed. Every STL checks as watertight and manifold, but nothing has been through the printer, and the fitter hole has not been measured against the real fitter. Measure the fitter first (see Open questions).

Files

  • barn_shade_UNO_STLs.zip: all three sizes (12in/, 13in/, 250mm/).
  • make_shade.py: the generator. It needs only numpy: python3 make_shade.py, with overrides like hole_d=45.5 diameter=280. style=cone gives a flatter schoolhouse cone. Edit the parameter block at the top (wall, hole diameter, cap and tier sizes, seam geometry) and re-run.

Sizes

Set Rim diameter Pieces Notes
12″ (recommended) 305 mm 9: 1 hub, 4 rim segments, 4 splice plates About 350 cm³, roughly 380 g in ASA
13″ 330 mm 9, split the same way Same parts, larger
One piece 250 mm (9.8″) 1 No seams, but it fills the P1S bed edge to edge, so there is no room for a brim

The 12″ parts

Part Qty What it is
A_hub 1 The fitter, both tiers and the upper dome, 238 mm across. A built-in sleeve reaches about 9 mm below the seam.
B_rim_segment 4 The lower rim in quarters, about 216 × 78 mm each, so two fit on one plate. They slide over the hub’s sleeve, which lines up the seam and gives the glue a large overlapping surface.
C_splice_plate 4 Small curved strips glued inside the four vertical seams between rim segments.

Printing

  • Orientation: print every piece rim-down, exactly as the files are oriented. All overhangs end up on the inside, so tree supports set to “build plate only” reach them through the open bottom and the outside surface stays clean.
  • Brim: on, about 5 mm. The rim and the hub’s sleeve sit on thin edges.
  • Supports: the hub also needs a little exterior support under its seam lip. It is hidden once the shade is assembled.
  • Walls: about 5–6 wall loops, so the 2.4 mm walls print solid.

Assembly and finish

  1. Glue the rim segments onto the hub’s sleeve and to each other with CA or 5-minute epoxy.
  2. Glue the splice plates over the vertical seams from inside.
  3. Fill and sand the outside seams, then apply a gap-filling primer.
  4. Paint. Matte black matches the LÄGERVALL. Gloss green outside with gloss white inside gives an enamel look, better suited to the style=cone schoolhouse variant.

Material

Assuming the lamp is outdoors (the lamp is meant for siding), use ASA, which the P1S’s enclosure handles well. PETG is the fallback. PLA painted black will sag in summer sun. Use an LED bulb either way.

Open questions

  • Fitter hole and ring: 44.8 mm is 1.75″ plus 0.35 mm clearance. Measure the outer diameter of the socket’s threaded section and of the UNO ring. The cap is 78 mm outside and about 73 mm inside, which should clear a standard UNO ring, but confirm it against yours. If anything is off, re-run the script, e.g. python3 make_shade.py hole_d=45.5 diameter=280.
  • Not printed yet: confirm the hub sleeve and rim segments slide together and that the 0.2 mm slip clearance suits the printer before gluing anything.
  • Match to the LÄGERVALL: the proportions were eyeballed from the product photo, not measured, so the dome height and tier sizes are approximate.

item.title: Hydroponics 101
item.description:
The short version of what a vertical tower needs: water + dissolved nutrients, oxygen at the roots, light, and a stable temperature. Everything else is detail.

How a vertical tower works

The tower in these notes (see The Tower) has a submersible pump in a 40+ L pot at the base. The pump pushes solution up a 20 mm center pipe to a sprinkler head at the top, and it rains down through the stack of grow pots, past the roots of plants held in net cups, and drains back through the pot floors into the reservoir. Roots get water, air, and a shallow standing layer in each pot between cycles; one commenter on the model found roots look healthier this way than in designs that drain dry.

 top sprinkler
^ | rain down
pipe | v
[cup][pot][cup] pots stack
[cup][pot][cup] on the pipe
^ |
+----+---v-----+
| pump tank |
+--------------+

A bigger reservoir is more forgiving: pH and nutrient concentration drift more slowly. This design’s 40+ L pot is a good size.

How often to run the pump

The model page gives no pump schedule, and the designer calls the system low-maintenance, so treat these as starting points borrowed from university-extension trickle towers, then adjust by watching the roots:

Stage Pump schedule (lights on) Notes
Seedlings just transplanted 15 min on / 15 min off Roots are short; keep them damp
Established plants 15 min on / 30–45 min off Cut back if the cups stay soggy or algae shows
Lights off Keep cycling, e.g. 15 min on / 45 off Don’t leave a trickle tower dry overnight; the pump runs 24 h on its own timer, separate from the light timer

Use a plain mechanical or digital outlet timer. Watch the roots, not the clock: white and fuzzy is healthy; slimy, brown, or smelling bad means too wet, too warm, or too little oxygen. Wilting at midday with a dry cup means run it more often.

A pump that fails while the lights are on can kill a tower in hours, so check it the first thing every day.

Feeding: pH and EC

  • pH — keep the solution at 5.5–6.5 (aim ~5.8–6.0). Outside that range, plants cannot take up some nutrients even though they are in the water.
  • EC (electrical conductivity, how strong the nutrient mix is) — the one number that tells you when to add nutrients. Measured in mS/cm.
Crop group pH EC (mS/cm)
Lettuce, arugula, bok choy 5.5–6.5 1.2–1.6
Basil, other herbs 5.5–6.5 1.0–1.6
Kale, chard 5.5–6.5 1.2–2.0 (the same solution as lettuce works)
Strawberries 5.5–6.2 1.8–2.2
Dwarf tomatoes 5.8–6.3 2.0–4.0
Peppers 5.8–6.3 lower than tomatoes, roughly 0.8–1.8

Start seedlings at roughly a quarter to half strength and work up. (Commercial growers feed seedlings at full strength; weak is the cautious choice for a first run.)

Routine for a small tower:

  1. Daily — look at the tank level and the roots. Top off with plain water (plants drink water faster than nutrients, so topping off with plain water keeps EC from creeping up).
  2. Daily for the first few weeks, then every 2–3 days once readings are stable — check pH and EC at the same time of day. Adjust pH after measuring EC. Adjust pH with small doses of pH-down (or up); add nutrients if EC has dropped below target.
  3. Every 2 weeks — drain, rinse, and refill the whole reservoir with fresh solution. Top-offs cannot fix an unbalanced mix.
  4. As needed — wipe slime off the pump intake and any drip points.

Use a complete hydroponic nutrient (two- or three-part) rather than garden fertilizer, and follow its label for the dilution. Miracle-Gro and similar lawn-and-garden products are not formulated for this.

Water temperature (important in a garage)

Keep the reservoir around 68–72 °F; treat 75 °F as the ceiling. Warmer water encourages root rot (often Pythium) and holds less oxygen; much colder water slows growth. In an unheated garage in winter, the problem is cold, not hot — see Garage Grow Setup.

Good first crops

Crop Why it works Roughly seed to first harvest
Loose-leaf and butterhead lettuce Fast, low EC, tolerates cool temperatures; cut-and-come-again 5–8 weeks
Basil Loves the tower, lots of leaf; needs warmth 5–7 weeks
Arugula, bok choy Fast and forgiving 4–6 weeks
Kale, Swiss chard Cold tolerant; good for a cool garage 6–8 weeks
Mint, parsley, cilantro Mint grows like a weed (give it its own spot); cilantro bolts quickly 6–10 weeks
Strawberries (day-neutral) A reasonable second project; buy bare-root crowns, not seed months

The tower is built for more (the designer lists tomatoes, cucumbers, broccoli, kohlrabi, peppers, and eggplant, with an optional ring support for heavy crops) and offers three pot sizes: GrowBig4 for large crops, Grow8 for radishes and small salad, GrowSmall4 for head lettuce, herbs, and flowers. For a first winter in a garage, fill it with the leafy crops above: fruiting crops need much stronger light and more heat than a winter garage gives them. Dwarf cherry tomatoes and peppers are a step-two project once the routine is working.

Common problems

Symptom Likely cause
Pale new leaves pH out of range, or EC too low
Brown, slimy roots Water too warm or low dissolved oxygen (root rot, often Pythium)
Brown leaf tips on lettuce Usually a calcium-delivery problem from fast growth under strong light with poor airflow: add a fan and ease the light. Very high EC causes a different, general leaf-edge burn
Algae in the tank or on the cups Light reaching the solution; cover the tank and use opaque parts
Tall, floppy plants Light too weak or too far away
Lettuce bolting (flower stalk) Heat or very long days

Safety

Water and mains power share a space. Plug everything into a GFCI-protected outlet, use drip loops on cords, and keep power strips and timers well above the reservoir.

item.title: Six Mocktails: Coconut, Citrus, a Not-a-Mule, and Three for the Beach
item.description:
Six no-alcohol drinks. The first three cover different ground — creamy/tropical, bright/citrus, ginger-forward. The second three (watermelon mojito, virgin paloma, mango chili-lime) were picked to travel: each adds just one new bottle to the cooler and reuses lime, mint, agave, and soda already on the list below, rather than needing its own dedicated shopping trip. No expertise assumed on my end either — these are straightforward builds, not bartending theory.

Tools and stock worth having on hand

  • Cocktail shaker (or any lidded jar/container that seals — a mason jar works)
  • Jigger or a set of measuring shot glasses (1 oz / 2 oz)
  • Citrus juicer or reamer — fresh juice matters a lot more than bottled here, especially for lime
  • Muddler (the back of a wooden spoon works in a pinch) — for mint
  • Fine strainer, if shaking anything with pulp or muddled mint
  • Copper mugs, if leaning into the mule presentation — not required, just traditional
  • Full-fat coconut milk (canned, not the carton beverage) and coconut water are different ingredients below — don’t swap one for the other
  • A bottle of good non-alcoholic ginger beer (strong ginger bite, well-carbonated) and a bottle of club soda or seltzer
  • Agave syrup (or 1:1 agave-and-water simple syrup) — shared by the citrus spritz, the paloma, and the mango chili-lime below
  • Coarse salt or Tajín, for rimming glasses — one small shaker covers the paloma and the mango chili-lime

Packing these for the 5-hour drive down

This is a drive to a beach house with its own kitchen and freezer, not a cooler-only day trip — so the plan is simpler than packing for a walk to the sand:

  • Ice and blending both happen on arrival, not in the car. No need to haul ice down — the house has a freezer, and the blender/muddler work is easiest done in an actual kitchen anyway.
  • Bring whole watermelons and mangoes, not pre-juiced bottles. Whole fruit travels fine at room temperature for 5 hours and blends better fresh at the house than juice that’s been sitting since before you left — this also skips worrying about fresh watermelon/mango juice oxidizing or losing flavor over the drive, which was a real concern for pre-blending, and isn’t one for whole fruit. Bottled watermelon juice or mango nectar are still fine fallbacks if you’d rather not deal with a whole watermelon at all.
  • Pre-mix the chili-lime salt in a small shaker or travel container (or just bring a bottle of Tajín) — no different whether you’re rimming a glass at home or at the beach house.
  • Cans of soda/ginger beer over open bottles — they hold carbonation better over a long drive and don’t go flat if the trip is bumpy.
  • Fresh lime, grapefruit, and blood orange juice travel fine for 5 hours if juiced ahead and kept in the car’s AC rather than a hot trunk; agave, salt, and canned coconut milk don’t need any special handling at all.

Coconut Colada

Creamy and tropical — the coconut mocktail to reach for over a piña colada. Full-fat canned coconut milk gives real body; coconut water alone comes out thin.

Ingredients (1 drink):

  • 2 oz full-fat coconut milk (canned, shaken well first)
  • 3 oz pineapple juice
  • 0.5 oz fresh lime juice
  • Splash of club soda or sparkling water, to top
  • Ice
  • Garnish: pineapple wedge or wheel, mint sprig

Method: Shake the coconut milk, pineapple juice, and lime juice hard with ice — the coconut milk wants the agitation to emulsify and get that piña-colada texture. Strain into a glass over fresh ice, top with a splash of soda, garnish.

Variation: swap the club soda for a splash of ginger beer if you want more spice against the coconut.

Source: Be Well Table — Pineapple Coconut Mocktail.

Blood Orange Citrus Spritz

Bright and a little tart — blood orange juice has more depth than regular orange juice, and the color is the best-looking drink of the three if blood oranges are in season (roughly winter into early spring in most US markets; regular orange juice works fine off-season, just less dramatic).

Ingredients (1 drink):

  • 3 oz blood orange juice (fresh-squeezed if you can get blood oranges; bottled is fine otherwise)
  • 0.5 oz fresh lime juice
  • 0.5 oz agave syrup or simple syrup, to taste
  • Sparkling water, to top
  • Ice
  • Garnish: orange wheel or twist

Method: Combine the juice, lime, and agave in a glass over ice, stir, then top with sparkling water. No shaking needed — this one’s built, not mixed.

Source: One Lovely Life — Blood Orange Mocktail.

The Not-a-Mule

A Moscow mule’s whole appeal is ginger heat against lime and fizz — none of that depends on the vodka, so dropping it loses less than you’d think. This is the one worth serving in a copper mug if you own them; the cold-metal thing is real, not just presentation.

Ingredients (1 drink):

  • 4 oz good non-alcoholic ginger beer (strong ginger, well-carbonated — the quality of the ginger beer is the whole drink here)
  • 0.75–1 oz fresh lime juice
  • Splash of club soda, optional, for extra fizz if the ginger beer alone isn’t lively enough
  • Ice
  • Garnish: lime wheel, mint sprig

Method: Fill a copper mug (or any glass) most of the way with ice. Add lime juice, top with ginger beer, stir gently — stir, don’t shake, or the ginger beer goes flat. Top with a splash of club soda if you want more sparkle. Garnish and serve immediately.

Source: Yummy Mummy Kitchen — Virgin Moscow Mule, Whisk Affair — Virgin Moscow Mule.

Watermelon Mojito (beach house-ready)

Reuses the lime and mint already on the list, plus club soda you’re already packing for the Not-a-Mule. The only new item is a whole watermelon — bring the fruit itself and blend at the house, rather than pre-juicing for the drive.

Ingredients (1 drink):

  • 3 oz watermelon juice (blended fresh from the whole fruit and strained, or bottled if you’d rather skip the blender entirely)
  • 0.5 oz fresh lime juice
  • 4–5 mint leaves
  • Club soda or sparkling water, to top
  • Ice
  • Garnish: mint sprig, watermelon wedge

Method: At the house — cube the watermelon, blend, strain out the pulp if you want a cleaner drink. Muddle the mint gently in the bottom of a glass, add lime juice and watermelon juice, fill with ice, top with soda, stir once.

Source: The Merry Thought — Watermelon Mojito Mocktail, The Real Food Dietitians — Watermelon Mojito.

Virgin Paloma (beach house-ready)

Same lime juice and agave as the Blood Orange Citrus Spritz, same sparkling water as everything else on this page — the only new bottle is grapefruit juice.

Ingredients (1 drink):

  • 3 oz grapefruit juice (fresh-squeezed if you’re juicing at home the night before; bottled is fine)
  • 0.5 oz fresh lime juice
  • 0.5 oz agave syrup, to taste
  • Sparkling water, to top
  • Ice
  • Salt (or Tajín) for the rim
  • Garnish: lime or grapefruit wedge

Method: Rim a glass with lime juice and dip in salt or Tajín, combine grapefruit juice, lime juice, and agave over ice, top with sparkling water, stir.

Source: Sweets & Thank You — Virgin Paloma, Mingle Mocktails — Paloma Mocktail.

Mango Chili-Lime (beach house-ready)

Reuses the lime, mint, and salt/Tajín already on the list — a whole mango (or bottled mango nectar, if you’d rather skip peeling and pureeing one) is the one new thing to bring.

Ingredients (1 drink):

  • 3 oz mango puree (blended fresh from a whole mango) or mango nectar
  • 0.5 oz fresh lime juice
  • 3–4 mint leaves
  • Sparkling water or club soda, to top
  • Ice
  • Chili-lime salt (Tajín, or your own chili/salt/sugar mix) for the rim
  • Garnish: lime wedge, mint sprig

Method: Rim the glass with lime juice and chili-lime salt, same as the paloma. Muddle or tear the mint into the glass, add lime juice and mango puree, fill with ice, top with soda, stir.

Source: Aura Bora — Mango Chili Lime Mocktail, Whole30 — Mango-Chili-Lime Mocktail.

item.title: Artisan on Headless Linux
item.description:
How to set up a headless Ubuntu server as a Phidget sensor hub, so that Artisan running on your Mac can read the VINT thermocouples as if they were plugged in locally.

Architecture: the Ubuntu server runs the Phidget Network Server — a lightweight daemon that makes all attached Phidget devices available over the LAN via WebSockets on port 5661. The Mac’s Phidget22 library discovers it automatically, and Artisan sees the remote sensors transparently. No Artisan instance, no virtual display, and no VNC needed on the server.

[Phidget VINT Hub] --USB--> [Ubuntu server]
|
phidget22networkserver
(WebSocket, port 5661)
|
LAN/WiFi
|
[MacBook]
Artisan + Phidget22
(reads sensors as local)

Hardware

  • Ubuntu server (22.04 or 24.04 LTS, headless)
  • Phidget VINT Hub (e.g. HUB0000_0) connected via USB
  • Thermocouple module(s) in VINT ports — e.g. TMP1101 (4-input K-type) or TMP1100 (single)
  • Mac on the same local network

1. Install the Phidget22 Library and Network Server

Phidgets provides an apt repository for Ubuntu.

# Add the Phidget repo
curl -fsSL https://www.phidgets.com/downloads/setup_linux | sudo bash

# Install the library and the network server daemon
sudo apt-get install -y libphidget22 libphidget22extra phidget22networkserver

If you prefer not to run the setup script, download the packages directly from phidgets.com/downloads.

2. USB Permissions (udev Rule)

By default, USB devices are only accessible to root. Add a udev rule so the network server process can reach the Phidget Hub without running as root.

sudo tee /etc/udev/rules.d/99-phidgets.rules <<'EOF'
SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ACTION=="add", ATTR{idVendor}=="06c2", MODE="0664", GROUP="plugdev"
EOF

sudo udevadm control --reload-rules

# Add the user that will run phidget22networkserver to plugdev
sudo usermod -aG plugdev $USER

Log out and back in (or reboot) for the group change to take effect.

3. Confirm the Phidget Hub is Visible

Plug in the VINT Hub, then verify USB enumeration and permissions:

# Device should appear
lsusb | grep -i phidget
# Expected: Bus 00X Device 00X: ID 06c2:XXXX Phidgets Inc.

# Your user should be in plugdev
groups $USER | grep plugdev

# Quick permission check — should print the device file with group rw
ls -la /dev/bus/usb/$(lsusb | grep 06c2 | awk '{print $2,$4}' | awk '{printf "%s/%03d\n", $1, $2+0}' 2>/dev/null) 2>/dev/null || \
 echo "check dmesg | tail -20 if device not found"

If lsusb doesn’t show a Phidget, try a different USB port, check dmesg | tail -20 immediately after plugging in, or try a different cable.

4. Run the Phidget Network Server

The phidget22networkserver package installs a systemd unit. Enable and start it, open the firewall port, then verify the server is listening:

sudo systemctl enable phidget22networkserver
sudo systemctl start phidget22networkserver

sudo ufw allow 5661/tcp
sudo ufw reload

sudo systemctl status phidget22networkserver
ss -tlnp | grep 5661
# Expected: LISTEN 0 ... 0.0.0.0:5661

The server listens on port 5661 and publishes all connected Phidget devices over a WebSocket interface. It also advertises itself via mDNS/Bonjour so the Mac’s Phidget22 library can discover it without needing a static IP.

Server IP

Note the server’s LAN IP — you’ll need it if mDNS discovery doesn’t work on your network:

ip addr show | grep 'inet ' | grep -v 127.0.0.1

5. Configure Artisan on macOS

Install the Phidget22 drivers on your Mac

The Mac needs the Phidget22 library to talk to the network server. Download and install the macOS package from phidgets.com/downloads.

You do not need to physically attach any Phidget to the Mac.

Open Artisan and configure the device

  1. Launch Artisan on your Mac.
  2. Go to Config > Device.
  3. In the device list, select the Phidget module that matches your thermocouple board — e.g. Phidget TMP1101 for a 4-input K-type board.
  4. Set the channel assignments for ET (environmental/drum temp) and BT (bean temperature) to match how your thermocouples are wired to the VINT ports.
  5. Click OK.

Auto-discovery (same LAN, mDNS)

If your Mac and the Ubuntu server are on the same subnet, the Phidget22 library discovers the network server automatically via Bonjour. No further config needed — just press ON in Artisan’s toolbar and you should see live ET/BT readings within a few seconds.

Manual server address (if mDNS doesn’t work)

If auto-discovery fails (e.g. across VLANs, or mDNS is blocked), set the server address explicitly. Open a terminal on your Mac and add the server:

# Run once — registers the server address persistently with the Phidget22 library
/usr/local/bin/phidget22admin -a <server-ip>

Or set it within Artisan: Config > Device, look for a Server or Remote field and enter <server-ip>:5661.

Confirming Everything Works

On the Ubuntu server:

# 1. Phidget hub is enumerated
lsusb | grep 06c2

# 2. Network server is running and listening
systemctl is-active phidget22networkserver
ss -tlnp | grep 5661

From the Mac:

# 3. Port is reachable from the Mac
nc -zv <server-ip> 5661
# Expected: Connection to <server-ip> port 5661 [tcp] succeeded!

In Artisan (Mac):

  1. Press ON — ET and BT should populate within a few seconds.
  2. The status bar should show the Phidget device name without an error icon.
  3. Wiggle a thermocouple gently — the temperature reading should respond.

Troubleshooting:

Symptom Check
lsusb shows no Phidget `dmesg
networkserver fails to start journalctl -u phidget22networkserver — likely a permissions issue; verify plugdev group
Port 5661 not reachable from Mac sudo ufw status; confirm server IP is correct
Artisan shows no readings Confirm Phidget22 drivers installed on Mac; try phidget22admin -a <ip> to force address
ET/BT swapped Swap channel assignments in Config > Device

item.title: Cherry Hallway Console (Proposed)
item.description:
A proposed build — fully dimensioned and detailed, but not yet cut. A narrow wall console for an entry/hallway: drop keys and mail on top, baskets or shoes on the lower shelf. Solid cherry, hand-tool build (stock ripped and thickness-planed by machine; all joinery cut by hand).

  • Overall size: 42" W × 14" D × 34" H
  • Top overhang: 1" all around the leg frame
  • Lower shelf: ~10" off the floor, resting on the lower rails
  • Joinery: mortise-and-tenon frame, drawbored; floating solid top

Drawings (true scale)

Drawn at 1″ = 12 px from the dimensions on this page. Click to open full size.

Front elevation

Side elevation

Plan view, top removed

Leg layout (mortise heights and drawbore pin positions)

The drawing shows the front-left leg. The back-right leg is the same part turned end for end, and the front-right and back-left legs are its mirror image. Mortise length depends on the tenon width (and any haunch at the top of the leg), which this plan doesn’t fix, so the shaded strips mark only where each mortise sits across the face and which height band it falls in.

Variant: want somewhere to sit and put shoes on? See Cherry Console + Slide-Under Chest Bench — the same console with an open lower half and a blanket-chest seat that slides underneath.

Why these proportions

The shallow 14" depth is the point of a hallway piece — it hugs the wall and stays out of the traffic path. 34" tall sits at about waist height, comfortable for setting things down (anywhere 30–34" works; taller reads more console-like). 42" long gives presence without dominating a corridor. Legs are 1½" square — slender but honest for this span; go to 1¾" if you want it chunkier. The lower shelf earns its keep both as storage and as a structural tie that stiffens the whole frame.

Materials

Species: solid cherry, clear finish. Cherry darkens dramatically with light over the first few months (pale pink → deep reddish-brown) — plan around that (see notes).

Stock Used for Rough qty (approx)
8/4 (2" rough) Legs only 5–6 bd ft
4/4 (1" rough) Top, aprons, lower rails, shelf 18–20 bd ft

Only the legs need stock heavier than 4/4. A finished 1½"-square leg cannot come out of 4/4 — rough 4/4 only nets ~¾" of flat, clean stock after jointing and planing out cup/twist. Buy 8/4 and keep the legs seamless. (6/4 is too close to 1½" finished to survive jointing unless you drop the legs to ~1⅜".)

Lamination alternative: two face-glued pieces of 4/4 make a ~1½" blank, but on a 1½"-square leg the glue line lands on two visible faces and will age to a slightly different shade. On a clear-finished cherry piece, 8/4 is worth it. If you do laminate, orient the seam to a back corner.

The 4/4 estimate leaves margin for grain-matching the top and shelf glue-ups and for working around cherry’s gum streaks and sapwood.

Cut list

Dimensions are thickness × width × length. Cut to the length in the table — the tenon lengths are already baked in.

Part Qty Stock T × W × L (cut to this) Tenons / notes
Legs 4 8/4 1½" × 1½" × 33¼" Mortised on two adjacent faces
Long aprons (front/back) 2 4/4 ¾" × 3½" × 39" 1" tenon each end, mitered tips
Short aprons (sides) 2 4/4 ¾" × 3½" × 11" 1" tenon each end, mitered tips
Long lower rails (front/back) 2 4/4 ¾" × 2½" × 39" 1" tenon each end, mitered tips
Short lower rails (sides) 2 4/4 ¾" × 2½" × 11" 1" tenon each end, mitered tips
Top 1 4/4 ¾" × 14" × 42" No joinery; floats on frame
Lower shelf 1 4/4 ¾" × 12" × 40" Notch corners 1½" × 1½"; rests on rails

Key reference dimensions

  • Shoulder-to-shoulder (what actually keeps the frame square):
    • Long aprons & long rails: 37"
    • Short aprons & short rails: 9"
  • The extra 2" on each part = two 1" tenons living inside the legs. Set your shoulder gauge to 37" / 9" and the tenon length falls out on its own.
  • Mortises: ~5/16" wide × ~1" deep. Two tenons meet inside each leg corner — miter their tips at 45° so they don’t collide.

Build sequence

  1. Mill 4/4 down to a true ¾" in stages, resting between passes — cherry moves as internal tension releases. Leave leg blanks a hair oversized off the planer and take the last shaving by hand.
  2. Lay out and cut all mortises and tenons. Fit each tenon to its mortise before any glue-up.
  3. Glue up two end units: each = a pair of legs + short apron + short lower rail.
  4. Connect the two ends with the long aprons and long rails.
  5. Dry-clamp the whole frame and confirm the 37" and 9" shoulder distances land square before committing.
  6. Drawbore the tenons — pins pull the joints tight without clamping across the 42" span. See Drawboring below for sizes and the step-by-step.
  7. Drop the shelf onto the four lower rails.
  8. Attach the top with figure-8 fasteners or wooden buttons so the solid top can float (expand/contract seasonally). Do not glue the top down.

Drawboring

Drawboring means the pin hole in the leg and the pin hole in the tenon are deliberately about 1/32″ out of line. A tapered pin driven through both pulls the tenon deeper into the mortise and closes the shoulder, then locks the joint mechanically. On a 42″ frame that replaces a long clamp, and the joint stays tight even if the glue ever lets go.

The blue hole is drilled in the leg; the red hole is drilled in the tenon, centered 1/32″ nearer the shoulder. The section looks down through a front leg at one of the front-apron pins. It also shows the side-apron tenon meeting the front-apron tenon at their mitred tips. The drawing is true to scale.

Sizes for this table

Item Value Why
Pin diameter 1/8″ The tenon is only 5/16″ thick; a 1/4″ pin would leave ~1/32″ of wood each side
Offset 1/32″ toward the shoulder Hardwood pins this small tolerate up to ~3/64″; more can crush or split the tenon
Pin position ½″ in from the leg face Mid-tenon on a 1″ tenon, clear of the end grain and of the mitered tip of the neighboring tenon
Pins per tenon 2 on the 3½″ aprons (about 1″ from each edge); 1–2 on the 2½″ rails Spreads the pull across the width of the tenon
Hole depth in leg Through the near wall, across the mortise, ¼″ into the far wall Blind, so no pin end shows on the far side

Stagger the pins at each leg corner. Two tenons meet inside the leg, and their pins are drilled from the two adjacent outer faces. If the long-apron pin and the short-apron pin sit at the same height they cross inside the leg. Put the long-apron pins at about ¾″ and 2¾″ below the top edge, and the short-apron pin at about 1¾″ (mid-height).

Steps

  1. Cut and fit every mortise and tenon dry. It should seat by hand or with light taps, not with force.
  2. Drill the leg. Use a sharp brad-point bit and a backing block. Start on the leg’s outer face (so the pin dots show on the faces that are meant to be seen) and drill square through the near wall, across the mortise, and ¼″ into the far wall.
  3. Mark the tenon. Seat the tenon fully, put the bit back into the leg hole and tap it so the point dimples the tenon cheek.
  4. Offset and drill the tenon. Pull the tenon, move the mark 1/32″ toward the shoulder, and drill at that new mark. A drill press with a fence keeps it square to the cheek; clamp scrap behind to prevent blowout.
  5. Make the pins. Straight-grain cherry or 1/8″ hardwood dowel, with a 3/8″ taper at the tip so it finds the offset hole.
  6. Glue-up. Glue on the tenon cheeks and shoulders, none on the pins. Seat the joint, then drive the pin until it stops; you should feel the shoulder draw in.
  7. When the glue has set, saw the pins flush and scrape them clean.

For this build

  • Do the end units first (short, easy), then assemble the long aprons and rails into both ends together. Use hide glue or an extended-open-time glue so you are not racing the clock over 42″.
  • Drive the pins one corner at a time. A single pipe clamp is only for starting the joints, not for holding them.
  • Test on scrap first: make one joint in cherry with the same 5/16″ tenon and 1/8″ pin. A good result is a closed shoulder with no cracks around the pin; if the tenon splits, reduce the offset.

Domino option

A Festool Domino can cut the apron joints instead of hand-cut tenons. The plan’s 5/16″ mortise is 7.9 mm, so an 8 mm Domino matches it, and a 40 mm Domino sits 20 mm (¾″) deep in each part.

The one rule at a leg corner: two mortises entering from adjacent faces cross inside a 1½″ leg. The hand-cut plan avoids that by mitering the tenon tips. Loose tenons can’t be mitered, so no two Domino mortises in a leg may be at the same height — stagger them.

Joint Domino Cut length (was)
Long aprons (×2) 1 × 8×40 per end, centred 24 mm (≈ 15/16″) below the apron’s top edge 37″ (39″)
Short aprons (×2) 1 × 8×40 per end, centred 66 mm (≈ 2⅝″) below the apron’s top edge 9″ (11″)
Lower rails (×4) Keep the hand-cut mitered tenons 39″ and 11″ (unchanged)
  • With the Domino, cut length = shoulder-to-shoulder (37″ and 9″); there is no tenon allowance to add.
  • Keep the aprons flush to the leg faces and centre each 8 mm mortise on the apron’s ¾″ thickness.
  • The 2½″ lower rails are too short to stagger two 40 mm Dominoes at the same corner, so they stay hand-cut. Their mortises sit well below the apron Dominoes, so nothing collides.
  • One 8×40 Domino has noticeably less glue area than the full-width tenon it replaces. That is fine for a hallway console; the lower rails and shelf stiffen the frame.
  • Drawboring does not carry over to the Domino joints (a 1/8″ pin through an 8 mm Domino is marginal). Clamp the aprons instead, with hide glue or an extended-open-time glue so you can square a 42″ frame before it sets.

Hand-tool & cherry notes

  • Tear-out: cherry planes beautifully but tears where grain reverses (near figure or the pith). Keep the smoother sharp and finely set, read grain direction before each pass, and keep a card scraper handy for the top glue-up and any tricky patches.
  • Color / clamps: don’t leave clamps, tape, or stickers on exposed surfaces during glue-up or curing — cherry tans unevenly and you’ll get pale patches that never catch up.
  • Squeeze-out: scrape off all glue squeeze-out before finishing. Finish over dried glue blocks the darkening and leaves permanent ghost lines.

Adjustments to consider

  • Stretch to 48" long, or drop height to 30".
  • Add a drawer in the front apron (would change the front apron to a rail + drawer pocket).
  • Bump legs to 1¾" square for a heavier look (still cut from 8/4).

item.title: Morgan Hand Mill
item.description:
Tom Morgan Bamboo Build Class

These are the notes from the class. They were given out on sheets of paper. I’ve re-written them here and amended them where I needed additional notes.

Split Culms

  • Choose culms. Bottom of the culms are used for the butts. Top of the culms are used for tips
  • Nodes are spaced closer together at the bottom. They’re wider at the top
  • The goal is for more power fibers at the bottom of the rod blank
  • Cut culms to 5-6’ sections: one for bottom & one for top
  • Inspect for depth of power fibers
  • Split into strip with star splitter, mallet & pipe. Put the tip of the culm up
  • Mark butt strips (B) and tip strips (T)

Strip Selection & Node Spacing

  • Lay out butt strips with lowest part of culm to the right
  • Stagger nodes into 3/3 configuration1
  • Mark 8 strips to cut off (4 for each stagger). That’s 3 + 1 extra
  • Cut strips to length with chop saw or with hack saw
  • Lay out strips again in same node spacing config
  • Mark right ends in 2 different colors, one for each node alignment
  • Mark right end of each strip as butt section (B)

Repeat for the tip sections.

Prepare Strips for Planing

  • Use froe to split & shave strips to consistent width and straightness
  • Sand dams with disc sander
  • Sand nodes on disc sander until flat & flush w/ enamel. Use a fancy sanding jig if you have one
  • Drill anchor screw hole 1" from right end
  • Separate butts and tips for separate planing
  • Soak strips in water overnight2

Rough Cut & Bevel Butt Sections

  • Set up butt-roughing anvil
  • Check for trueness
  • Set butt taper from spreadsheet
  • Plane all butt strips to rough dimensions 0.070 over
  • Check for and repair curves using heat gun as needed
  • Choose 6 best strips and continue. Shelve the rest for future use

Rough Cut & Bevel Tip Sections

  • Set up tip-roughing anvil
  • Check for trueness
  • Set tip taper from spreadsheet
  • Plane all tip strips to rough dimensions 0.070 over
  • Check for and repair curves using heat gun as needed
  • Choose 6 best strips and continue. Shelve the rest for future use

Heat Treat Strips

  • Bundle strips and place in 325 degrees oven for 45 minutes
    • 45 minutes at 325 produces a “blond” color
    • 20 minutes at 350 can also be used
    • Reference needed for results of this
  • If using a forced air oven3, flip end-to-end after approx 20 minutes

Plane Butt & Tip Strips to 0.30 Over

  • Soak butt strips in water
  • Set up butt-finishing anvil
  • Zero out each station
  • True the anvil if necessary
  • Set butt taper from spreadsheet
  • Plane butt strips to 0.030 over final taper dimensions

Dry Bind Strips

This should be done at least once. Do this twice if time allows.

  • Lay out butt strips using alternating color coded ends
  • Number the strips from 1 to 6. This is the order for the strips for the rest of the build
  • Lay out strips on tape in order, 1 to 6
  • Roll strip 6 to strip 1 then work the strips together
  • Bind butt once in a binder

Check Sections for Fit

This step is to remove glue seams (gaps) twists, and bends

  • Mark gaps and irregularities with a pencil
  • Sand and straighten strips at gaps using a sanding jig

This step consists of slowly working down each of the strips, starting at the butt-end of the strip, and looking for gaps surrounding the nodes. If there was a gap at the node, place arrows on the enamel-side around the node. After all nodes are inspected, place the non-enamel side up in the sanding jig and sand this side. The gap

The gap (eventually will be a glue seam) exists because there is a “scoop” in the planed face. The intent of sanding is to lengthen that scoop so that when bound again, the strip can interface properly with its neighbor strip.

Final Planing of Strips

  • Plane butt strips to 0.003 over final taper dimensions

This 0.003 over is to allow for enamel removal in a future step, plus moisture.

Glue Up Section

  • Lay butt sections in order (1-6) on tape. Place tape at both ends of strips
  • Spread glue with toothbrush on all surfaces of strips. Work from right to left spreading glue but skip the portions above the tape. After glue is spread everywhere, also spread onto the strips over the taped sections. Goal is to keep the tape dry enough for it to stick
  • Roll strip 6 to strip 1
  • Bind butt twice in binder (once in both directions)
  • Roll out blank on marble slab with palms, checking and correcting gaps and twists
  • Roll out blank on marble slab with tape roller, gentle pressure down rod
  • Hang vertically until dry, tip-side up, with a weight at the bottom to encourage straightness

Sand Enamel from Blank

  • Cut off base of butt section
  • Sand each facet with rough and fine sanding blocks
  • When working on tip section, measure sanding strokes on each facet to ensure even removal on all sides
  • In class we were using Norton ProSand sandpaper in either 200 and 320 grit

  1. Common node spacings are Garrison-style, 3x3, and 2x2x2. See pg. 71 of Maurer & Elser’s Fundamentals of Building a Bamboo Fly-Rod ↩︎

  2. An easy solution is vinyl gutters. Lowes items #279187 & #279191 combined with silicone or similar. ↩︎

  3. Check out Frank’s Personal Waste of Time Website. If that page goes down, try the Wayback Machine archive ↩︎

item.title: Cherry Console + Slide-Under Chest Bench (Proposed)
item.description:
A proposed two-piece build: the Cherry Hallway Console reworked so its lower half is open, plus a separate blanket chest that doubles as a seat and slides underneath. Sit on the lid to put shoes on; push the chest in and the hallway looks like a plain console. Solid cherry, drawbored mortise-and-tenon frame, dovetailed chest.

Everything here is my own design, so there are no maker dimensions to match. Every number is a design choice or derived from one, and the fit checks below show how the two pieces close.

What changes from the original console

Original This version Why
Overall 42″ × 14″ × 34″ 42″ × 15″ × 35″ 1″ deeper so the seat is 13″ deep (shoe-tying depth); 1″ taller so the lid can open fully under the apron
Lower shelf Yes, ≈ 10″ off floor Removed The chest lives there
