Front lower rail Yes Removed The chest slides in through the front
Back lower rail Yes Kept — now the chest’s stop
Side lower rails Yes Kept The chest passes between them
Leg frame 40″ × 12″ 40″ × 13″

How the two pieces fit

Check Working Result
Opening between front legs 40 − 2 × 1½ 37″
Chest width 37 − 2 × ½ clearance 36″
Side rails, inner faces 40 − 2 × ¾ 38½″ apart — chest never touches them
Clear height under the apron 35 − ¾ top − 3½ apron 30¾″
Seat (lid top) height design choice 17″ — a normal bench height
Space above the lid 30¾ − 17 13¾″
Lid depth (hinged at the back) 13″
Lid front edge, open to vertical 17 + 13 30″, so ¾″ below the apron
Back stop 15 − 1 − ¾ (back rail) chest back at 13¼″ from the front edge
Chest front 13¼ − 13 ¼″ behind the top’s front edge, ¾″ proud of the legs

The lid opens all the way with the chest pushed fully under — the lid’s front edge swings up an arc of radius 13″ and clears the apron by ¾″. A deeper chest or a taller seat would break that, so the 17″ × 13″ pair is the limit for this console. For comfortable access to blankets, slide the chest out a few inches first.

Drawings (true scale)

Drawn at 1″ = 12 px (the two chest drawings at 1″ = 16 px). Click to open full size.

Front elevation, chest pushed in

Side elevation, lid open to vertical

Plan view, top removed

Chest end section

Chest front elevation

Console

Joinery and finishing are the same as the original plan: mortise-and-tenon, 1″ tenons, drawbored, floating top on buttons or figure-8s. See its Drawboring section for pin sizes and steps.

Cut list

T × W × L, cut to length. Tenon lengths are baked in.

Part Qty Stock T × W × L Notes
Legs 4 8/4 1½″ × 1½″ × 34¼″
Long aprons (front, back) 2 4/4 ¾″ × 3½″ × 39″ 37″ shoulder to shoulder
Short aprons (sides) 2 4/4 ¾″ × 3½″ × 12″ 10″ shoulder to shoulder
Side lower rails 2 4/4 ¾″ × 2½″ × 12″ Top edge ≈ 9¼″ off the floor, flush to the leg outer face
Back lower rail 1 4/4 ¾″ × 2½″ × 39″ The chest’s stop; glue a ¼″ felt strip on its inner face
Top 1 4/4 ¾″ × 15″ × 42″ Floats; 1″ overhang all round

Stiffness without a front lower rail

With the front rail gone, the base is braced on three sides (two side rails and the back rail) and the top is a rigid box of four 3½″ aprons. That is enough for a hallway piece, but it relies on the joints: drawbore the apron joints, and dry-assemble to check there is no racking along the 42″ length before you glue. If the front legs still flex, add a hidden gusset block at each front leg-to-apron corner.

Chest bench

Cut list

Cherry for everything visible. T × W × L.

Part Qty Stock T × W × L Notes
Lid 1 5/4 1″ × 13″ × 36″ Glue up from two boards; cleat underneath (below)
Case front, back 2 4/4 ¾″ × 13¾″ × 36″ Through dovetails; ¼″ groove for the bottom
Case ends 2 4/4 ¾″ × 13¾″ × 13″ Through dovetails; ¼″ groove for the bottom
Bottom 1 ½″ ½″ × 11⅞″ × 35″ Cherry or ply; floats in the grooves, grain along the length if solid
Plinth front, back 2 4/4 ¾″ × 2¼″ × 35¼″ Mitered corners, inset ⅜″ all round
Plinth ends 2 4/4 ¾″ × 2¼″ × 12¼″ Mitered corners
Lid cleats 2 4/4 ¾″ × 1¼″ × 11¼″ Underside, 2″ in from each end; slotted screw holes so the lid can move

Height is 1″ lid + 13¾″ case + 2¼″ plinth = 17″. The interior is about 34½″ × 11½″ × 13″ (the ½″ bottom sits in grooves ¼″ up from the case’s bottom edge).

Hardware

  • Hinge: one 36″ continuous (piano) hinge, 1½″ open, mortised into the back edge of the lid and case.
  • Lid support: two soft-close lid stays rated for the lid’s weight (≈ 10 lb), so it can’t slam on fingers.
  • Glides: four PTFE or felt glide pads under the plinth so the chest slides on a hard floor.
  • Edges: ease the lid edges ⅛″–¼″; they are where you sit.

Build sequence

  1. Mill case, lid and plinth stock and let it settle between passes.
  2. Cut and fit the through dovetails on the case. Plow the ¼″ bottom grooves before assembly.
  3. Glue up the case with the bottom dry (unglued) in its grooves.
  4. Make the plinth, miter the corners, and glue it to the case bottom edge — long grain to long grain, so glue is fine.
  5. Glue up the lid, add the cleats, and mortise the hinge into lid and case.
  6. Hang the lid and fit the stays. Check the lid opens to vertical with the chest in place under the console.
  7. Finish with hand-rubbed linseed oil and wax; add glides last.

Open questions

  • Seat depth. 13″ is comfortable for shoes but shallow for general sitting. Going deeper means a deeper, taller console so the lid still clears; the arc check above is the thing to redo.
  • Console leg section. 1½″ legs were fine for the original shelf version; with the front rail gone you may prefer 1¾″.
  • Floor type. Glides assume a hard floor; for carpet use rigid plastic skids instead.

item.title: Dog Biscuits: Pumpkin and Peanut Butter
item.description:
A simple, crunchy dog biscuit with five ingredients and no mixer: whole wheat flour, pumpkin, peanut butter, and eggs. Makes about 3 dozen 2-inch biscuits.

Two label checks before you start.

  • Peanut butter must have no xylitol. Xylitol (sometimes labeled “birch sugar”) is toxic to dogs. Plain peanut butter with just peanuts and maybe salt is the safe choice; check the label even on brands you trust.
  • Pumpkin must be 100% pure puree, not pumpkin pie filling. Pie filling has sugar and spices (nutmeg is harmful to dogs in quantity).

Ingredients

Amount Ingredient
2½ cups whole wheat flour, plus more for dusting
½ cup 100% pure pumpkin puree
¼ cup natural peanut butter, xylitol-free (unsalted if you can)
2 large eggs
½ tsp ground cinnamon (optional)
2–4 tbsp water, only if the dough is too dry

Equipment

  • Large bowl and a sturdy spoon
  • Rolling pin
  • Cookie cutter (about 2 inches), or a knife or pizza wheel for squares
  • Parchment-lined baking sheets

Method

  1. Heat the oven to 350°F. Line two baking sheets with parchment.
  2. Mix the wet ingredients. In the bowl, whisk the pumpkin, peanut butter, and eggs until smooth. Stir in the cinnamon if using.
  3. Add the flour a little at a time, stirring until a stiff dough forms. If it is crumbly and won’t come together, add water a tablespoon at a time; if it is sticky, work in a little more flour.
  4. Roll it out on a floured surface to about ¼ inch thick. Cut out biscuits and set them on the sheets, close together; they don’t spread.
  5. Bake 20–25 minutes, rotating the sheets halfway, until the biscuits are firm and the edges are lightly browned.
  6. Dry them out for a crunchier biscuit: turn the oven off and leave the biscuits inside for 1–2 hours, or until hard. Cool completely on a rack.

Storage

  • Airtight container at room temperature for up to 1 week (they are drier and last longer if you did the oven-off step).
  • In the refrigerator for up to 2–3 weeks.
  • In the freezer for up to 3 months.

Notes

  • Treat these as treats, not a meal. As a rule of thumb, treats should be no more than about 10% of a dog’s daily calories.
  • If your dog has a wheat or egg allergy, or you’re not sure these ingredients are right for them, check with your vet first.
  • Skip raisins, chocolate, onion, garlic, and xylitol in any variation of this recipe; all are harmful to dogs.
  • For a wheat-free version, swap in oat flour (or ground rolled oats) and expect a slightly crumblier dough; add a little extra flour if it is sticky.

item.title: Seed Starting for Hydroponics
item.description:
Seeds start in a small plug of growing medium, under light, then the whole plug drops into a net cup in the tower. No soil is involved.

Mediums

Medium Notes
Rockwool cubes (1″) Cheap, standard. Needs a pre-soak: saturate in nutrient solution at pH ~5.5 until the air bubbles stop (a few minutes), drain, and don’t squeeze. Wear gloves and avoid breathing the dust; the fibers irritate skin.
Rapid Rooter / peat-based plugs Easy, no pre-soak pH step; pop the seed in and keep moist
Coco coir plugs Good water retention; rinse if not pre-buffered
Oasis cubes Foam; works but holds a lot of water

For a first try, rockwool or plugs are the least fiddly. Whichever you pick, it has to fit the tower’s net cups.

Step by step

  1. Soak the plug in pH ~5.5 solution and let the excess drain. It should be damp, not dripping.
  2. Sow 1–2 seeds per hole (3 for tiny seeds like lettuce, thinned later). Do not bury light-dependent seeds such as lettuce; barely cover them.
  3. Cover the tray with a clear humidity dome until the seeds sprout.
  4. Warm — most crops want 65–75 °F at the plug. In a cold garage, a seedling heat mat under the tray does more good than a space heater. Lettuce germinates poorly above ~80 °F; peppers and basil like it warmer.
  5. Light as soon as they sprout — take the dome off and put a light a few inches above the seedlings, 14–16 hours a day. Raise it as they grow. Too far away means stretched, leggy seedlings.
  6. Water from below — keep an inch of very weak nutrient solution (a quarter of the label strength, EC ~0.4–0.8) in the bottom of the tray. Do not let the plugs dry out.
  7. Transplant into the tower when roots show out of the bottom of the plug and the seedling has 2–3 true leaves (not counting the first pair), usually 2–3 weeks for lettuce and herbs (longer under dim light).

Germination quick reference

Crop Germination temp Days to sprout
Lettuce 60–70 °F 2–7
Arugula, bok choy 60–75 °F 3–7
Kale, chard 60–75 °F 4–10
Basil 65–75 °F (best ~70) 5–10
Cilantro 60–70 °F 7–21
Parsley 65–80 °F 12–21+
Peppers 80–85 °F 7–14
Tomatoes 70–80 °F 5–10

Staggering

Sow a few new plugs every 1–2 weeks. A tower planted all at once gives one big harvest and then nothing; staggered sowing gives a steady supply, and a spare seedling ready when a plant fails.

Troubleshooting

  • Nothing sprouts — too cold, too dry, or old seed. Check the plug is damp and the temperature is within the range above, ideally mid-range.
  • White fuzz or mold on the plug — too wet and too still. Vent the dome and lower the moisture.
  • Seedlings fall over at the base — damping off, usually from wet, cool, stagnant conditions. Add airflow (a small fan on low) and let the surface dry a bit.
  • Leggy seedlings — light too far or too weak.

item.title: Converting a Threaded SodaStream/Drinkmate to a 5 lb CO2 Tank
item.description:
Swapping the tiny 14.5 oz cylinder that ships with a threaded (screw-in) SodaStream or Drinkmate for an external 5 lb tank — same carbonation, without buying $15–20 exchange cylinders every 60 liters.

This only applies to screw-in machines. The connection depends on the TR21-4 thread — the “blue label” screw-in cylinder standard shared by classic SodaStream machines and Drinkmate. SodaStream Terra and Art use a push-in quick-connect cylinder and are not compatible with this approach — they need a different adapter, if one exists at all. Confirm your machine actually screws the cylinder in before buying anything.

The core idea: no regulator

The stock 14.5 oz cylinder feeds the machine unregulated, at something like 850 psi (CO2 tank pressure is a function of temperature, not fill level, until the tank runs dry — so a “full” 5 lb tank and an almost-empty one both sit around the same pressure at a given room temperature). The machine’s own trigger valve is what meters gas into the bottle in short bursts; it’s designed for that pressure already.

That means the standard approach is a direct adapter hose — CGA320 (the tank’s valve standard) on one end, TR21-4 (the machine’s cylinder thread) on the other — with no separate pressure regulator in between. Adding a regulator dialed down to, say, 130 psi would just give weaker carbonation than stock, not a safety improvement; the machine already expects full cylinder pressure.

Parts

  • 5 lb aluminum CO2 cylinder, CGA320 valve. Aluminum over steel — lighter, won’t rust internally. Buy new, not refurbished, DOT-approved with a current hydro-test date (5 lb aluminum cylinders in the US are DOT-3AL, hydro-tested every 5 years; the date’s stamped on the collar and a gas supplier will check it before filling or exchanging). VEVOR and Beverage Elements both make commonly-recommended 5 lb aluminum CGA320 cylinders.
  • CGA320 → TR21-4 direct adapter hose, 36–60 in, braided stainless or reinforced food-grade hose, rated well above tank pressure (most listings claim 4500–5000+ psi, which is the hose/fitting rating, not an indication you need that much pressure). Get one with a gauge and bleed valve — the bleed valve lets you depressurize the line before disconnecting, which matters (see below). Grab spare nylon washers/o-rings while you’re at it.
  • Tank strap or wall bracket. A pressurized 5 lb cylinder becomes a genuine projectile hazard if the valve gets sheared off in a fall — secure it upright, always. Upright also isn’t optional for a different reason: these adapters pass gaseous CO2 only. A tipped tank can send liquid CO2 into the machine, which the setup isn’t built for.

Tools/consumables: adjustable wrench, a spray bottle of soapy water for leak-checking every threaded joint, spare washers.

Where to buy

Cylinder — buy local if you can. A welding or beverage-gas supplier will sell a 5 lb aluminum cylinder and fill it on the spot with beverage-grade CO2, and you skip shipping a pressure vessel entirely. If ordering online, the VEVOR 5 lb aluminum CGA320 cylinder is the commonly-recommended budget option; homebrew retailers like MoreBeer and Williams Brewing carry better-vetted tanks and are reputable for this whole category.

Adapter hose:

Product Notes
Soda Helper Universal CO2 Adapter Hose (OmniFizz/Aarke Carbonator 3), 60" Low-profile hose rather than a metal-shell braided one — won’t scratch counters. Spare washers included.
Soda Helper CO2 Adapter Hose & Base Kit for OmniFizz Same hose plus a machine base — tidier countertop setup.
GURUDAR CO2 Direct Adapter, 60" stainless Listing explicitly names DrinkMate compatibility. Label warns gaseous CO2 only, tank upright.
Tiiyee CGA320 → TR21-4 with gauge and bleed valve, 60" The gauge + bleed valve combo is worth having over a bare hose.

Other reputable non-Amazon sources for the hardware in general: MoreBeer, Williams Brewing, Soda Dispenser Depot, or a local welding/gas supply shop for the tank itself.

Gas purity

An in-line filter is not the real control here, and a cheap one won’t reliably catch what actually matters: industrial and welding-grade CO2 can carry compressor oil and hydrocarbon residue that a basic filter doesn’t remove. Two things that do the real work:

  1. Specify beverage-grade / food-grade CO2 at the fill counter, every time — not the general-purpose industrial tank.
  2. Buy a new cylinder, so you’re not inheriting rust or residue from whatever the tank held in a past life.

An activated-carbon in-line gas filter from a homebrew supplier is a reasonable belt-and-suspenders addition, but largely redundant if the gas source is clean — and check its pressure rating before adding it to this unregulated, full-tank-pressure line, since most are speced for regulated low-pressure use downstream of a proper regulator.

Safety notes

  • The cylinder is the real hazard, not the gas connection. Standing, strapped, away from heat and direct sun. A cylinder is not a countertop decoration — treat it like the pressure vessel it is.
  • CO2 displaces oxygen. It’s heavier than air and pools low in a room. This is a real risk for any large-volume leak, not just a slow one — don’t store or operate the tank in a small closed cabinet with no airflow, and if you ever smell/hear a active leak, ventilate before troubleshooting.
  • Bleed the line before disconnecting. The gauge/bleed-valve hose exists specifically for this — open it to vent residual line pressure before you unscrew anything, rather than cracking a pressurized fitting open by hand.
  • Leak-test every threaded joint with soapy water after assembly — bubbles mean it’s not sealed.
  • Don’t overtighten the TR21-4 end. The washer does the sealing, not torque.
  • Drinkmate’s own warranty generally doesn’t cover damage from third-party CO2 sources — know that going in.

Before you order

  • Confirmed the machine is screw-in (TR21-4), not the push-in quick-connect used on SodaStream Terra/Art
  • Cylinder ordered/sourced: new, aluminum, CGA320, current hydro-test date, filled with beverage-grade CO2
  • Adapter hose ordered: CGA320 → TR21-4, with gauge and bleed valve if available
  • Tank strap or bracket sourced and installed before the tank goes anywhere near the counter
  • Every joint leak-tested with soapy water on first hookup

item.title: Morgan Hand Mill Manual
item.description:
The Morgan Hand Mill — Manual Reference

A re-written, factual reference for the Morgan Hand Mill — the machine, its parts, and the taper-setting model — distilled from the Morgan Hand Mill Manual (chapters A–R, rev. 2005–2013) by Tom Morgan Rodsmiths (Tom Morgan & Gerri Carlson, Manhattan, MT).

Note. This page is a derived, factual digest — specs, procedures, and the taper-setting model summarized in my own words for reference and education. The manual itself is copyrighted and is not reproduced here. Source machine and maker contact: troutrods.com.

It is the human-readable companion to the caneDNA mhm_kb.json knowledge base, which grounds caneDNA’s Mill Settings and anvil-position visualizer in the actual machine.

What the Machine Is

The Hand Mill is two self-aligning parts: an adjustable plane that holds the cutters, and an adjustable bed that holds the strip. The cutters shave both sides of a strip at once at a fixed bevel; the taper is set by the bed, which raises the strip into the cutters station by station. The plane follows the grain rather than fighting it.

The redesigned plane (2004, developed with Dennis Detloff) has shipped since late 2005 and adds an adjustable hard stop (from Joe Byrd) that repeats the finish depth for every strip.

The Base

key value
what Chrome-plated cold-rolled steel bar the plane rides on — the taper reference surface
dimensions 5/8 × 1¾ × 72¾ in
mounting Bolts to a 2 × 2 × 3/8 in, 75 in aluminum angle at 7 points (idea from John Miller) so accuracy doesn’t depend on bench flatness
capacity Two-piece rods up to ~9 ft and various three-piece rods

Install the aluminum angle with a slight ~1/8 in upward bow so the plane doesn’t dip in the middle; check by rocking the plane along the base. The vertical face has 7 slots on 12-in centers for the anchor screws.

The Adjustable Bed

A steel bar sitting on top of the base, raised above it by push/pull screws every 5 in to set the taper. The anvil sits on the bed; the strip sits on the anvil.

key value
dimensions 5/8 × 3/4 × 68 in
stations #0 through #13 (14 stations) on 5-in centers, spanning 0–60 in
station #0 No adjusting screw, only a locking screw — always held tight against the base
push screw 5/16-18 flat-head set screws
pull/lock 1/4-20 cap-head screws (bed attaches to base with 14 of these)

To set a taper: loosen the cap-head (pull) screw, turn the hex-head (push) set screw in or out to change the bar gap. Do not over-tighten — it warps the bed. Never adjust the bed by more than 0.020 in between adjacent 5-in stations or you may permanently damage it (matters for 3-piece / spey shim setups).

The Anvils

Anvils are white HDPE with embedded brass inserts. Critically, anvils only support the strip — they do not set the taper (the bed does), so they don’t wear as the taper changes.

  • 5 anvils shipped: butt-roughing, tip-roughing, butt-finishing, and two tip-finishing.
  • Hold-down stations: finishing anvils have 11 lettered (A–K) positions; roughing anvils have 3 (long / medium / short — short is for ~3-piece rods).
  • Top widths (finishing): tip ~0.150 in, butt ~0.225 in. Top widths (roughing): tip ~0.175 in, butt ~0.225 in.
  • Truing: finishing anvils must be shaved flat between stations (with a carbide insert in the dial-holder/shaver) before use — target ±0.001 in (0.002 in TIR). Never recut the factory-installed reference anvil. Never mill an anvil narrower than the smallest strip.

The A–K Hold-Down Letters & the Mill Stop

The base has tapped holes on its right front labeled A–K; matching letters are stamped on the bed just below the finishing anvils’ 11 hold-down screws. A movable mill stop screws into one lettered hole and does two jobs: it stops the plane so the cutters can’t hit the strip’s hold-down screw, and it gives an automatic plane stop matched to the rod section’s length.

Selection rule. The strip’s tip always anchors between bed stations #12 and #13 (as close to #13 as possible) so the anvil stays widest at its tip. Choose the mill-stop letter from the bamboo hold-down screw’s position: set the mill so the cutters just clear the hold-down screw, then mount the stop just behind it — in most cases the mill-stop letter equals the hold-down letter. Untapered rough cutting uses hole A (rightmost).

Worked example (7 ft rod). The strip is fastened in hole D (4th from the right), putting the ferrule/tiptop point at station #12 with ~3 in of strip past it; the butt taper is set from station #3 (stations #2/#1/#0 left at zero).

For one-piece rods on the extension bed, use hole B for rough/finish butt and hole A for finish tip. Short (3-piece) sections may anchor farther up the anvil for support.

Cutter Heads

Swappable heads for 8-, 6-, 5-, or 4-strip rods (6-strip is standard).

head included angle hold-down shoe angle
8-strip 46° —
6-strip 61.5° 61.5°
5-strip 73.5° 73.5°
4-strip 92° 91.5°

Morgan uses 61.5° for 6-strip (not the traditional 60°), per Winston practice, to reduce visible glue seams.

Inserts. Two carbide inserts, 3 edges each; a set planes ~3–5 rods. Cut depth ≤ 0.010 in/pass green, 0.001–0.003 in/pass heat-treated. Regular inserts are TPGW-321, 3/8 in inscribed circle, 0.015 in tip radius; since July 2011 supplied inserts are C5 carbide (harder), 15% relief, TiN-coated relief edge, diamond-lapped top. Install with tops parallel to the pocket; rotate/pair inserts to double edge life.

The Measuring Block

A caliper-mounted 6061-T6 aluminum block that reads strip height in per-geometry grooves. Calibrate with a #38 drill blank (0.100 in).

groove constant (drill height)
61+ (6-strip) 0.152 in
73+ (5-strip) 0.140 in
91+ (4-strip) 0.123 in

Add 0.100 / 0.200 in when a strip exceeds 0.100 in. Glue up ~6 measured sections to verify your own constants, since glue and pressure shift results slightly.

The Taper-Setting Model

This is the heart of the machine, and the part most often confused.

Two separate steps.

  1. Set the taper. Using the plane’s dial indicator, raise the bed at each 5-in station to the correct height above the base.
  2. Mill. Measure the strip height with calipers / the measuring block as you cut, and stop at target. The hard stop then repeats that depth for every strip.
  • The station “setting” is the cumulative rise of the bed at each station relative to a chosen reference (typically #2 = 0.000). It equals (half-dimension at reference) − (half-dimension at that station) = caneDNA’s total_increase. It is not the strip height.
  • The strip height is half the flat-to-flat rod dimension at that station (one strip). It is measured during milling, never set by the bed.
  • Reference station. Register the taper so the strip tip is near the anvil tip; for shorter rods start the taper at station #2 (or higher), not #0/#1, to avoid cutting the anvil too narrow at its tip.
  • Extend past length. Continue the taper one or more stations past the rod’s end so strips have extra length for straight gluing (Morgan likes ≥ 5–6 in extra; min 3 in on tips).

The Plane’s Dial

Calibrated dial reads 0–50 in 0.002-in steps; one revolution = 0.050 in of cut depth (clockwise lowers). Dial indicator travel is 0–1 in at 0.001 in accuracy. A dovetail slide + gib runs the plane; backlash is removed by a spring-loaded Teflon plug (never remove it). Nylon side pads (moly-impregnated) let it slide — set them 0.628–0.629 in apart with the supplied jig.

RodDNA caveat (from manual chapter J). Of RodDNA’s MHM Settings Report, use the Station #, Increment, Rod Dim, and Increase columns; disregard “Form Depth” (should be strip height) and “Settings” (wrong on some tapers). This is why caneDNA computes strip_depth + total_increase itself rather than porting RodDNA’s report. Free taper sources with Hand Mill station settings: RodDNA.com and hexrod.net (Frank Stetzer, with Chris Obuchowski).

Workflow, End to End

Split → prep / straighten nodes → drill anvil hole → rough cut (taper preset) → swap anvil → finish anvil, set taper, finish cut in many light passes.

Always mill butt → tip, and mark the butt end. Grip behind the adjusting head (never on it) with centered downward pressure; take many light passes and re-cut the first 2–3 in of each pass to full depth.

Strip Preparation

  • Buy ≥ 10 poles (ideally 20+). Reject deep cuts, big dark splotches, and node heat marks; power fibers must run the full glued-section depth.
  • Wall thickness: butt 5/16–1/2 in, tip 3/16–5/16 in.
  • Node spacing: butt 9–14 in, tip 14–20 in. Common three/three node match; avoid nodes at cut ends, ferrules, and tiptop.
  • Straighten with heat (gun 350–450 °F) and remove twist, especially the first 18 in of butts; square or slightly inward-taper the strip sides.
  • Heat-treat to light brown (raises MOE, resists set); black = brittle. Remove maximum material before treating (harder afterward); rest treated strips ≥ 1 week to regain moisture.
  • Rough sections ≥ 6 in over finish (+~2 in on the butt for the anvil screw); split ~1/8 in wide.

Milling

  • Rough on a wide roughing anvil (strip + mill stop in hole A) to a 61.5° bevel just wider than the anvil; mount the hold-down shoe once an apex forms. The stainless, spring-loaded hold-down shoe mounts in the head’s center hole and rides ahead of the cutters, so it doesn’t affect accuracy — critical for slender tips and stiff quad strips. Clean it with alcohol / dry graphite only (never oil).
  • Then switch to a finishing anvil and set the taper.
  • Measure strip height three ways: micrometer + height/width chart, thread-wrapped strips, or the aluminum measuring block (most accurate). Don’t measure the apex directly (leftover “fuzz”).
  • Finish in two stages: cut ~0.015 in oversize, then install fresh sharp cutters and finish at 0.001–0.002 in/pass. Remove apex fuzz before gluing and saw off the thick held-down butt.
  • Minimum strip width: tip 0.200 in / butt 0.250 in. Tip hold-down 2-56 (#43 drill), butt hold-down 4-40 (1/8 in), hole ~1 in from the butt.

7 ft #4 wt example (#12 ferrule): strip height 0.096 in at the ferrule (station #12), 0.033 in at the tiptop.

Accessories

accessory what it does
Hollow fluting cutter Hollows strip centers to cut weight (Stoner/Winston cross-section). Rollers 64/76/94° (64 std for 6-strip). Suggested wall 0.070 in (trout) / 0.085 in (steelhead-salmon). Leave the rod solid under ferrules with a ~2.5 in transition; hollow after finish-cutting, butt→tip. Hollowing loses stiffness — increase section area ~2–5% to compensate.
Swelled butt kit Shims to raise the finishing anvil for a swelled butt. Max swell 0.060 in per strip / 0.120 in finished — do not exceed (anvil damage). 100 shims (0.060/0.030/0.020/0.010 in) combine in 0.020-in steps; initial rise over 2.5 in.
Magic star cutter Alternate hollowing — an inverted-T with central support spokes (width 0.030–0.065 in). Square inserts remove more but leave ~80% of the triangle’s glue seam (weaker). Suggested wall 0.060–0.070 in (trout) / 0.075–0.085 in (steelhead-salmon).
Extension bed 36 in bolt-on bed for one-piece rods up to ~7 ft 6 in. The strip is cut on both finishing anvils, switching once; the tip-butt transition lands between stations #7–#8. Strip length = rod + 4 in tip + 5 in butt + 2 in hold-down (e.g., 7 ft → 95 in).
Enamel scraper 60°-groove anvils (with the dial-holder/shaver) to scrape enamel off beveled strips. The bed must have no taper when shaving.

Reference & Further Reading

No book covers the Hand Mill itself. The manual recommends:

  • Garrison & Carmichael, A Master’s Guide to Building a Bamboo Fly Rod — the amateur’s “bible”
  • Howell, The Lovely Reed
  • Maurer & Elser, Fundamentals of Building a Bamboo Fly-Rod
  • Ray Gould; and the Stoner / McLane encyclopedias

Tom Morgan runs a private owners’ list server (join by email via troutrods.com). Free taper sources with Hand Mill station settings (including quads and pentas): RodDNA.com and hexrod.net.

Source: The Morgan Hand Mill Manual (chapters A–R, rev. 2005–2013), Tom Morgan Rodsmiths. This is a factual reference re-written in my own words; the manual is copyrighted and not reproduced here.

item.title: 3D-Printed Shop Tools
item.description:
Printable jigs and shop tools for woodworking projects — the woodworking counterpart to the rodmaking tool set. This page covers the printed parts that the Adjustable Scarf Jig plan already calls for, plus table-saw accessories that fit any SawStop (they key off the standard ¾″ × ⅜″ miter slot and the flat table, not a model).

All are FDM-printable, generated parametrically, and validated watertight. STLs export in print orientation. Print in PETG, 4+ perimeters, 40% infill — the ratio gauge at 100%.

Parametric source: generate_woodworking_stls.py — edit the parameter block and re-run (pip install manifold3d trimesh numpy matplotlib). The scarf-jig parts come straight from the plan’s dimensions.

Scarf jig

Ratio setting gauge

For: setting the bed’s drop d (= 12″ ÷ ratio) without calipers.

A stepped block whose steps are exactly the drop at the 12″ mark for each ratio, tallest to shortest:

Step Ratio Height
1 1:8 1.500″ (38.1 mm)
2 1:10 1.200″ (30.5 mm)
3 1:12 1.000″ (25.4 mm)
4 1:16 0.750″ (19.1 mm)
5 1:20 0.600″ (15.2 mm)
6 1:23.3 (Rod 002 splice) 0.515″ (13.1 mm)
7 1:24 0.500″ (12.7 mm)
8 1:30 0.400″ (10.2 mm)

Stand it on the bed at the 12″ line and raise the bed until the step for your ratio just touches a straightedge across the rails. It prints on its side so the heights lie in the print plane and come out exact; check them with calipers once after your first print, and adjust the print scale if your printer is off.

ratio_gauge.stl · print 1 · no hardware

Hold-down bar and knobs

For: the plan’s ¾″ × ¾″ × 3″ hold-down across the stock’s top flat.

The bar has two clearance holes 2″ apart, matching an insert pair in the bed (¼-20 inserts, 1″ either side of center), and a shallow pocket for a cork or rubber pad. Print it with the pocket facing up, then flip it over when you fit the pad. Pair it with two fluted knobs, each with a hex pocket that captures a ¼-20 hex-head bolt.

hold_down_bar.stl · print 1 + hold_down_knob.stl · print 2 · hardware: two ¼-20 × 1¼″ hex-head bolts (length to suit your inserts), cork or rubber pad

Pegged fence

For: keeping the stock square to the hinge line without taping a fence on.

A ¼″ × ½″ strip with Ø6 mm pegs that drop into the bed’s ¼-20 inserts on the 2″ pitch, so it registers the same way every time. Print pegs up. Two two-peg segments plus one single-peg end piece cover the five pairs at 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15″ from the pin. The strip is ¼″ thick (the plan’s ⅛″ hardboard fence is thinner) because the peg needs the width; account for that when you set the stock against it.

The hold-down bar uses an insert pair across the bed, so leave that pair’s fence peg out — stop the fence before the bar.

fence_pair.stl · print 2 + fence_single.stl · print 1 · no hardware

Table saw (any SawStop)

These are model-agnostic: they use the miter slot (standard ¾″ × ⅜″, 19.05 × 9.5 mm — measure yours to confirm) or the flat table. Nothing here replaces the saw’s guard, riving knife or brake; the push devices are accessories.

Safety. Push blocks and push sticks sit between your hand and the blade. Printed PETG is not rated for that: inspect before each use, discard anything cracked or crazed, never print them in PLA, and keep a commercial push block as a backup. Print the first one and push scrap with the saw off before trusting the shape.

Push block

For: pushing stock past the blade under your hand’s full control.

A heel-and-toe block: a raised grip, a flat base for pressure on the stock, and an 8 mm heel at the back that catches the end of the workpiece so you push it rather than rubbing it. The base underside has a shallow pocket for a ⅛″ rubber pad (spray adhesive). Print it standing on its side (the profile lies flat on the bed); it is solid and fairly heavy, so use 3–4 perimeters and 20–30% infill.

push_block.stl · print 2 · hardware: ⅛″ rubber pad

Push stick

For: narrow rips, where there’s no room for a block between the blade and the fence.

A 250 mm stick with a wide handle (finger hole included), a slim shaft and a 15 mm hook at the tip that catches the back of the stock. Print it flat with the hook pointing up. The hook is only 15 mm deep, so it is for stock about ¾″ and thicker; for thin stock, use a block.

push_stick.stl · print 2 · no hardware

Featherboard (prototype)

For: holding stock against the fence on rips.

Ten fingers leaning 30° toward the feed, on a base with a friction-fit miter-slot runner. This one is a prototype and is friction-only: a plain miter slot has no undercut, so there is nothing for a printed part to lock against, and the runner’s two crush ribs give a light grip. Treat it as a hold-down for light work, not as a kickback preventer, and test-fit it in a scrap slot first — tune RUNNER_CLEAR and CRUSH_RIB in the script until it needs a firm push. If you want a positive lock, bolt the base to a commercial expanding miter bar instead. Print it upside down (runner pointing up) so the fingers stand as vertical walls and flex along their layers.

featherboard.stl · print 1 · no hardware

Setup depth blocks

For: setting blade height or dado depth without a ruler.

Eight steps, ⅛″ to 1″ in ⅛″ increments. Stand a block next to the blade, lay a straightedge across it, and raise the blade until it just touches. Print it on its side so the heights lie in the print plane, and check them with calipers once.

setup_steps.stl · print 1 · no hardware

90° / 45° blade-angle checker

For: a quick check that the blade is square to the table (and at 45°) after you tilt it.

A 100 mm right isosceles triangle, 6 mm thick. Stand a leg on the table and the other against the blade body (between the teeth). The accuracy is only as good as your printer, so check it against a known-good square before relying on it.

angle_checker.stl · print 1 · no hardware

Crosscut-sled runner

For: the miter-slot bars of a crosscut sled.

The tenoning jig uses one of these. A 240 mm segment, 18.6 mm wide (0.45 mm under the slot width) and 8.8 mm tall so it stays below the table surface, with six M5 nut pockets on a 40 mm pitch. Lay the sled base on the runners and screw down through it with M5 flat-head machine screws into the nuts. Print 4 and butt them end to end for two 480 mm runners. A runner this tight is a clearance fit, so tune it with masking tape or thin shims until it slides without side play, and keep the sled’s runners parallel to each other.

sled_runner.stl · print 4 · hardware: 6 M5 nuts and M5 × 25 flat-head screws per segment

Tenoning jig

These print the parts of the Miter-Slot Tenoning Jig; the wood and the clamp are on that page. It also uses one sled runner.

Tenon shim set

For: setting the tenon thickness: s = A − (t + T) ÷ 2, stacked between the fence and the stock.

Five plates — 1/16″, 1/8″, 1/4″, 1/2″ and 1/2″ — laid out on one bed (226 × 222 mm), so any 1/16″ step from 0 to 1-7/16″ is reachable. Print them flat; the thickness is set by layer count, so check each plate with calipers and adjust the print scale or layer height until they match. Each has a pull hole. Print two sets: one for the foot of the fence and one near the clamp.

tenon_shims.stl · print 2 · no hardware

Fence bracket

For: holding the fence square to the base.

A right-angle bracket with a web and two screw holes per flange (Ø4.6 mm, for #8 screws). Screw it into the base and the back of the fence, one at each end. Print it on the base flange.

jig_bracket.stl · print 2 · hardware: four #8 × 1″ wood screws each

Jig handle

For: pushing the jig past the blade.

A flange with two screw holes, a 28 mm post and a rounded top. Screw it to the base behind the fence.

jig_handle.stl · print 1 · hardware: two #8 wood screws

Not yet designed

The plans also call for these printed parts; none of them has an STL yet:

  • Scarf jig: the end-alignment gauge and the beam handles.
  • Table saw: a flip-stop and a sled stop block; a positively locking featherboard.

item.title: Logging Roasts to This Site
item.description:
How to export a roast from Artisan and add it as a page on this site.

Roast Phase Buttons

Artisan’s toolbar has one button per roast phase — press each the instant it happens. Use the trier (the little sampling scoop on the roaster) to judge color for Dry End, and listen for the cracks:

Button Press it when…
CHARGE Beans go into the roaster. This is the zero point everything else is measured from — no CHARGE, no ∆BT curve.
DRY END The beans finish drying and start browning (Maillard) — pull a sample with the trier and watch the color shift from green to tan/yellow.
FC START First crack audibly begins — a popcorn-like popping.
FC END First crack’s popping tapers off.
SC START Second crack begins, if roasting past first crack — a faster, higher-pitched crackle than first crack.
SC END Second crack’s crackling tapers off.
DROP Beans come out of the roaster into the cooling tray.

Turning Point isn’t a button. Artisan auto-detects it as the lowest bean-temp reading shortly after Charge — the moment the cold beans stop dragging the temperature down and it starts climbing. That makes it the one phase mark that can go wrong even when you press every button correctly: if the probe glitches right after Charge, like on the first roast logged here, the auto-detected TP is meaningless even though every button-marked event on the same roast is fine.

What to Capture Per Roast

Enter bean and weight data straight into Artisan’s own Roast Properties dialog (Roast menu, or click the roast title above the graph) as you go — it’s saved into the .alog file automatically, so there’s nothing to transcribe later:

  • Roast tab: Beans (origin, variety, processing — e.g. “Ethiopia Yirgacheffe, washed”), Green Weight, Roasted Weight (Artisan computes weight loss % from these two)
  • Title: batch identifier, shown on the graph itself
  • Notes tab: roasting notes during the session, cupping notes once it’s rested

Charge, turning point, first crack, and drop don’t need writing down either — mark each one live with Artisan’s phase buttons/hotkeys as it happens, and the exact time and temp land on the graph and in the saved profile on their own.

Exporting from Artisan

Roast Curve Image

After the roast completes (or during):

  1. File > Save Graph — saves the roast curve as a .png (also offers PDF and social-media-sized exports).

For a clean export, use View > Full Screen first so the graph fills the window before saving.

Roast Data (Artisan .alog)

  1. File > Save As — saves the full roast as an Artisan .alog file (JSON format), including every temperature sample, event marker, and the Roast Properties entered above.

Keep this file alongside the page as a data archive even if you don’t embed it in the site — it’s the only copy of the raw curve data, and it’s what ArtisanViewer or a future Artisan version would need to re-open the roast.

Optional: Artisan’s Autosave feature (Config > Autosave) can write both the .alog and a rendered image/PDF automatically at the end of every roast, using a filename template built from the roast date and bean name — worth setting up once instead of doing the File > Save Graph / File > Save As dance by hand every time.

Where to Store Files 

static/static/coffee-roasting/
└── YYYY-MM-DD-bean-name/
├── roast-curve.png ← exported graph image
└── roast.alog ← Artisan data file (optional, for archiving)

Example:

static/static/coffee-roasting/2025-01-15-ethiopia-yirgacheffe/roast-curve.png

The file will be served at:

/static/coffee-roasting/2025-01-15-ethiopia-yirgacheffe/roast-curve.png

Creating a Roast Page

Each roast gets its own Markdown file under content/docs/coffee-roasting/.

hugo new docs/coffee-roasting/2025-01-15-ethiopia-yirgacheffe.md

Page Template 

---
title: "2025-01-15 Ethiopia Yirgacheffe"
date: 2025-01-15
weight: 200
---

**Bean**: Ethiopia Yirgacheffe, washed
**Source**: [Roaster name]
**Green weight**: 250g | **Roast out**: 210g (16% loss)

## Roast

| | Temp | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Charge | 195°C | 0:00 |
| Turning point | 92°C | 1:45 |
| First crack | 196°C | 9:30 |
| Drop | 207°C | 11:00 |

![Roast curve](/static/coffee-roasting/2025-01-15-ethiopia-yirgacheffe/roast-curve.png)

## Notes

Notes on the roast — airflow adjustments, gas changes, anything that
went well or needs adjustment next time.

## Cup

Tasting notes after resting 5–7 days.

Keeping Pages Ordered

Use weight in front matter to control sidebar order. Lower numbers appear first. A convention that works well:

  • Section _index.md: weight: 100
  • Individual roast pages: use the date as a weight, e.g. weight: 20250115 for 2025-01-15

This keeps roasts sorted chronologically from oldest (top) to newest (bottom). Reverse it by assigning descending weights.

Publishing

Add the new page and static files, then push to main — CI deploys automatically.

git add content/docs/coffee-roasting/ static/static/coffee-roasting/
git commit -m "roast: 2025-01-15 Ethiopia Yirgacheffe"
git push

item.title: Modern Craftsman 2-Drawer Console (Proposed)
item.description:
A proposed build — a copy of the Vermont Woods Studios / Vermont Furniture Designs Modern Craftsman 2-Drawer Console Table (product page, archive), with the proportions held to the maker’s published numbers. A long, low console: a wide, thin top that overhangs the leg frame by a lot at the ends, two shallow drawers hung right under the top, and a narrow lower shelf carried on chunky side rails.

Provenance of the numbers. Dimensions marked (stated) come straight from the maker’s Dimensions and Construction Details panels. Dimensions marked (derived) are worked out from the stated ones so everything closes. Dimensions marked (est.) are measured off the maker’s front and three-quarter photos — good to roughly ±¼″ — and are the ones to sanity-check against the real piece, or against your own taste, before cutting.

Stated by the maker

Item Value
Overall 60″ W × 16″ D × 29″ H (stated)
Top overhang, ends 8″ (stated)
Top overhang, front/back 1″ (stated)
Drawer front (exterior) 19.75″ W × 3.5″ H (stated)
Drawer interior 18″ W × 7.5″ D × 2″ H (stated)
Bottom shelf 41.5″ W × 9.75″ D (stated)
Species Cherry, maple or walnut (stated)
Drawers Dovetailed; beech sides, back and bottom; metal slides; walnut pulls (stated)
Finish Cherry/walnut: hand-rubbed linseed oil + wax. Maple: tung oil + wax (stated)

Drawings (true scale)

All five are generated from the dimensions on this page and drawn true to scale. The elevations and plan are at 1″ = 12 px, so they can be measured against each other; the drawer-bay detail and leg layout are drawn larger (scale on each). Click to open full size.

Front elevation

Side elevation

Plan view, top removed

Drawer bay and drawer box

Leg layout

The ratios

Everything hangs off the 60″ overall width and the 8″ / 1″ overhangs. The frame is whatever is left:

Derived Working Result
Leg frame, width 60 − 2 × 8 44″ (derived)
Leg frame, depth 16 − 2 × 1 14″ (derived)
Frame opening between front legs 44 − 2 × 1¾ 40½″ (derived)
Two drawer fronts + divider + reveals 2 × 19.75 + ¾ + 4 × 1/16 40½″ (derived — fills the opening exactly)
Shelf width 44 − 2 × 1¼ (side-rail thickness) 41½″ (derived — matches stated shelf width)
Shoulder-to-shoulder, front↔back 14 − 2 × 1¾ 10½″ (derived; shelf is 9¾″, leaving ¾″)

That the two independent checks (drawers fill 40½″; shelf lands on 41½″ with 1¼″ rails) both close is the evidence that the 1¾″ legs and 1¼″-thick side rails are right.

Proportion Value
Width : height 60 : 29 ≈ 2.07 : 1
Width : depth 60 : 16 = 3.75 : 1
Frame width ÷ overall width 44 ÷ 60 ≈ 0.733 (each end overhang = 13.3 %)
Drawer front width ÷ overall width 19.75 ÷ 60 ≈ 0.33
Drawer front height ÷ overall height 3.5 ÷ 29 ≈ 0.12
Leg width ÷ overall height 1¾ ÷ 29 ≈ 0.06
Shelf top height ÷ overall height ≈ 10½ ÷ 29 ≈ 0.36 (est.)

To resize: multiply every dimension by one factor k (so 48″ long → k = 0.8) and the proportions hold. Round leg and rail sections to stock, but do not change the 8″-end / 1″-front overhang ratio independently of the width — the long ends are the look.

Dimensions that are estimates

Item Value Basis
Top thickness ¾″ (est.) ≈ 14 px against a 3.5″ drawer front at ≈ 66 px in the front photo. Could be 1″; ¾″ keeps the 8″ cantilever light
Leg section 1¾″ square (est.) ≈ 1.85″ measured, and 1¾″ is what makes both closures above work
Shelf top above floor ≈ 10½″ (est.) Front photo, scaled against the 29″ height
Lower drawer rail ¾″ thick × 1″ tall (est.) Thin strip under the drawers in the front photo
Center divider ¾″ wide (est.) Narrow stile between the drawers
Side aprons 4½″ tall (est.) Solid panel under the top at the ends in the three-quarter photo
Pull 8″ × ⅝″ × 1″ (est.), walnut ≈ 8″ long against the 19.75″ drawer front; stand-off finger pull

Cut list

T × W × L, cut to length — 1″ tenons are baked into rail and apron lengths. Species: cherry (or maple/walnut) for the case; beech (or maple) for drawer boxes.

Case

Part Qty T × W × L Notes
Legs 4 1¾″ × 1¾″ × 28¼″ 8/4 stock. Height = 29 − ¾ top
Lower front rail 1 ¾″ × 1″ × 42½″ Under the drawers; 40½″ between shoulders; 1″ tenons
Back apron 1 ¾″ × 4½″ × 42½″ 1″ tenons
Side aprons 2 ¾″ × 4½″ × 12½″ 10½″ between shoulders; 1″ tenons
Center divider 1 ¾″ × ¾″ × 3⅝″ Underside of top to lower front rail; pinned to the front of the center runner
Center runner 1 ¾″ × 3″ × 12½″ Lower front rail to back apron, centered; slides mount on both faces. Housed in both
Slide spacers 2 1″ × 3″ × 9″ Screwed to the inside of the side aprons so the slide face sits at the drawer-box edge
Shelf side rails 2 1¼″ × 2½″ × 12½″ Flush to leg outer faces; 10½″ between shoulders; top ≈ 11″ off floor
Shelf cleats 2 ¾″ × ¾″ × 9¾″ Glue/screw to rail inner faces to carry the shelf
Shelf 1 ¾″ × 9¾″ × 41½″ Sits between the side rails, centered front-to-back (⅜″ setback each side)
Top 1 ¾″ × 16″ × 60″ Floats; buttons or figure-8s, never glued

As listed, the spacers and runner put the slide faces 19⅞″ apart in each bay, which leaves 7/16″ per side beside the 19″ drawer box — 1/16″ per side less than the ½″ most side-mount slides need (see Open questions). Adjust them to the clearance of the slides you buy.

Drawers (×2, identical)

Part Qty each T × W × L Notes
Front 1 ¾″ × 3½″ × 19¾″ Cherry, grain-matched to the case; 1/16″ reveals all round
Sides 2 ½″ × 2½″ × 8½″ Beech; dovetailed to front and back
Back 1 ½″ × 2½″ × 18″ (between sides) Beech
Bottom 1 ¼″ × as fitted Beech; in a groove, floating
Pull 1 8″ × ⅝″ × 1″ Walnut; two screws from the inside

The stated 18″ × 7½″ × 2″ interior sets the drawer box: 18″ clear between ½″ sides gives a box 19″ wide overall, which leaves 7/16″ per side in the 19⅞″ bay — not quite the ½″ per side that standard slides need (see Open questions). The 7½″ box depth sits in a 14″ frame, so there is room behind the drawers — decide whether to close it with a back panel (the maker uses plywood backs on case pieces) or leave it open.

Build sequence

  1. Mill legs from 8/4 and everything else to size; let stock sit between passes — cherry moves.
  2. Cut mortises and tenons (5/16″–⅜″ mortises, 1″ deep). Miter tenon tips where two meet inside a leg.
  3. Dry-fit the two end frames: leg pair + side apron + shelf side rail. Confirm the 10½″ shoulder distance and that the rail sits flush to the leg outer face.
  4. Glue up the ends, then join them with the front and back aprons and the lower front rail. Dry-clamp first and check the 40½″ opening and the 44″ × 14″ frame for square. Drawbore if you like — optional here, since the top and drawers add little racking load.
  5. Fit the center runner and divider and check the two drawer openings are equal (≈ 19⅞″ each with 1/16″ reveals).
  6. Screw on the slide spacers, add the shelf cleats and drop in the shelf. The shelf carries load, so keep the cleats glued and screwed.
  7. Build and dovetail the drawers, fit the slides, then trim the fronts to a 1/16″ reveal.
  8. Make the walnut pulls and fit them.
  9. Finish: hand-rubbed linseed oil and wax for cherry and walnut (tung oil and wax for maple), matching the maker. Scrape off all squeeze-out first.
  10. Attach the top with buttons so it can move seasonally. Center it: 8″ at each end, 1″ front and back.

Domino option

A Festool Domino can cut most of the joints instead of hand-cut tenons. The 5/16″ mortise in this plan matches an 8 mm Domino; a 40 mm Domino goes 20 mm (¾″) into each part, a 50 mm Domino 25 mm (1″).

Rule at a leg corner: two mortises entering from adjacent faces cross inside the leg, so no two Domino mortises in a leg may be at the same height — stagger them. (The hand-cut plan avoids this by mitering tenon tips, which a loose tenon can’t do.)

Joint Domino Cut length (was)
Back apron (¾″ × 4½″) 1 × 8×40 per end, centred 25 mm below the apron’s top edge 40½″ (42½″)
Side aprons (×2) 1 × 8×40 per end, centred 70 mm below the apron’s top edge 10½″ (12½″)
Lower front rail (¾″ × 1″) 1 × 4×20 per end, centred on the rail 40½″ (42½″)
Shelf side rails (×2, 1¼″ × 2½″) 1 × 8×50 per end, centred 10½″ (12½″)
Center runner Keep it housed in the lower front rail and back apron 12½″ (unchanged)
  • With the Domino, cut length = shoulder-to-shoulder (40½″ and 10½″).
  • At the back legs the back apron (upper) and side apron (lower) are staggered. At the front legs the side apron (lower-middle of its 4½″) stays clear of the lower front rail’s 4×20.
  • The 1″ lower front rail is the weak spot — a 4×20 is the largest Domino that fits. It is lightly loaded and the center runner and divider support it, but if you want more, use a shop-made stub tenon.
  • Keep the aprons flush to the leg outer faces and centre each mortise on the part’s thickness.

Open questions

  • Top thickness — ¾″ is estimated; if the real piece reads chunkier, 1″ is the likely answer. Re-check drawer front height (3.5″) against it.
  • Shelf height — about 10½″ to the shelf top is estimated from photos.
  • Frame joinery — the maker’s page does not say how the legs and rails are joined, so mortise-and-tenon here is my choice, to match the other console plan on this site.
  • Space behind the drawers — see the note above.
  • Slide clearance — the stated 18″ interior with ½″ sides makes a 19″ box, but each bay is 19⅞″ between slide faces: 7/16″ per side, where ½″ slides need ½″. To fit them, either plane the drawer sides to 7/16″ (box 18⅞″, keeps the stated interior), take 1/16″ off each spacer and make the runner ⅝″ (bays 20″), or keep ½″ sides on a 17⅞″ interior.

item.title: Adjustable Scarf Jig (Proposed)
item.description:
A proposed shop jig for cutting long, accurate scarf bevels in strip stock: the 4½" splice on Rod 002’s bamboo sections, and also scarfed trim, bow and paddle laminations, and anything else that needs a feathered lap joint. It’s a permanent tool, not a one-off. One knob sets any ratio from 1:8 to 1:40, and the setting doesn’t depend on the stock’s thickness.

How it works. Two hard-maple rails form a flat reference plane. A sanding beam rides on them and can’t cut below that plane. Between the rails is a tilting bed hinged so that its top surface pivots on the rail plane. Clamp the stock with its end on the hinge line and drop the far end of the bed. The stock then rises above the rails by exactly the wedge you want removed. Sand until the beam rides the rails, and the bevel feathers out precisely at the end of the stock. The only setting is the ratio: the bed’s drop at the 12″ mark is d = 12″ ÷ ratio, for any thickness of stock.

Drawings

All dimensions are in inches. The X axis runs along the jig, Y across it, and Z up.

Holding the work

A C-clamp won’t work on the bed itself. The bed sits recessed in a 3″ channel between 3″-tall rails, with the base underneath, so a clamp’s lower jaw has nowhere to go. Anything sticking up above the rail plane inside the scarf would also be hit by the beam. The hold comes in three layers instead:

  1. Double-sided tape under the scarf zone (the primary hold). Use thin cloth carpet tape or turner’s tape, along the whole scarf and a few inches past it. It’s the only thing that can hold the feather, the last thin inch that no clamp can reach. On bamboo, press the section down hard for a minute. Release it afterward with a putty knife and a little naphtha.
  2. The hold-down bar goes across the stock’s top flat, knobbed into the nearest insert pair past the beam’s travel. It resists the pull of each stroke. For a scarf of length L, use the first pair beyond L + 3″, and use a short beam (6″ long) on short scarfs so it stops short of the bar. For the 4½″ bamboo splice, that’s the 9″ pair. Pad the bar so it doesn’t mark the enamel side.
  3. The outboard end gets the C-clamp. A rod section is 39″ long and leaves the jig sloping gently downhill (2.5° at 1:23). Support it on a block or roller stand at that height, and C-clamp it there. That’s where a C-clamp is useful: it keeps the long lever arm from rocking the stock on the bed.

Sand with light strokes toward the feather. That pulls the stock toward the hinge, against the tape and the bar, and keeps bamboo fibers from lifting at the thin end.

Settings

Drop d is measured at the 12″ setting mark, from a straightedge laid across the rails down to the bed’s top. Use a depth gauge or the depth rod of your calipers.

Ratio d at 12″ mark Bed angle Max stock thickness (L ≤ 15″)
1:8 1.500″ 7.1° 1.88″
1:10 1.200″ 5.7° 1.50″
1:12 1.000″ 4.8° 1.25″
1:16 0.750″ 3.6° 0.94″
1:20 0.600″ 2.9° 0.75″
1:23.3 (Rod 002 splice) 0.515″ 2.5° 0.64″
1:24 0.500″ 2.4° 0.62″
1:30 0.400″ 1.9° 0.50″
  • Any other ratio: d = 12 ÷ r. For a scarf of length L on stock of thickness t, r = L ÷ t.
  • Capacity: stock up to 2-3/4″ wide. Scarf length L up to 15″, so the maximum thickness is 15 ÷ r.
  • Ratio range: at 1:8 the bed’s far end still clears the base by 0.27″, which sets the steep limit (~1:7.5). Shallow ratios are only limited by how small a d you can measure.

Parts

Part Qty Material Size (T × W × L) Notes
Base 1 ¾″ Baltic birch ¾ × 4-1/2 × 24 Flat; check it on the table saw
Rails 2 Hard maple, quartersawn ¾ × 3 × 24 Glued and screwed to the base edges. Their tops are the reference plane
Bed 1 Hard maple, quartersawn ¾ × 2-15/16 × 16-3/8 16″ from the pin to the far end, plus a 3/8″ nose behind the pin, rounded to a 3/8″ radius about it
Feet 2 Hardwood 1 × 1-1/2 × 4-1/2 Under each end; clearance for the lift knob
Hinge pin 1 ¼″ drill rod (or ¼″ shoulder bolt) Ø¼ × 4-1/2 Through rail, bed, rail at X = 5″, 2-5/8″ above the base’s top. Press fit in the rails, turning fit in the bed
Lift screw 1 ¼″-20 knurled thumb screw, 3-1/2″ — Up through a T-nut in the base at X = 17″, with a jam nut. At d = 0 it stands 2-1/4″ above the base
T-nut 1 ¼″-20 — Base, underside
Bearing pad 1 ½″ brass washer — Epoxied under the bed where the screw tip bears
Threaded inserts 10 ¼″-20 — Five pairs in the bed, at 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15″ from the pin and 1″ either side of center, for the hold-down
Hold-down bar 1 Hard maple (or 3D-printed) ¾ × ¾ × 3 Two ¼″-20 knobs, and a cork or rubber pad on its underside. Sits past the beam’s travel
Fence strip 1 ⅛″ hardboard ⅛ × ½ × 15 Double-sided tape along one edge of the bed; keeps the stock square
Sanding beam 1 ¾″ MDF (or ¼″ aluminum plate on MDF) ¾ × 6 × 10 Wider than the jig, with a handle on top and PSA paper (80 / 120 / 220) underneath
Screws 10 #8 × 1-1/4″ — Rails to base, from underneath

3D-printed parts

A 3D printer makes several of the fiddly parts easier, and repeatable. Print them in PETG, which is tougher than PLA and doesn’t creep under a clamp, at 4+ perimeters and 40% infill.

Part Why print it
Ratio setting gauges A stepped block whose steps are the drop d for 1:8, 1:12, 1:16, 1:20, 1:23.3 and 1:24. Set it on the bed at the 12″ line and raise the bed until the step for your ratio touches a straightedge across the rails. No calipers needed, and the setting repeats. Print it on its side so the steps are accurate, and check them with calipers once.
Hold-down clamps Low-profile cam clamps or bars with a TPU pad, sized to sit under the beam’s path where they can. For narrow stock, a bar with a shallow relief so it presses on the center of the top flat.
Fence strip A thin printed fence with tabs that key into the insert holes, so it registers square to the hinge line every time instead of being taped on.
End-alignment gauge A small block that rests on both rails and drops a lip exactly to the hinge line. Push the stock’s end against the lip, then lift the gauge away. It’s faster and more accurate than sighting with a square.
Beam handles A comfortable handle (and a short-beam version) bolted to the MDF or aluminum beam.

STLs and the parametric source for the ratio gauge, hold-down bar and knobs, and pegged fence are on the 3D-Printed Shop Tools page.

The rails, bed and base should stay wood: their flatness and stiffness are the whole tool. Printed parts only hold, locate and set.

Build

  1. Mill the rails and bed from the same quartersawn board. Plane them to final thickness together so they move together.
  2. Glue and screw the rails to the base’s long edges, with their outside faces flush. Put the screws in from underneath so nothing is near the rail tops. Add the feet.
  3. Drill the hinge together. Shim the bed so its top is flush with the rail tops, and clamp everything. Then drill one ¼″ hole straight through rail, bed, and rail at X = 5″, 3/8″ below the top. That’s 2-5/8″ above the base’s top. Drilling it in one pass is what keeps the bed’s top surface pivoting on the rail plane.
    • The pin goes through the bed. The hole is centered in the bed’s ¾″ thickness, with ¼″ of wood above and below the pin. Leave 3/8″ of bed behind the hole and round that nose to a 3/8″ radius about it. Because the nose is centered on the pin, its highest point stays at the rail plane at every tilt, so it never sticks up into the beam’s path.
    • Fits: the pin is a press fit in the rails. Open the bed’s hole just enough for the bed to turn without play, with a ¼″ reamer or 320 grit wrapped on a dowel. A sloppy 17/64″ hole would let the feather point wander.
  4. Flatten the reference plane. With the bed shimmed flush and clamped, sand the rail tops and the bed top together on a flat surface, such as PSA paper on a jointer bed, a cast-iron wing, or glass. They must be one continuous plane. Check with a straightedge: the bed flush to the rails within 0.002″ is d = 0.
  5. Lift screw: install the T-nut under the base at X = 17″. Epoxy the brass pad under the bed at that spot, and thread in the thumb screw and jam nut.
  6. Marks: scribe the hinge line (X = 5″) and the 12″ setting line (X = 17″) across both rail tops, and ink them.
  7. Hold-down: install the two inserts in the bed, and make the bar and the fence strip.
  8. Sanding beam: flatten the MDF, stick on the PSA paper, and add a handle. Wax the rail tops so the beam glides.

Using it

  1. Zero: with d = 0, a straightedge should lie flat across rails and bed.
  2. Set the ratio: turn the lift screw until d at the 12″ line matches the settings table, then lock the jam nut.
  3. Load the stock: lay it on the bed against the fence, with its end exactly on the hinge line. Sight down the scribed line with a square, then hold it as described in Holding the work.
  4. Sand: take long, light strokes along the jig, starting with 80 grit. Keep the beam flat on both rails. You’re done when the beam rides the rails along the whole scarf and the end has feathered to nothing. Finish with 120 and then 220.
  5. The mating piece gets the same setting and the same procedure. Joined face to face, the two bevels restore the full section.

Accuracy. The pin sits 3/8″ below the bed’s top surface, so the pivot line moves very slightly as the bed tilts. At 1:8 the feather point shifts 0.05″ along the stock and drops 0.003″; at 1:23 it’s about a third of that. That’s well inside the material you trim off the feathered tip anyway.

Rod 002 splice, worked example

  • Joint: 4½″ scarf at the 39″ joint, where the hex measures 0.193″ across the flats.
  • Ratio: r = 4.5 ÷ 0.193 = 1:23.3, so d = 12 ÷ 23.3 = 0.515″.
  • Tip section: lay it flat-side down on the bed with its end on the hinge line. A hex rests stably on a flat, so the bevel runs across the flats. Tape it and hold it down at the far end, then sand with light strokes. Bamboo fibers want to lift at the feather: finish with 220 and keep strokes going toward the feather.
  • Butt section: same setting, same procedure.
  • Mate them: rotate one section 180° about its axis so the bevels face each other. Line up the guide flats, whip the feather ends, and tape the joint, as described on the Rod 002 page.

Variations

  • Router sled for thick stock. A 6″ × 12″ sled spanning the rails can carry a trim router with a flat-bottom bit set flush with the sled’s underside. Run it back and forth along the rails. It’s faster than sanding on 1″+ hardwood. Take conventional (not climb) passes, and use a full hold-down.
  • Longer scarfs: lengthen the rails and bed together. Keep the 12″ setting mark, and capacity grows with the bed.
  • Metric: scribe a second mark 300 mm from the hinge; d = 300 mm ÷ r there.

item.title: Miter-Slot Tenoning Jig (Proposed)
item.description:
A proposed shop jig for cutting the cheeks of tenons on the table saw: the stock stands on its end against a vertical fence, the jig rides in a miter slot, and one pass per face cuts each cheek. Plywood base and fence, a printed runner, shim set and brackets, and a plain C-clamp. It uses only the standard ¾″ × ⅜″ miter slot, so it fits any SawStop (measure your slot to confirm).

How it works. The blade’s distance from the fence is fixed once the jig is set up. Call the distance from the fence face to the blade’s near plane A (1¼″ here). Stack shims between the fence and the stock to move the stock toward the blade. The blade’s near plane then lands at (t + T) ÷ 2 from the stock face, where t is the stock thickness and T is the tenon thickness. Cut, turn the stock end for end, cut again, and the tenon is centered. The only setting is the shim stack: s = A − (t + T) ÷ 2.

This jig cuts the cheeks only. The shoulders are cut afterward on a crosscut sled or miter gauge with a stop, which also frees the waste.

Safety. The stock stands on end with its top well above the blade, so always clamp it — never hold it by hand — and stand to the side of the blade’s plane. Check that the guard or riving knife you are using clears the stock; the cheek kerf is only as deep as the tenon is long, so the riving knife usually runs in the kerf. Run a scrap through with the saw off first.

Drawings

All dimensions in inches. Slot-to-blade distance depends on the saw, so the drawing shows a typical layout; the runner is slotted in the base so you set A once for your saw.

End view looking along the feed

Plan view

Cut sequence (detail)

Shim table (A = 1¼″)

The shim set is 1/16″, 1/8″, 1/4″, 1/2″ and 1/2″, so every 1/16″ step from 0 to 1-7/16″ is reachable. The stock stands between the fence and the blade, and s is the stack between fence and stock.

Stock t Tenon T s = A − (t + T)/2 Shims
¾″ ¼″ ¾″ ¼ + ½
¾″ ⅜″ 11/16″ 1/16 + ⅛ + ½
¾″ ½″ ⅝″ ⅛ + ½
¾″ ⅝″ 9/16″ 1/16 + ½
1″ ¼″ ⅝″ ⅛ + ½
1″ ⅜″ 9/16″ 1/16 + ½
1″ ½″ ½″ ½
1″ ⅝″ 7/16″ 1/16 + ⅛ + ¼
1½″ ¼″ ⅜″ ⅛ + ¼
1½″ ⅜″ 5/16″ 1/16 + ¼
1½″ ½″ ¼″ ¼
1½″ ⅝″ 3/16″ 1/16 + ⅛

For any other size, s = A − (t + T) ÷ 2, in 1/16″ steps; T = 2 (A − s) − t. If s comes out negative, the stock is too thick for this A — widen A by moving the base (see “Setting A”).

Parts

Wood and hardware

T × W × L.

Part Qty Material Size Notes
Base 1 ¾″ Baltic birch ¾ × 7 × 16 Three cross slots, 7/32″ wide × 1⅜″ long, 80 mm (3.15″) apart, centered on the base, over the runner’s nut pockets 1, 3 and 5 (40 mm pitch)
Fence 1 ¾″ Baltic birch ¾ × 10 × 16 Glued and screwed to the base’s long edge, standing on it; its face, square to the base, is the reference
Runner 1 Printed 18.6 × 8.8 × 240 mm The crosscut-sled runner from the printed-tools page; nuts in the pockets
Brackets 2 Printed One at each end, on the back of the fence (see below)
Handle 1 Printed Screwed to the base behind the fence
Shims 2 sets Printed One set near the foot of the fence, one near the clamp, so the stock stays parallel
Runner screws 3 M5 × 25 flat-head Down through the base slots into the nuts in the runner
Bracket screws 8 #8 × 1″ wood screws 4 per bracket
Clamp 1 4–6″ C-clamp Fence back to stock face, above the blade

Printed parts

STLs and the parametric source are on the 3D-Printed Shop Tools page: the tenon shim set, the fence brackets, the handle and the sled runner.

Build

  1. Cut the base and fence to size from the same sheet. Cut the three cross slots in the base.
  2. Glue and screw the fence to the base’s long edge, with its face flush to the base edge. Square it to the base with a machinist’s square before the glue sets.
  3. Add the brackets on the back of the fence, one near each end, screwed into both the fence and the base. They hold the fence square under load.
  4. Fit the runner under the base: lay it in the miter slot, set the base on top, and run the M5 screws down through the base slots into the nuts. Leave them just snug.

Setting A (once per saw)

  1. Set the blade’s height to about 1½″ and the jig in the slot with no shims.
  2. Slide the base across (the runner slots allow ±⅜″) until the blade’s near plane is 1¼″ from the fence face. Measure with calipers from the fence face to the near side of the blade.
  3. Tighten the screws. Make a test cut in scrap with a known shim stack, and measure the tenon. Nudge the base if the tenon is off, and note the final A.

Using it

  1. Set the blade height to the tenon length. Use the setup depth blocks to check.
  2. Stack the shims for your stock and tenon sizes (table above) at the foot of the fence and again near the clamp.
  3. Stand the stock on its end against the shims, with the face you want against them. Clamp it with the C-clamp, fence back to stock face, above the blade.
  4. Push the jig past the blade. The kerf is the first cheek.
  5. Turn the stock end for end (180° about its length) so the opposite face is against the shims, clamp, and cut the second cheek. Both cheeks sit the same distance from their faces.
  6. Cut the shoulders on a crosscut sled or miter gauge with a stop block, freeing the waste.
  7. Test the fit in the mortise and adjust the shims by 1/16″ if needed.

Open questions

  • Slot-to-blade distance on your saw determines whether the jig’s base fits left of the blade with A = 1¼″. If your slot is closer, shorten the base; if it is far, the base can be wider.
  • Guard clearance. A crown guard may interfere with tall stock; remove it only if you have a safe alternative.
  • Stock width. The clamp and fence are set for stock up to about 5″ wide; wider stock needs a taller fence.

item.title: Dog Chews: Banana and Oat
item.description:
Soft, chewy, four-ingredient dog treats made from ripe banana, oats, and an egg. They are a good counterpart to the crunchy pumpkin biscuits: no nut butter, no rolling out, and they mix in a single bowl. Makes about 2 dozen treats.

Check before you start. Use plain rolled oats (not instant packets with sugar or flavoring) and nothing else added. If you add a spoonful of peanut butter, make sure it is xylitol-free.

Ingredients

Amount Ingredient
2 very ripe bananas (about 1 cup mashed)
1 large egg
2 cups old-fashioned rolled oats
½ cup oat flour (or whole wheat flour), plus a little extra if needed
1 tsp ground cinnamon (optional)

Equipment

  • Large bowl and a fork or potato masher
  • Spoon or cookie scoop
  • Parchment-lined baking sheet

Method

  1. Heat the oven to 350°F and line a baking sheet with parchment.
  2. Mash the bananas in the bowl until smooth. Stir in the egg and cinnamon.
  3. Stir in the oats and oat flour until the mixture is thick and sticky and holds together. If it is too wet to scoop, add oat flour a tablespoon at a time.
  4. Scoop tablespoon-size mounds onto the sheet and press each flat to about ½ inch thick. They won’t spread much.
  5. Bake 15–18 minutes, until firm and lightly golden on the edges.
  6. Cool on the sheet for a few minutes, then move to a rack. They stay soft in the middle; for a firmer chew, leave them in the turned-off oven for 20 minutes.

Storage

These are moist, so they keep less well than dry biscuits:

  • Refrigerator, airtight, up to 1 week.
  • Freezer, up to 3 months. Freeze them flat on a tray, then bag them; they thaw in a few minutes.

Notes

  • Bananas are high in natural sugar, so keep these to a treat or two a day, and fewer for small dogs.
  • Treats should stay under roughly 10% of a dog’s daily calories.
  • If your dog has a grain or egg sensitivity, or you aren’t sure these ingredients are right for them, check with your vet.
  • Skip raisins, chocolate, onion, garlic, and xylitol in any variation of this recipe; all are harmful to dogs.

item.title: Barrel Sauna Roof and Porch Plan
item.description:
Plan for an Almost Heaven four-person cedar barrel sauna with an electric heater. Goals: stop rain drips through knots and seams, add insulation for cold-weather heating, and add a covered spot to change at the door.

Note: This is general building guidance gathered from Almost Heaven’s own roof suggestions, product listings, and common practice. It is not from the Almost Heaven manual, so confirm key details with Almost Heaven or a sauna builder before committing. Product and spec claims were checked against public listings on 2026-11-04 (see Verification notes); anything still unconfirmed is marked unverified.

Quick expectations

  • Cedar swells when wet, so small drips through knots and seams are common. A roof greatly reduces them but may not eliminate them. Almost Heaven itself says some seepage is normal.
  • Do not caulk or foam the tongue-and-groove joints. The wood moves with heat and moisture, and rigid fill will crack or split boards.
  • Keep some airflow at the roof edges so moisture can escape. Trapped moisture causes mold and rot.
  • In 30°F weather, expect a longer preheat, often 60 to 90 minutes (a rule of thumb, not a measurement). A roof with insulation helps more than sealing gaps, though the ends, door and floor still lose heat.
  • Heater: 4-person Almost Heaven barrels are commonly listed with a 6 kW Harvia (some Watoga listings show 4.5 kW; the larger Essex lists 8 kW on a 240 V, 40 A hard-wired circuit). Check the label on your own heater and put it on a dedicated circuit; have an electrician confirm the wiring.

The plan in pictures

The three diagrams below cover the whole job. Layer thicknesses are exaggerated, and the barrel dimensions are placeholders until you measure yours.

Roof options from Almost Heaven’s guidance

  1. Removable canvas rain jacket. Easiest, clips on with bungees, can stay on while the sauna is running, and Almost Heaven sells one (listings show roughly $245 to $280). It is a cover and not insulation. Cheap, reversible first step.
  2. Corrugated metal roof screwed on with short (about 3/4 inch) sheet metal screws. Their staves are 1-3/8 inch thick, so short screws are safe going straight into the staves.
  3. Roofing shingles over underlayment, covering as much of the top as you like.
  4. A full shelter or structure with a roof.

Recommended build: insulated roof over the barrel

From the inside out:

  1. Barrel staves (existing cedar, 1-3/8 inch).
  2. Insulation strips. Rockwool Comfortboard 80, 1.5 inch (R-4.2 per inch, so about R-6.3), cut lengthwise into strips roughly 4 to 6 inches wide and laid along the barrel like extra staves. At that width a flat strip sits within about 1/8 inch of a 6 ft diameter curve, so the board does not need to bend. Stagger the end joints. Buy one pack first and test the fit.
  3. Furring strips running around the curve (over the top from one side to the other, like hoops), spaced about 1 foot apart. They hold the insulation down and give the roof something to fasten to. Use thin, bendable strips, or rip quarter-inch plywood into narrow strips.
  4. Underlayment (roofing felt or synthetic), which keeps the mineral wool dry.
  5. Roof surface: corrugated metal or shingles, with a drip edge at the bottom so water sheds clear. Corrugated panels need to be curved with the ribs running around the barrel; shingles follow the curve more easily.

How it is fastened (this corrects the first draft, which only mentioned short screws):

  • Furring to staves: the screw has to pass through the furring and the insulation, so use about 3 inch screws (3/4 inch furring + 1.5 inch insulation + about 3/4 inch into a 1-3/8 inch stave). Pre-drill, and test on a spare stave or a hidden spot so the tip does not reach the sauna interior.
  • Roof to furring: 1 to 1-1/4 inch roofing screws with washers that stop in the furring. The original 3/4 inch screws are Almost Heaven’s advice for fastening metal straight to the staves, not through a furring layer.

Cautions:

  • Mineral wool loses insulating value when damp, so the underlayment and roof edges must shed water cleanly.
  • Account for the steel hoops on the barrel. The flat strips and furring can ride over them; confirm they sit flat.
  • Wear gloves, eye protection and a dust mask when cutting mineral wool; use a serrated blade.
  • Unverified: I could not find a Rockwool maximum service temperature for Comfortboard 80, or a statement on sauna use. It sits on the cool, outer side of the cedar, but ask Rockwool technical service before ordering a lot of it.

Sealing and airflow

Seal the outside against rain, and leave the inside and bottom edges able to breathe. These two goals pull in opposite directions, so each gets its own rule.

Seal the outside:

  • Lap the underlayment shingle-style (upper layer over lower) so water sheds.
  • Fit drip edge or flashing at the bottom edges.
  • Seal roof fasteners and seams, since the metal or shingles are the actual waterproofing.
  • Tuck or tape the underlayment at the ends so wind cannot blow rain up under it.

Do not seal the inside face:

  • Do not caulk or foam the cedar joints. The wood moves with heat and moisture and will crack the seal or split boards.
  • Do not put a plastic vapor barrier or foil directly on the cedar. It can trap moisture in the wood and cause rot. (The first draft suggested an optional foil layer under the insulation; that contradicts this rule, so it is dropped.)

Leave the bottom edges open:

  • Sauna heat pushes moist air through the cedar into the insulation. If every edge is sealed, that moisture condenses and soaks the mineral wool and staves, leading to mold or rot.
  • Let the roof surface and drip edge hang about 1 inch below the end of the insulation. That leaves an open pocket under the roof edge. The drip edge still sheds rain outward.
  • Cover the opening with insect screen or mesh so wasps and mice cannot move in.
  • Do the same at the two end walls: overhang 1 to 2 inches, drip edge, mesh.

Insulation product names to search for

All from Rockwool (formerly sold as Roxul):

  • Comfortboard 80: semi-rigid stone wool board, R-4.2 per inch. Thicknesses run from 1 inch up through 5 inches. Common sizes are 2 ft by 4 ft, 4 ft by 6 ft and 4 ft by 8 ft, and Rockwool’s own charts differ on which thicknesses come in which size. A Canadian retailer lists 1.5 inch as a 24 x 48 inch pack of 48 square feet (six panels) and as a 48 x 72 inch pack of 24 square feet. Check dimensions on whatever you buy; the 2 x 4 ft size is easiest to cut into strips.
  • Comfortbatt R-15: flexible batt, 3.5 inches thick, 15.25 or 23 inches wide, 47 inches long. Easy to find, but likely thicker than you want.
  • Safe’n’Sound: 3 inch batts, 15.25 or 23 inches wide, 47 inches long. Same stone wool, but sold for sound and fire rating in interior walls. It has no official R-value (forum guesses are R-11 to R-13), so it is a poor pick for this job.

Porch roof at the door

A separate freestanding porch roof, so you can dress and undress out of the rain and so weight stays off the barrel staves.

  • Size: about 4 feet deep from the door, wider than the door (about 4 to 5 feet), with room to stand, hang a towel, and maybe fit a small bench.
  • Frame: four posts: two at the front and two beside the door at the back (this fixes the first draft, which had no support at the back edge short of resting on the barrel). Put a beam across each pair and run rafters between them.
  • Slope: 3 inches of drop per foot (3:12), draining forward and away from the barrel. The first draft said 1 inch per foot, which is too flat: corrugated metal generally wants 3:12 or more, and asphalt shingles need at least 2:12 with extra underlayment at low slopes (one code summary says 4:12, so check your local code). Taller front posts or a steeper pitch also give you more headroom.
  • Height: aim for about 6 ft 8 in clear under the front edge. At 3:12 over 4 ft the back edge then ends up about 1 ft higher, which is above the top of a 6 ft barrel on its base. That is fine, because the porch then sits in front of the barrel instead of under its roof.
  • Barrel joint: keep the back edge at least 2 inches clear of the barrel and its roof overhang. Give it an upturned lip and a metal cap flashing, and do not screw anything into the staves. Measure your barrel’s height at the door end first and set the post heights from that.
  • Lumber: cedar or pressure-treated 4x4 posts, 2x6 beams and rafters, with roof material to match the barrel roof. Set posts on piers or footings suited to local frost depth and code.

Air circulation for cold feet

A heat-rated sauna fan can move air. Ordinary fans are not safe inside: motors and plastic can fail or become a fire risk at sauna temperatures. Check this section’s assumptions before buying; the first draft overstated what the fan does.

  • Product to look for: MMotors MM-S 100, a 4 inch (100 mm) sauna exhaust fan: about 105 m³/h, 16 W, IP44, rated for 140°C when running (180°C switched off) and 100% humidity, housing and back-draft damper in glass-filled polyamide. Listings include versions with a back valve. These specs come from retailer pages, not an official datasheet.
  • Where to buy: the listings I found were European sauna shops (for example esaunashop.com and orotech.lt). The first draft named Sauna Experts, Saunainter and SaunaBee, which I could not confirm. Unverified: supply voltage. EU listings are often 230 V, so find a 120 V version or a different fan before ordering.
  • Not the SaunaBox Flow: it is a cordless USB-C fan for SaunaBox models only (SmartSteam, Pulse PRO, Solara, Forge), and often sold out. Its “up to 30% more heat transfer” is a vendor claim.
