  • Placement: the first draft claimed a low fan near the heater pulls warm air down along the floor. I could not find support for that. The MM-S is sold as an exhaust fan, and mounting one means cutting a 4 inch hole in a stave, which may affect your warranty. Ask Almost Heaven before cutting.
  • Try first: Almost Heaven barrels usually have a low intake vent and a high exhaust vent. If both are wide open in winter, cold air may be flooding in, so try partly closing the intake. That costs nothing.
  • Wiring: use high-temperature (silicone) wire near the fan, and have an electrician check the wiring.

Shopping list (starter)

  • Rockwool Comfortboard 80, 1.5 inch (one pack to test, then more as needed)
  • Thin furring strips or quarter-inch plywood to rip
  • About 3 inch exterior screws for the furring (pre-drill)
  • Roofing underlayment
  • Corrugated metal panels or shingles, plus drip edge
  • 1 to 1-1/4 inch roofing screws with washers, and sealant for the roof fasteners
  • Insect mesh for the open slots
  • Metal flashing and cap flashing for the porch back edge
  • Porch lumber: four posts, two beams, rafters; piers or footings
  • Dust mask, gloves and eye protection for the mineral wool
  • Optional: heat-rated sauna fan (MMotors MM-S 100, in a voltage you can use) plus high-temperature wire

Open questions

  • Heater size and circuit (confirm kW rating against your model and barrel volume, and the circuit with an electrician).
  • Barrel diameter and height at the door end, to set the porch post heights.
  • Whether the barrel’s steel hoops need notching or shimming under the furring.
  • Rockwool’s maximum service temperature for Comfortboard 80 and sauna suitability.
  • Whether Almost Heaven allows cutting a fan hole or fastening a roof without voiding the warranty.
  • Local permit rules for the porch roof and the heater circuit.

Verification notes

Checked 2026-11-04 against public pages. Confirmed items are fine as written; corrections are in the sections above.

Claim Result
Almost Heaven rain jacket, can stay on during use Confirmed (listing, archive)
Corrugated metal and shingles as roof options Confirmed in Almost Heaven’s roof blog post (archive)
Stave thickness 1-3/8 in per Almost Heaven’s Watoga page (archive); resolves the earlier open question
Comfortboard 80, 1.5 in, about R-6 R-4.2 per inch, so about R-6.3; 24 x 48 in pack of 48 sq ft listed by BMR (archive); Rockwool’s own page (archive) lists sizes differently
Comfortbatt R-15 and Safe’n’Sound sizes Confirmed (3.5 in and 3 in, 15.25 or 23 x 47 in); Safe’n’Sound has no official R-value
MMotors MM-S 100, 140°C rating Confirmed by retailers (orotech.lt, archive); it is an exhaust fan; voltage unverified
Sauna Experts, Saunainter, SaunaBee as suppliers Not confirmed; replaced
SaunaBox Flow suits a barrel Not so; it is for SaunaBox models (maker, archive)
6 kW heater typical Commonly listed on 4-person models; varies by model
Porch slope 1 in per ft Too flat; 3:12 for corrugated metal, 2:12 minimum for asphalt shingles (GAF, archive); check local code
Comfortboard 80 temperature limit in a sauna No source found; ask Rockwool

item.title: Garage Grow Setup
item.description:
A winter garage changes three things: there is no sunlight, it is cold, and there is moisture around electricity. All three have fixes.

Light

Garage windows will not do it. Plants need a dedicated light.

  • Seedlings: roughly 100–200 µmol/m²/s (PPFD) at the canopy, 14–16 h/day.
  • Leafy greens and herbs in the tower: roughly 200–400 µmol/m²/s, 14–16 h/day.
  • Fruiting crops (tomatoes, peppers, strawberries): considerably more, 400+ (a rule of thumb; not checked against a source).

A light delivering ~300 µmol/m²/s for 16 h works out to a daily light integral of about 17 mol/m²/day, a good target for lettuce. Without good airflow, aim a little lower (13–14) to avoid tip burn.

The tower stands up to 180 cm (about 6 ft) with all three pot sizes stacked, so you want light that covers its height, not just the top. A 1 m bar covers roughly half of a full-height column; use two per side, or build the tower shorter. A commenter built LED strips into the optional support rings. Options:

  • Full-spectrum LED bars or strips mounted vertically alongside the tower, one per side. This is usually the best fit.
  • Full-spectrum LED panel or bar above the seedling tray for the starting area.
  • T5 high-output fluorescents — work well for seedlings, cheaper but bulkier and less efficient.

Look for a manufacturer-stated PPFD (or PAR) figure at a stated distance, not just “equivalent to 1000 W” claims. Give the light its own timer (14–16 h on). The pump runs its interval cycle around the clock on a separate timer.

Heat

Unheated garage lows will drop the reservoir towards freezing, which stops growth and can split pumps and fittings.

  1. Insulate — wrap or place the reservoir in foam board or a cooler-style enclosure; keep it off the cold concrete floor on a pallet or foam.
  2. Aquarium heater (adjustable) in the reservoir, set about 68 °F, plugged into a GFCI. This is the single most useful heat item. It must stay fully submerged: a heater exposed by a falling water level gets very hot very fast.
  3. Freeze protection for everything else — the reservoir heater only protects the tank. The tower column, tubing, net-cup roots, and pump all sit in garage air. If the forecast is near 32 °F, bring the tower inside or drain the column and lines, and keep the plants somewhere warm.
  4. Room-level heat — insulation plus the reservoir heater is the preferred plan. If you add an electric space heater, plug it directly into a wall outlet (never a power strip or extension cord), keep 3 ft of clearance, use one with tip-over shutoff, and don’t leave it running unattended; NFPA advises unplugging it when you leave. No fuel-burning heaters in the garage (carbon monoxide), and keep fuels and solvents away from any heater.
  5. Seedling heat mat with a thermostat for germination.

Timers and power

  • A timer for the lights (14–16 h on) and a separate timer for the pump (15 min on, 15–45 off, around the clock) so the schedules are independent.
  • GFCI outlet or GFCI adapter — not optional.
  • Surge-protected power strip mounted above the water line (for the lights and timers, not for a heater).
  • Low-water protection — as the tank drops, the pump can run dry (which damages it) and the heater can end up in air. Check the level daily; a float switch or low-water cutoff is cheap insurance.

Meters and supplies

  • pH meter (digital pen type) with calibration solution (pH 4 and 7); calibrate regularly and store as directed. Cheap pH test drops or strips work for rough checks only.
  • EC meter — buy EC, not just TDS. TDS is calculated from EC with a 0.5 or 0.7 factor, so ppm readings from different meters don’t match.
  • pH Down (and pH Up) — small bottles last a long time.
  • Complete hydroponic nutrient — a two- or three-part set designed for leafy greens.
  • Seed-starting tray, humidity dome, heat mat, rockwool or plugs — see Seed Starting.
  • Small clip-on fan for airflow. Seedlings need it, and grown lettuce needs it too to prevent tip burn and damp mold, especially in a closed tent.
  • Measuring syringes or a graduated cylinder for doses.
  • Opaque tubing and a lid on the reservoir to keep out light and algae. Print or paint the tower parts opaque too (check the model for PETG vs PLA; PETG copes better with a cold, wet garage).

Water and mixing

  • Know your tap water. Check your utility’s water-quality report. Very soft water (Asheville’s runs about 24 ppm alkalinity) starts near zero EC and has little pH buffering, so pH swings fast, and some nutrient formulas need a Cal-Mag supplement. Chlorine is fine; chloramine is not removed by letting water sit. Well water needs a water analysis first.
  • Mixing: add each nutrient part to the water separately and stir; never combine the concentrates. Measure EC first, then adjust pH. pH Down is acid: wear gloves and eye protection.

Shopping list

Grow lights below don’t list a PPFD figure at a distance (see the Light section). Archive links are omitted where the Wayback Machine has no snapshot of a product page yet. Links and prices were checked against each product page on 2026-11-01. On the same day the list was re-checked against the tower’s own parts list (see The Tower): the pump was replaced with the designer’s Sicce (the earlier pumps could not lift to the top), the light counts were sized to the 180 cm height, the TriPart nutrient was added, and rows were added for the reservoir pot, center pipe, screws, filter foam, net pots, and grow media. Prices change; no links are affiliate links.

Item Pick Why / key spec Price (2026-11-01)
Vertical LED grow lights Spider Farmer SF600 (archive), one per side
or Barrina T5 2 ft, 5000K, 4-pack (archive)		 SF600: 39.4″ × 5.9″ bar (100 cm), ~74 W, 2.3 µmol/J, hanging kit included; not daisy-chainable. Barrina: 10 W per 2 ft (61 cm) strip, links up to 16, clips/ties included; budget option, much less light per side. For the full 180 cm tower: 2 SF600 end to end per side (200 cm), so one 2-pack per side; or 3 Barrina strips per side (183 cm), so two 4-packs light two sides and leave two strips for the seedling tray. A shorter build may need only one SF600 or two strips per side. Neither page gives a PPFD figure at a distance. A “Hydroponic tower light kit” by StarFactory on MakerWorld is an add-on idea for this tower; it was not checked (MakerWorld blocks fetching). SF600 $65.99 (2-pack $121.99); Barrina $41.99 (4-pack)
Seedling light Spider Farmer SF300 (archive)
or two strips from the Barrina pack above		 23.6″ bar, ~33 W, 74 µmol/s, rated for a 2′×2′ area, so it covers one 1020 tray. No PPFD figure on the page; start about 12″ above the tray and adjust for stretch. $49.99
Seedling heat mat + thermostat VIVOSUN 10″×20.75″ heat mat + digital thermostat (archive) Sized for a 1020 tray; thermostat holds 68–108 °F with a probe in the plugs. MET listed. $30.99
Aquarium heater Aqueon Pro Adjustable Heater, 50 W (archive) Plastic shatterproof housing (better than glass in a garage), 68–88 °F, fully submersible, shuts off if it overheats or tips past horizontal. 50 W is rated for up to 20 gal; go up a size if the reservoir is bigger or the garage gets very cold. Not shown (dealer list)
pH meter Apera PH60 (archive)
or Apera PH20 (archive)		 PH60: ±0.01 pH, ATC, IP67, replaceable probe, comes with pH 4/7/10 buffers. PH20: ±0.1 pH, ATC, IP67, but the probe is not replaceable (the whole pen is replaced when it wears out). PH60 $110; PH20 $72
EC meter Apera EC60 (archive)
or Apera EC20 (archive)		 Both read 0–20 mS/cm directly (no TDS conversion needed), ATC, IP67, with calibration solution. EC60 has a replaceable probe; EC20 does not. EC60 $112; EC20 $79
Nutrients General Hydroponics FloraSeries Quart Trial Pack
or CropKing Hydro-Gro Leafy, 5 lb (archive)
or the designer’s Terra Aquatica TriPart (archive)		 FloraSeries: 1 qt each of Micro, Gro, Bloom; liquid, sold in most hydro shops; use the vegetative ratios on GH’s feed chart. Hydro-Gro Leafy: 4.3-9.3-35 powder made for leafy crops, about 125 gal of solution per lb, but calcium nitrate must be bought separately. TriPart: a three-bottle Micro/Grow/Bloom system like FloraSeries, with Micro sold in hard- and soft-water versions (soft suits Asheville water). The TriPart name has not changed; the brand has. Terra Aquatica is the French maker formerly sold as General Hydroponics Europe (GHE), and its FAQ still calls its products “GH nutrients”. It is a European product and no US retailer was found, so FloraSeries is the practical US stand-in. Its FAQ says its feed charts use a lower EC than GH’s US charts. FloraSeries not shown (dealer list); Hydro-Gro $51; TriPart not shown (no US retailer)
pH Down / pH Up General Hydroponics pH Control Kit (archive) 8 oz pH Up + 8 oz pH Down plus an indicator dye for rough checks. Enough for a winter of a small tower. Not shown (dealer list)
Starter plugs General Hydroponics Rapid Rooter, 50-cell tray + plugs (archive) Peat/bark plugs, no pre-soak pH step; the 50-cell insert fits in a 1020 tray. The page does not give the plug diameter, so check it against the tower’s net cups. For rockwool (the designer’s choice), see the rockwool row below. $25.96
Tray + humidity dome Bootstrap Farmer 1020 tray, no holes (archive)
+ Bootstrap Farmer 1020 humidity dome (archive)		 Thick tray, 2.5″ deep, no holes, for bottom watering. Dome is 5.4″ tall with two vents and rests on the rim. Both made in the USA. Tray $6.69; dome $8.19
Outlet timers Lights: Autopilot 7-day digital timer (TM01715) (archive)
Pump: Autopilot analog dual-outlet timer (TM01015D) (archive)		 The digital timer only allows 8 on/off cycles a day, fine for lights but too few for a 15-on/15-off pump. The analog timer has 15-minute pins for the full 24 h, so it can do 15/15 or 15/30–45. Both grounded, 15 A, UL listed, indoor use. List price $25.19 (digital) / $19.94 (analog)
GFCI adapter Southwire 14650013-6 single-outlet GFCI adapter (archive) 120 V/15 A, trips at 4–6 mA, manual reset (stays off after a power cut until you reset it, so check the pump after outages). Skip it if the garage outlet is already a GFCI that passes its test button. Not shown (dealer list)
Air pump + airstone EcoPlus Eco Air 1 Plus
+ AquaVita 2″ cylinder airstone		 Single outlet, 2 W, 44 GPH; plenty for a small reservoir. Keeps the water oxygenated when the pump is off. Add airline tubing and a check valve; keep the pump above the water line. Pump $12.03; stone $3.11
Tower pump Sicce Syncra Silent 2.0 (archive) (designer’s pump)
or Sicce Syncra Silent 1.5 (archive) for a shorter tower
Specs: Sicce Syncra Silent page (archive)		 Size by lift, not flow: flow falls to zero at max head. Lift is the height from the pot’s water surface to the sprinkler, about 1.4–1.6 m on a full 180 cm tower (assuming the 180 cm includes the 40 cm pot). 2.0: 568 GPH, 6.5 ft (2.0 m) max head, 35 W, ¾″ outlet (US 120 V listing); Sicce’s own page (230 V/50 Hz) gives 2150 L/h, 200 cm, 32 W. 1.5: 357 GPH, 6 ft (1.8 m), 23 W, ½″ outlet; Sicce gives 1350 L/h, 180 cm. At full height the 2.0 runs near 80% of its max head (low flow, but the designer’s tower works), and the 1.5 would be marginal. Shorter build: measure the lift and pick a pump whose max head is comfortably above it (aim for about 1.3–1.5× lift; a rule of thumb, not from a source). With a 1.2 m lift the 1.5 has that margin. The printed base is built around the Syncra outlet, so check the fit if you use a different pump. The cheaper pump with a commenter’s connector (MakerWorld 1625658) could not be checked, so it is not listed. The AC Infinity pumps listed here before top out at about 1.5–1.6 m of lift and will not reach the top of a full tower. 2.0 $119.99; 1.5 $89.99
Reservoir pot (≥40 L, no drain) Veradek Pure Series Nobleton 18″ (archive) The tower is sized for a square 38 × 38 × 40 cm pot with no holes. Nobleton 18″: 16″ × 16″ × 18″ (40.6 × 40.6 × 45.7 cm) outside, 12.2 gal (46.4 L), made in Canada, tested −20 to +120 °F. It has drainage holes with removable plugs, so seal the plugs (silicone) and leak-test before use. The page says “commercial-grade plastic” without naming the resin, and doesn’t say whether it tapers. It is bigger than 38 cm, so adapt the printed 36.8 cm lid using the model’s STEP files, or screw the lid to a board cut to the rim. A commenter’s 5-gallon bucket works but holds about 19 L, under the designer’s 40 L minimum. $59.99
Center pipe, 20 mm OD × 2 m KIPP K0493.0220X2000 aluminum round tube (archive) 20 ± 0.1 mm OD, 14 mm bore (so a 3 mm wall), 2000 mm, anodized aluminum (the designer used aluminum). Cut it to length. A commenter used stainless instead; no stainless 20 mm listing was checked. US ¾″ tube is 19.05 mm OD, not 20 mm, so test the fit in the printed parts before substituting. AFT has a $75 minimum order. $141.52
Screws and nuts M4×16 A2 flat-head socket screws, about 28
+ M4×8 A2 flat-head socket screws, 2 (filter flap)
+ M4 A2 hex nuts
+ M5 A2 hex nuts, 12		 Stainless A2-70 throughout (better than zinc in a wet garage). The screws are ISO 10642 countersunk with a 90° head, hex drive (2.5 mm key). The nuts are ISO 4032. The base lid takes 12 M5 screws, but their length and head type weren’t captured from the model page, so confirm them before buying (the same store stocks A2 M5 screws). The grow pots also take nuts (4 per big pot, 2 per small): confirm their size on the model page and buy spares. Hand-tighten only; the designer warns that power drivers crack the parts. M4×16 $0.14 each ($0.10 each in 100s); M4×8 $0.10; M4 nut $0.07; M5 nut $0.08
Lid filter foam (3 cm) Swiss Tropicals Poret foam sheets (archive) 3 cm is about 1.2″. Poret comes in 1″ (2.5 cm) or 1.5″ (3.8 cm), both in 30 PPI (“fine”) black, and is aquarium/aquaponics safe. A 19.5 × 19.5″ sheet covers the 36.8 cm lid, and the shop cuts rectangles free. Cut the center hole and slit yourself, with the slit facing away from the filter flap. 1″ 19.5×19.5 $17; 1.5″ 19.5×19.5 $26
Net pots AC Infinity 2″ mesh net cups, 50-pack (archive)
or AC Infinity 3″, 25-pack (archive)		 Confirm the net-pot size on the model page first: our printout of it doesn’t give one. These are candidates only. Wide-lip, slotted, BPA-free polypropylene. 2″: 1.96 × 2.59 in (5.0 × 6.6 cm) listed size. 3″: 2.55 × 3.54 in (6.5 × 9.0 cm). 2″ $17.99; 3″ $16.99
Clay pebbles Mother Earth Hydroton Original, 25 L (archive)
or GROW!T clay pebbles, 10 L (archive)		 The designer adds clay pebbles to the net pot once roots develop. Hydroton: 8–16 mm, made in Germany, reusable; out of stock on 2026-11-01, and doesn’t ship to AK/CA/HI. GROW!T: 4–16 mm, in stock. Rinse before use. Hydroton $33.51 (sale); GROW!T $15.92 (sale)
Vermiculite PVP Vermiculite (archive) The designer tops rockwool cubes with vermiculite. An 8 qt bag of medium grade is plenty for one tower. The page also lists coarse grade in 20 qt and 4 cu ft. Medium 8 qt $4.99; coarse 20 qt $9.99
Rockwool starter cubes Grodan A-OK 1″ starter plugs (713020) (archive) 1″ stonewool plugs, 200 per sheet (fits a 1020 tray). The page lists a case quantity of 30 but doesn’t say whether one sheet or a case is the purchase unit, so check before ordering. The designer’s choice: start in rockwool, add vermiculite on top, then clay pebbles. Check the 1″ plug against the net-pot size. Not shown

item.title: Heartwood Shaker 3-Drawer Nightstand (Proposed)
item.description:
A proposed build — a copy of the Vermont Furniture Designs Heartwood Shaker 3-Drawer Nightstand (product page, archive), with the proportions taken from the maker’s photos and drawing. Three equal drawers stacked under a top that flares out past the case at the ends, four straight legs, an arched apron across the front, and frame-and-panel sides.

Provenance of the numbers. The maker publishes only the overall size and the construction notes. (stated) = from the maker’s page. (derived) = worked out from other numbers here so everything closes. (est.) = measured off the maker’s front photo, dimensioned drawing and three-quarter photo — good to about ±¼″ at best. The front/back overhang in particular is borrowed from a sibling model (the Heartwood Shaker End Table), because it cannot be read from a front view. Check the (est.) items before cutting.

Stated by the maker

Item Value
Overall 24″ W × 18″ D × 28″ H (stated)
Drawers 3, dovetailed; beech sides, backs and bottoms; high-end metal slides (stated)
Knobs Matching hardwood (stated)
Case Solid-wood sides; hardwood-plywood back (stated)
Species Cherry, maple or walnut (stated)
Finish Cherry/walnut: hand-rubbed linseed oil + wax. Maple: tung oil + wax (stated)

Drawings (true scale)

Drawn at 1″ = 16 px (the arched rails at 24 px) from the dimensions on this page. Click to open full size.

Front elevation

Side elevation

Plan view, top removed

Leg layout

Arched rails

The ratios

Derived Working Result
Case width 24 − 2 × 2½ (end overhang) 19″ (derived)
Case depth 18 − 2 × 1¼ (front/back overhang) 15½″ (derived)
Drawer opening between legs 19 − 2 × 1½ 16″ (derived — matches the ≈16″ measured on the photo and drawing)
Drawer front width 16 − 2 × 1/16 15⅞″ (derived)
Drawer stack 3 × 6″ + 2 × ¾″ rails + 6 × 1/16″ reveals 19⅞″ (derived)
Floor to bottom of lowest opening 28 − 1 (top) − 19⅞ 7⅛″ (derived — matches ≈ 7¼″ measured)
Front apron, ends / centre 7⅛″ band: ends 2⅝″, centre 1⅝″ 1″ rise (est.)
Proportion Value
Width : height 24 : 28 ≈ 0.86 : 1
Width : depth 24 : 18 = 4 : 3
Case width ÷ overall width 19 ÷ 24 ≈ 0.79 (each end overhang ≈ 10.4 %)
Drawer front height ÷ width 6 ÷ 15⅞ ≈ 0.38
Drawer stack ÷ overall height 19⅞ ÷ 28 ≈ 0.71
Floor to opening ÷ overall height 7⅛ ÷ 28 ≈ 0.25

To resize: multiply every dimension by one factor k and the proportions hold; round the stock thicknesses (¾″ rails, 1½″ legs) to what you have and keep the drawer fronts equal.

Dimensions that are estimates

Item Value Basis
End overhang 2½″ ≈ 2½″ scaled off both the front photo and the dimensioned drawing
Front/back overhang 1¼″ Not visible from the front; matches the maker’s Heartwood Shaker End Table (listed 1¼″ front/back, 2″ sides)
Top thickness 1″ (thin edge, bevelled underneath) ≈ 1″ in the front photo; the three-quarter photo shows the edge tapered to roughly ⅜″
Leg section 1½″ square ≈ 1.5″ in the drawing; ≈ 1.1–1.4″ in the photos, so it may be a little lighter. 1½″ makes the 16″ opening close
Drawer front height 6″ ≈ 6.0″ in both straight-on views
Rails between drawers ¾″ ≈ 0.85″ visible including reveals
Knob 1¼″ diameter, centred on each front Round, ≈ 1¼″ in the front photo
Top side rail / muntin 1½″ / 1″ Three-quarter photo shows a top rail, one centre muntin and two panels per side
Slide clearance ½″ per side Typical side-mount metal slide; confirm against the slide you buy

Cut list

T × W × L, cut to length. 1″ tenons are baked into rail lengths. Cherry for the case and drawer fronts; beech (or maple) for drawer boxes.

Case

Part Qty Stock T × W × L Notes
Legs 4 8/4 1½″ × 1½″ × 27″ Height 28 − 1 top. Soft radius on the foot end, as in the photo
Front apron (arched) 1 4/4 ¾″ × 2⅝″ × 18″ Arch cut on the bottom edge: 1″ rise over the 16″ between shoulders (radius 32½″) — see the arched-rail drawing
Front rails 2 4/4 ¾″ × ¾″ × 18″ Between drawers. 16″ between shoulders
Back top rail 1 4/4 ¾″ × 1½″ × 18″ Grooved for the back panel
Back bottom rail 1 4/4 ¾″ × 2⅝″ × 18″ Straight; grooved for the back panel
Back panel 1 ¼″ hardwood ply ¼″ × 16⅜″ × 18¾″ Floats in ¼″ grooves; width and height include groove depth, less ⅛″ (stated: plywood back)
Top side rails 2 4/4 ¾″ × 1½″ × 14½″ 12½″ between shoulders; flush to leg outer face
Bottom side rails (arched) 2 4/4 ¾″ × 2⅝″ × 14½″ Same 1″-rise arch as the front, here over 12½″ (radius ≈ 20″)
Side muntins 2 4/4 ¾″ × 1″ × as fitted Between top and bottom side rails (18⅜″ apart); grooved both edges
Side panels 4 4/4 resawn ½″ × 6⅜″ × 19″ Two per side; float in ⅜″ grooves (width and height include groove depth, less ⅛″)
Slide spacers 2 4/4 ¾″ × 2″ × 12″ Screwed to the inside of the side frames so the slide face sits at the drawer-box edge
Top 1 4/4 1″ × 18″ × 24″ Floats on buttons; underside bevelled toward the edge

(Rails and aprons are shown flush to the leg faces on the outside. Side-rail tenons are about 5/16″ thick; the front-rail tenon is short because the rail is only ¾″ tall — use ¼″ × ½″.)

Drawers (× 3, identical)

Part Qty each T × W × L Notes
Front 1 ¾″ × 6″ × 15⅞″ Cherry, grain-matched top to bottom; 1/16″ reveals
Sides 2 ½″ × 5″ × 12″ Beech; dovetailed
Back 1 ½″ × 4½″ × 15″ Beech; dovetailed (full box width)
Bottom 1 ¼″ × as fitted Beech; floats in a groove
Knob 1 1¼″ ⌀ Matching cherry, turned or shaped

The box is 15″ wide overall (½″ slide clearance each side of the 16″ opening), so its interior is about 14″ wide — close to the 14¼″ the maker lists for a sibling nightstand. Box length of 12″ fits a 12″ slide with room behind for the back panel.

Build sequence

  1. Mill the 8/4 for legs, then the 4/4 in stages, resting between passes.
  2. Cut mortises and tenons for the legs. Cut the two arches on the front apron and the bottom side rails before assembly.
  3. Groove the side rails, muntins and legs for the panels. Make the four panels, finish them before assembly so no bare wood shows when they move.
  4. Glue up each side frame (legs + top rail + bottom rail + muntin + two panels). Drawbore the leg joints if you like.
  5. Join the two sides with the front apron, the two front rails and the back rails. Dry-clamp first; the opening must be 16″ and the case 19″ × 15½″.
  6. Slide the back panel into its grooves before the last rail goes in.
  7. Screw on the slide spacers, then build and dovetail the three drawers and hang them on the slides.
  8. Make and fit the knobs.
  9. Finish with hand-rubbed linseed oil and wax (cherry), matching the maker.
  10. Attach the top with buttons so it can move seasonally. Centre it: 2½″ at each end, 1¼″ front and back.

Domino option

A Domino is a poor fit for the leg joints on this piece, and a good fit for the muntins.

Why: the 1½″ legs take several joints at the same height. At each back corner, the back top rail and the top side rail both enter at the top; at every corner the arched aprons and bottom rails (2⅝″ tall) meet at the same level. Two Domino mortises from adjacent faces cross inside the leg, so they would have to be staggered in height, and 1½″ and 2⅝″ parts don’t have room to stagger. The hand-cut plan avoids the collision by mitering tenon tips.

Joint Option Notes
Leg joints (rails, aprons) Hand-cut or router-cut tenons, tips mitered As in the cherry console plan
Front rails (¾″ × ¾″) Stub tenon A ¾″-tall rail is too small for a standard Domino (a 4×20 does not fit)
Side muntins (¾″ × 1″, ×2) 1 × 4×20 Domino per end Fits the 1″ width; cut the muntin shoulder-to-shoulder
Back panel, side panels Unchanged Float in grooves
  • If you still want Dominoes at the leg corners, stagger by height and widen the legs to 1¾″ so the mortises have room — but that changes the 16″ opening, so every other dimension on the page moves with it.

Open questions

  • Front/back overhang — 1¼″ is borrowed from the sibling model; the three-quarter photo suggests it is in that range but doesn’t prove it.
  • Leg section — 1½″ closes the 16″ opening, but the photos read as slightly lighter. If you go to 1¼″, either narrow the case to 18½″ (2¾″ end overhang) or widen the opening to 16½″ and the drawer fronts to 16⅜″.
  • Drawer depth — 12″ box length is my choice; the maker doesn’t state it.

item.title: Top Ten Market Products
item.description:
What to build for craft fairs and Christmas markets. The goal is a table that sells: a few cheap impulse items, a solid middle of gift-priced pieces, and one or two “hero” pieces that draw people in.

Numbers are planning estimates, not market data. Prices, material costs and build times below are my own rough figures for a small one-person shop selling at regional craft markets. Replace them with your own after the first market, using real receipts and a stopwatch. Check booth fees and your state’s sales-tax rules before the first sale. This is not tax advice, so talk to a CPA about how a hobby-versus-business classification affects deductions.

The ten, ranked

Ranked by how well each fits a table at a market: sells fast, builds in batches, uses cheap stock and ships nowhere.

# Product Price Materials Build time Why it sells
1 Mitered picture frames $25–60 $4–10 30–45 min (batch) Cheap to make, everyone needs one, easy upsell
2 Cutting and serving boards $35–90 $8–25 45–90 min (batch) Top gift category; people pick them up and handle them
3 Birdhouses and nest boxes $25–50 $5–12 45–60 min Scrap-friendly, and kids and grandparents both buy them
4 Wall boxes (“pipe box” / salt box) $45–85 $8–20 1.5–2.5 h Distinctive look, and you can make them in several finishes
5 Small ornaments and stocking stuffers $6–20 $0.50–3 5–15 min Impulse buys that fill the gaps in a sale
6 Shaker peg rails and wall shelves $35–75 $8–25 45–90 min Fast, classic, easy to display on your booth wall
7 Step stools $45–95 $10–25 1.5–2 h Useful, sturdy, and good for kids and kitchens
8 Small keepsake boxes $50–120 $12–35 2–4 h Higher price point, feels like “real” woodworking
9 Serving trays and carry totes $40–85 $10–25 1–2 h Seasonal, and they use the same stock as the boards
10 Entryway bench (the hero piece) $175–350 $45–90 5–8 h Draws a crowd; one sale covers the booth fee

Mix to aim for: roughly 50% of units from items 5, 1 and 3 (impulse), 35% from items 2, 4, 6 and 9 (gifts), and a few pieces from items 7, 8 and 10 (hero). Most of the revenue still comes from the middle.

1. Mitered picture frames

You already have the dimensioned plan: Mitered Picture Frame, 1¼″ × ⅞″ profile.

  • Cut a standard size run: 5×7, 8×10, 11×14 and 16×20. People buy to a size they already own a photo or print for.
  • Offer two or three species or stains (maple, walnut, cherry or oak). Contrast is what makes a rack of frames read well.
  • Batch the work: mill all stock at once, cut all miters on one stop-block setting, then glue up in sets of four.
  • Sell them with a cheap mat and backer already fitted. Frames with glass sell for more, but glass breaks in transit, so sell glass-free frames with an acrylic option.

2. Cutting and serving boards

  • Edge-grain boards in maple, walnut and cherry are the easy volume. End-grain boards sell for more but cost more time and glue-up risk.
  • Use food-safe finishes only: mineral oil with beeswax. Say so on a small tag. Avoid exotic woods with irritant dust or unknown food safety.
  • Batch: glue up six to eight blanks at once, then do all the roundovers, handle holes and finishing in one pass.
  • Sell a board with a small tin of board butter as a bundle. The margin on the add-on is high.

3. Birdhouses and nest boxes

  • Decide whether each one is decorative or functional and label it. A functional nest box needs the right hole size, no perch, ventilation and drain holes, and a way to open it for cleaning. Wren, chickadee and bluebird boxes have different hole diameters, so check a reliable source (the NABS or Audubon plans) before you cut.
  • Cedar or cypress needs no finish and weathers well. Pine plus a nice finish suits the decorative ones.
  • Cut kits from a single template: one pattern board, one stop setting, and a pocket of screws makes these fast.

4. Wall boxes (“pipe box” / salt box)

A salt box has a sloped, hinged lid over a small box, and a pipe box has an open rack above a small drawer. Both are the same idea: a small box with a shaped back plate that hangs on a wall.

  • Typical size is about 5–7″ wide, 14–18″ tall and 4–5″ deep, with a scalloped or ogee back and either a hinged lid or an open front.
  • Sell them as candle boxes, salt boxes, key holders or wall storage. The same body can carry four different labels.
  • Vary the back shape (ogee, scallop, flat-top) and sell them in cherry, walnut or painted pine.
  • One jig for the shaped back saves the most time here. A bandsaw template plus a spindle or drum sander gets repeatable curves.

5. Ornaments and stocking stuffers

This is the cheap category that earns more than it looks like it should at Christmas markets.

  • Ideas: scroll-saw or laser-cut ornaments, turned or lathe-made tree toppers, wooden spoons and spatulas, bottle stoppers, keychains, coasters, small cheese knives and ring-toss games.
  • Use cutoffs and offcuts from items 1 to 4. This is where the scrap pays for itself.
  • Price in round numbers ($6, $10, $15, $20) so cash and card handling stays fast. Put a basket at the front of the table.

6. Peg rails and wall shelves

  • Shaker peg rails (a 24–36″ board with 4–6 pegs) are one of the fastest products to make, and they look right on a rail hung on your booth wall.
  • Small ledge shelves, plate rails and key-and-mail racks use the same stock and tooling.
  • Buy turned pegs by the hundred rather than making them. It saves hours.

7. Step stools

  • A two-step stool in pine or poplar costs little, and a well-built one in oak or ash is a “forever” piece.
  • A kids’ step stool with a hand hole also sells well. Round every edge, check the stability, and keep finishes non-toxic.
  • Design for load: use thick enough stretchers and glue plus screws or dowels at every joint. These items get stood on, so do not skimp.

8. Small keepsake boxes

  • Keep it simple: butt or mitered corners with splines, a lift-off or hinged lid, and a nice finish. Add a felt or velvet liner if you want a higher price.
  • Sell them in maple, walnut and cherry with contrasting splines. They show your skill and sell as gifts.
  • Time is the cost here, so make only a few. They also work as a showcase for the booth.

9. Serving trays and totes

  • A flat-bottom serving tray with cut-out handles and a simple tote or caddy (tool, cutlery, garden, picnic) share stock and techniques with the boards.
  • The drawing shows a cheese tray. It makes sense around the holidays: a cheese tray, a coffee-and-tea tray or a wine caddy.

10. Economical entryway bench

Your largest piece, and it should be a display anchor, not a volume item. A person who stops for the bench ends up buying a frame as well.

  • Keep it affordable to build: a 36–48″ pine, poplar or ash bench with a plank top, apron and four legs, or a slab top with simple stretchers. About $45–90 in lumber.
  • Use simple, strong joinery: pocket screws plus glue, or mortise-and-tenon if you want to show off. Match the joinery to the price.
  • Build two for the season, not ten. Take photos and offer to build to order in a different finish or size.
  • Related existing plans on this site: the Shaker coffee table and the console plans can be adapted into higher-ticket commissions.

3D-printed draw-ins and hybrids

You have a printer, so use it for two jobs: traffic builders that get people to the table, and print + wood hybrids that sit in the gift tier. Print-and-forget items also run while you build everything else.

Small printed pieces for sale are fine, but check any model licence before selling prints. Many free STLs are personal-use only, so print your own designs (see the parametric tools already on this site) or models whose licence allows commercial use.

Free or near-free draw-ins

These cost cents each and give someone a reason to stop and talk.

Item Cost each Print time How to use it
Fidget spinner or print-in-place fidget $0.20–0.60 20–60 min Free with any purchase, or “free if you tell me what you’d make”
Bottle-opener or keychain with your logo and QR code $0.30–0.80 15–30 min Free giveaway; the QR links to your page or newsletter
Print-in-place flexi animals $0.20–0.50 30–60 min Kid magnet; parents stop too
Business-card holder or coaster with logo $0.40–1.00 30–60 min Gives your card a reason to be kept
  • Keep giveaways cheap and fast. Print a batch the night before on a multi-part plate. Count on 2–3× more than you hand out, since some get taken without a conversation.
  • Always attach a card or QR code. A free item with no way back to you is just a cost.
  • One per person, with a sign. “Free fidget with any purchase” protects margin; “free fidget, ask me how it’s made” brings in the curious.
  • Do not skip safety. For anything kids may mouth, avoid tiny loose parts and sharp edges, and sand or deburr every print.

Print + wood hybrids to sell

Item Price Wood part Printed part
Desk phone stand $18–30 Maple or walnut block, routed slot Printed angle insert or cable guide
Pen and phone caddy $25–40 Turned or squared base Printed dividers
Bottle stoppers $10–18 Turned or sawn wooden top Printed core or decorative cap
Name-sign or house-number plaque $30–65 Cedar or walnut board Printed raised letters or logo, painted
Coaster set in a wooden holder $22–40 Small wooden stand Printed inserts in school or team colours
Wall hook rail $25–45 Maple board (see the peg rail above) Printed hooks in custom shapes
Birdhouse accessories $8–15 (sold with item 3) Printed predator guard, hanging bracket
Tool and jig sets $20–60 Hardwood base Printed fences, holders (reuse shop designs)
  • Use print where wood is worst: curves, repeated small parts, text and logos. Use wood where it shows: bases, boards, faces.
  • Personalisation sells. A printed name or number on a wooden plaque lets you charge more and make to order. Take orders at the market and deliver the next week.
  • Be honest on the tag. Label “wood and 3D-printed” so nobody feels misled; many buyers like the mix.

Making the numbers work

  • Price floor: a common rule of thumb is price ≥ 2–3× materials plus your time at a minimum hourly rate you choose. If an item cannot clear that at a price the market will pay, cut it.
  • Track from day one: log each sale, each material receipt, booth fees, mileage and show-specific costs in one sheet. Good records matter for any tax treatment.
  • Time per unit drops with batches. The times above assume batch work. A one-off takes 2–3× longer.
  • Test first: take about 40 pieces to a small market before investing in a big run, and note what people pick up and what they buy.

A starting plan for this season

Christmas markets are weeks away, so start with the quick builds and add the rest after your first market.

  1. Week 1: frames (1), ornaments (5), peg rails (6), and a batch of printed giveaways. Fast, uses stock you already have.
  2. Week 2: boards (2), birdhouses (3), trays (9).
  3. Week 3+: wall boxes (4), step stools (7), and the bench (10) if time allows.

Open questions

  • Which markets, and what are the booth fees and dates?
  • Is there an existing shop capacity limit (how many hours a week)?
  • Do you want to stay food-safe-only for boards, or also sell decorative ones?
  • Which species can you source cheaply and locally?

item.title: Fall Vegetable Soup with Tiny Pasta
item.description:
A cozy vegetarian soup built on a celery-onion-carrot base, with canned tomatoes, sweet potato, and tiny pasta. Serves 6. About 35 minutes of cooking.

Ingredients

Amount Ingredient
2 Tbsp olive oil
1 medium yellow onion, diced
3 stalks celery, diced
3 medium carrots, diced
3 cloves garlic, minced
1 Tbsp tomato paste
1 tsp dried oregano
½ tsp dried thyme
1 large sweet potato, peeled and cut into ½-inch chunks
1 can (14 oz) diced tomatoes, with juices
6 cups vegetable broth
1 bay leaf
1 cup ditalini or other tiny pasta
1 tsp salt (a pinch goes in early, the rest at the end)
½ tsp black pepper
2 Tbsp fresh parsley, chopped
¼ cup grated Parmesan or Pecorino, for serving (optional)

Method

  1. Build the base (8 min). Heat the olive oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the onion, celery, and carrots with a pinch of the salt. Cook, stirring often, until softened.
  2. Add aromatics (2 min). Stir in the garlic, tomato paste, oregano, and thyme. Cook until fragrant and the tomato paste darkens slightly.
  3. Simmer with tomatoes and sweet potato (15 min). Add the sweet potato, tomatoes with their juices, broth, and bay leaf. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a simmer, partially covered, until the sweet potato is just tender.
  4. Cook the pasta (9 min). Stir in the pasta and cook until al dente, stirring occasionally so it doesn’t stick. Remove the bay leaf.
  5. Season and serve. Season with the remaining salt and the pepper, adjusting to taste. Ladle into bowls and top with parsley and cheese.

Notes

  • The pasta keeps absorbing broth as it sits. For leftovers, cook the pasta separately and add it to each bowl, or thin the soup with extra broth when reheating.
  • Swap the sweet potato for cubed pumpkin or butternut squash.
  • Stir in a handful of chopped kale or spinach in the last few minutes for extra greens.
  • Skip the cheese (or use a vegetarian-friendly one) to keep it fully vegan.

item.title: Jeweler's Traveling Tool Chest (Proposed)
item.description:
A tool chest for a jeweler who solders rings and pendants and teaches lapidary workshops (domed cabochons and flat/faceted stones). It has to do two jobs: sit on a bench as a daily soldering kit, and travel to a workshop with a lapidary teaching kit. Two classic chest styles fit; this page compares them, then lays out a proposed build modeled on Mike Pekovich’s traveling tool chest, resized and re-organized for jewelry and lapidary tools.

Provenance of the numbers. Pekovich’s chest is a course product, and its page publishes no dimensions, species or drawer count, so this is a design inspired by it, not a copy. (stated) = from the course page. (derived) = worked out from the sizes I chose so everything closes. (est.) = typical sizes of tools and supplies, which vary by brand: put your own tools on the bench and check them before cutting.

The finished chest (concept rendering)

Nothing here is built yet, so this is a drawing from the plan sizes, not a photograph.

Two styles to choose from

Pekovich traveling chest Dutch tool chest
Shape Rectangular case, flat frame-and-panel lid, drawers under an open well Sloped lid, two tiers, fall front (see below)
Made to Be carried: side handles, lock, modest size Hold a full set of woodworking hand tools
Strength Tidy small tools: lift-out tray, two drawers, lockable Big tools: planes, saws, chisels, in a light pine box
Weak point here A well too shallow for long tools Jeweler’s tools are small and need separating; a big open well does not give you that

Pick: the Pekovich style. A jeweler’s kit is hundreds of small, fragile or expensive pieces (stones, laps, burs, solder). They want dividers, a lock, and a carry size, and not a big open well. The standard Dutch chest, described next, is the better answer for planes and saws.

The standard Dutch tool chest

For comparison, this is the chest the Dutch style is known for: a woodworker’s tool chest, not a jeweler’s. I read two pages for it, so what follows is what they say and little more. Christopher Schwarz’s book Dutch Tool Chests is the place for dimensions and joinery; I could not open that page.

Item What the sources say
Lid “Perhaps the chest’s most distinctive characteristic is its sloped lid” (stated, Fine Woodworking). A search summary of a Schwarz video gives about 30°; I did not confirm it
Tiers A top tier for chisels, saws, planes and layout tools, and a bottom sized for molding and joinery planes and tool rolls (stated, Fine Woodworking)
Fall front Has battens; they work best when set no more than ⅛″ inside the case sides (stated, Fine Woodworking)
Joinery Dovetails at the bottom only, plus dadoes, rabbets and cut nails (stated, Fine Woodworking); screws are not required, and cut nails or wooden pegs work (stated, Popular Woodworking)
Wood Pine “or another lightweight wood”; “the cheapest, lightest wood that is available” (stated)
Size One build’s interior depth is 11¼″, the width of a 1×12 (stated, Fine Woodworking). Overall sizes are not stated in what I could read; the “big” chest is said to hold as many tools as a full-size English floor chest (stated, Popular Woodworking)
Hardware and finish Strap hinges and lifts; commonly painted, historically often blue (stated, Popular Woodworking)
Not found Overall dimensions, the side profile, dado heights, and any sliding or saw till

What it means for a jeweler’s chest. The Dutch chest suits a woodworker’s long, heavy tools in a light box that is simple to build. A jeweler’s kit is small and needs separating, which is why this page builds the Pekovich style. The one idea worth borrowing is the two tiers: small tools on top, heavier ones below. The proposed chest already does this with its tray and drawers.

What Pekovich’s course covers (stated)

From the course page (archive), titled Build a Traveling Tool Chest with Mike Pekovich:

Item Value
Corner joints Dovetails at the bottom corners, tails cut at the table saw (stated)
Shelf Through-tenons, laid out together with the mortises (stated)
Case assembly Glued up, tenons wedged, then drilled and pinned (stated)
Case front Mortised for a lid lock (stated)
Lid Frame-and-panel, with bridle joints at the corners (stated)
Drawers Pinned rabbet drawers (stated)
Storage Lift-out mitered trays, slotted blocks for saws, other tool-holding features (stated)
Level / length Intermediate; over 10 hours of instruction; downloadable plans (stated)
Not stated Overall size, species, drawer count, hinge type, handles

If you build from this page, buy the course for the joinery: this page does not teach it.

What the chest has to do

  • Hold two kits that are never used at the same time. Soldering (daily, bench) and lapidary (workshop days) go in separate drawers, so you can lift out one kit.
  • Stay light enough to carry. The case alone is about 22 lb in cherry (derived: ½″ case parts, ¾″ shelf and bottom, cherry at about 35 lb/ft³). Tools add roughly 15–20 lb (est.). Plan on two bail handles and, at about 40 lb loaded, a second person for stairs.
  • Keep the abrasives apart. In cabbing, a single grain of a coarse grit on a fine pad leaves scratches that cost a whole polishing step. Each grit gets its own sealed jar, and laps stay in their own sleeves.
  • Keep acid and water out. Pickle (Sparex or citric) and wet lapidary slurry corrode steel tools and stain wood. The chest holds dry, clean tools only; carry wet items in a separate tub.
  • Protect metal and stones. Many woods give off organic acids, and oak is the usual one to avoid near steel and silver. Use cherry or maple, finish the inside with dewaxed shellac, and wax it. Keep loose stones in lidded boxes or gem papers, not in open tray compartments.
  • Be lockable. A half-mortise lid lock (the course installs one) deters casual theft but does not stop a determined one. A chest with stones and precious metal also needs insurance, which a lock does not replace.

The proposed chest

Overall 22″ W × 12″ D × 13¾″ H (derived: chosen so a 21″ interior fits files and a 12″ mandrel with room), with a lift-out tray and a drawer bay of two equal drawers.

Item Value
Overall 22″ × 12″ × 13¾″ (derived)
Case height / lid 13″ case + ¾″ lid (derived)
Case parts ½″ sides, back and well front; ¾″ bottom and shelf (derived)
Well front 4½″ tall (derived)
Drawer bay 7″: two openings 3¼″ with a ½″ rail between (derived)
Drawer fronts 20⅞″ × 3⅛″, ¹⁄₁₆″ reveals all round (derived)
Drawer interior about 20⅛″ × 9⅝″ × 2¾″ (derived)
Tray 20¾″ × 10¾″ × 1¾″, resting on ½″ cleats (derived)
Species Cherry or maple case, maple drawer sides (proposed)

Drawings (true scale)

Drawn at 1″ = 24 px from the sizes on this page. Click to open full size.

Front elevation

Cross-section at centre

Side panel joint layout

Lift-out tray

Drawer layouts

What goes where

Zone Contents Why here
Tray Pliers and cutters (jaws up in a slotted block), needle and hand files, dividers, calipers, steel rule, ring sizer, burnishers, pushers, scribes, burs in index cases, loupes Used constantly on both kinds of day; lift the tray out and the well is clear
Well (about 2¼″ under the tray) Hammers and mallets, a 12″ ring mandrel (bracelet mandrel if it fits), saw frame and blades, torch tips Heavier, longer, or used less often
Top drawer: soldering Solder sheet and wire in labeled tubes, flux, borax dish, tweezers, third hand, a ceramic tile, ring clamp, spare bench-pin inserts, lidded boxes for work in progress Daily bench kit; sits right under the tray
Bottom drawer: lapidary Dop sticks on edge in a slotted rack, dop wax, one sealed jar per grit and polish, cabochon templates, calipers, loupes, gem tweezers, wrapped stones, faceting laps in padded sleeves Heavy, so it rides low; opens fully for a workshop table
Not in the chest Torch, hoses and fuel; pickle pot; wet grinders, saws and the faceting machine; anything wet Fire, acid and water; the workshop venue normally supplies the machines (see Open questions)

Fire. The chest is a wooden box. Close it before lighting a torch, keep it out of the soldering area, and never leave a hot tile, torch or alcohol lamp on or inside it.

Cut list (proposed)

Finished sizes in inches, thickness × width × length. Check against your own layout before cutting.

Joint allowances are not included. The 21″ lengths of the well front, back, bottom and rail, and the 10″ drawer sides, are the sizes between the parts they join. Add the depth of your dovetails, grooves, rabbets and drawer-front rabbets before you cut. Only the shelf already includes its through-tenons.

Part Qty Size Notes
Sides 2 ½ × 12 × 13 Dovetailed to the well front and back; grooved for the bottom and shelf
Well front 1 ½ × 4½ × 21 Mortised for the lid lock
Back 1 ½ × 21 × 13 Rabbeted into the sides; full case height, so the lid closes on it
Bottom 1 ¾ × 11½ × 21 In grooves in the sides
Shelf 1 ¾ × 11½ × 22 Through-tenoned into the sides: 22″ includes the tenons
Drawer rail 1 ½ × 11½ × 21 Full depth, in grooves in the sides; the top drawer runs on it
Lid frame 4 ¾ × 2 × 22 (long), ¾ × 2 × 12 (short) Bridle corners, grooved ¼″ for the panel
Lid panel 1 ¼ × 8⅜ × 18⅜ Floats in the groove
Drawer fronts 2 ¾ × 3⅛ × 20⅞ Pulls: small wire rings
Drawer sides 4 ⅜ × 3 × 10 Maple
Drawer backs 2 ⅜ × 2¾ × 20⅛
Drawer bottoms 2 ¼ × 9⅝ × 20⅛
Tray cleats 2 ½ × ½ × 21 Top face 10¾″ above the floor
Tray 1 set ⅜ sides, ¼ bottom, ¼ dividers Mitered

Hardware: two butt hinges and a cord or chain stay (as in the photo), one half-mortise lock, two bail handles, two ring pulls.

Build order

  1. Mock up and check the tools. Lay your actual tools on the tray and drawer footprints. Move dividers before cutting any wood. Most fixes here cost nothing.
  2. Mill the stock and cut the sides, well front, back, bottom and shelf to length.
  3. Cut the joints: dovetails for the well front and back, grooves for the bottom, rabbet for the back, mortises for the shelf’s through-tenons.
  4. Dry-fit, then glue the case. Wedge and pin the shelf tenons.
  5. Make the lid: bridle-jointed frame, floating panel, then hang it with two butt hinges and fit the stay and the lock.
  6. Fit the drawer rail, make the drawers, then plane the fronts to ¹⁄₁₆″ reveals.
  7. Make the tray and cleats, and cut the dividers last so they fit the finished drawers.
  8. Finish: dewaxed shellac inside, shellac and wax outside. Let it cure fully before you load the tools.
  9. Handles and pulls.

Open questions

  • What the workshops supply. This plan assumes the venue provides the grinders, trim saw and faceting machine, so the chest carries only hand tools and consumables. If you bring a faceting head or a small cab machine, it needs its own case.
  • The meaning of “flat/faceted ground.” I read it as flat-lapped and faceted stones next to domed cabochons. If it means something else, the laps and dops section changes.
  • Lap size. The laps drawer assumes 6″ discs. 8″ laps do not fit a 9⅝″ drawer with their sleeves, so check yours.
  • Weight. About 22 lb empty is heavy for a chest that will go up stairs. Basswood or poplar drawers, or ⅜″ case parts, save about 4 lb; I kept ½″ for the dovetails and handles.
  • Hinge, lock and handle choices. The course page does not name them; the ones above are my choice.

item.title: 3D-Printed Garrison Binder
item.description:
A Garrison-style rod binder built almost entirely from 3D-printed parts. The architecture follows E. Garrison’s original — vertical face board, cradle on the top edge with a belt gap, guide wheels and drive wheel on the face, a weight riding the belt’s slack loop, and a disc-drag cord tensioner — as documented in detail on the Garrison Binder page. Read that page first; all of its tuning guidance applies directly to this build.

Every wheel runs on two 608 skateboard bearings. All bolt holes, counterbores, captive-nut pockets, and adjustment slots are printed in place — the only drilling in this project is a handful of holes in the wooden face board.

How it works

Crank the drive wheel → the belt circulates → the full turn of belt around the rod spins it → the binding cord (spool → eye 1 → tensioner → eye 2) wraps onto the spinning rod as you feed it through the cradle. The weight keeps constant belt pressure regardless of crank speed. Guide 3 sits just below the cradle on the drive side so the belt’s return run enters the gap vertically instead of scraping the left cradle block.

Printed parts

All STLs are exported already in print orientation — import, slice, print. No supports needed on any part. (One caveat: the feed head’s dowel socket ceiling is a flat internal bridge — it prints fine, and it lands on the non-critical dowel end face.)

Part Qty STL Preview
Drive wheel (Ø64) 1 drive_wheel.stl
Idler wheel (Ø40) 4 idler_wheel.stl
Bearing spacer 5 bearing_spacer.stl
Cradle block 2 cradle_block.stl
Feed-support head 2 feed_head.stl
Feed-support base 2 feed_base.stl
Crank arm 1 crank_arm.stl
Crank grip 1 crank_grip.stl
Weight hanger 1 weight_hanger.stl
Tensioner base 1 tensioner_base.stl
Tensioner disc 2 tensioner_disc.stl
Tensioner knob 1 tensioner_knob.stl
Cord guide post 2 cord_guide.stl
Spool bracket 2 spool_bracket.stl
Board foot 2 board_foot.stl

Parametric source: generate_binder_stls.py. All dimensions (board thickness, bearing fit, trough size, belt diameter) are parameters at the top of the script — pip install manifold3d trimesh numpy matplotlib and re-run to regenerate every STL for your hardware. The script validates that every mesh is watertight before export.

Print settings

Setting Value
Material PETG (PLA acceptable for non-wheel parts)
Layer height 0.2 mm
Perimeters 4
Infill 40% (wheels and cradle: 60%)
Supports None

The bearing pockets are sized at Ø22.15 for a light press fit. Print one idler first and test: if the bearing falls out, reduce POCKET_D to 22.05 and regenerate; if it won’t seat with firm thumb pressure, raise it to 22.25.

Hardware

Item Qty Used for
608-2RS bearings (8×22×7) 10 2 per wheel
M8 × 60 bolts + nyloc nuts 4 drive + 3 guide wheel axles (through board)
M8 × 50 bolt + nyloc nut 1 weight-pulley axle (through hanger)
M8 × 80 bolt (or rod) + washers 1 spool axle
M8 washers 16 axle stacks
M5 × 40 bolts + hex nuts 2 cradle clamp bolts (hex or socket head — the counterbore fits an 8 mm socket)
M5 × 45 bolt + hex nut 1 tensioner stack
M5 × 50 bolt + nyloc nut 1 crank handle (grip spins on shank)
M4 × 25 screws 2 crank arm → drive wheel (self-tap into printed pilots)
M4 × 10 screws 6 pinch screws: feed heads ×2, feed bases ×2, board feet ×2 (all counterbored)
#8 × 3/4" wood screws ~20 tensioner, cord guides, spool brackets, feet, feed bases
Compression spring ~Ø10 × 15 1 tensioner (smooth drag adjustment)
Face board: 500 × 300 × 18 mm ply 1 measure actual thickness — see note
Mounting plank: ~600 × 200 mm ply 1 feet screw to this; it overhangs the bench edge
1" hardwood dowel ~650 mm feed-support posts, cut to height
3/16" braided mason line 2 m drive belt (braided, not twisted)
1/8" brass rod, ~300 mm 1 optional: fly-off take-off loop above the spool (per the article)
Rodmaker’s binding cord 1 spool
Small jar + hardware 1 weight, 450–680 g (1–1.5 lb per the article)

Board thickness note: the cradle channel and foot slots are generated for 18.0 mm stock + 0.35 mm clearance. Plywood sold as 3/4" varies from 17.5–19 mm — measure yours and set BOARD_T in the script before printing the cradles and feet.

Board drilling plan

The only drilled holes in the project. Coordinates are (distance from the board’s left edge, distance down from the top edge) on a 500 × 300 board:

Hole Position Size For
Cradle bolt L (232, 7.5) Ø5.5 M5 clamp bolt
Cradle bolt R (268, 7.5) Ø5.5 M5 clamp bolt
Drive wheel (150, 150) Ø8.5 M8 axle
Guide wheel 1 (300, 130) Ø8.5 M8 axle — sets the belt’s exit angle: the outgoing strand departs the rod at ~168° of wrap
Guide wheel 2 (330, 250) Ø8.5 M8 axle
Guide wheel 3 (262, 190) Ø8.5 M8 axle — brings the return strand into the gap vertically

Everything else attaches with wood screws through printed counterbores — no drilling, just drive the screws.

Assembly

1. Feet and board

Screw the two board feet to the mounting plank ~400 mm apart, slots aligned, then clamp the plank to the bench so the board’s front face overhangs the bench edge by at least 25 mm. The belt plane runs 12 mm in front of the board face and the weight loop hangs below the board — both need clear air in front of the bench edge along the whole loop span. Drop the board into the slots and drive the pinch screws.

2. Wheels

Press two 608 bearings into each wheel with a vise or thumb pressure. Drop a printed spacer between them (it clamps between the inner races so the nyloc can be fully torqued without binding the wheel).

Axle stack, inside to out: bolt head → washer → board → washer → bearing/wheel/bearing → washer → nyloc. Torque the nut fully — the spacer takes the clamp load and the wheel spins free.

Fasten the crank arm to the drive wheel face with two M4 × 25 screws — they self-tap into the printed pilot holes (any two opposite pilots) and stop inside the wheel, so nothing protrudes from the back face spinning next to the board. Then bolt the grip to the arm end with the M5 — nyloc snug but the grip must spin.

3. Cradle

Drop the two cradle blocks over the board’s top edge, one each side of the belt-gap position. Each clamps with an M5 bolt through the printed slot — the hex nut sits captive in the track on the back face. The slots give ±4.5 mm of slide per block: start with a 6 mm gap between the blocks (within the article’s 3/16–1/4" range, with a little margin around the 4.8 mm belt) and close it down later only if the cord-wrap spacing demands it. The gap-facing bottom edges of each trough slab carry printed 45° relief chamfers so the departing belt clears the blocks.

The trough axis sits 12 mm in front of the board face — the same plane as the wheel grooves. This is by design; don’t shim it.

4. Drive belt

Make a knotless loop from the mason line (this is the same splice described in the Garrison Binder article):

  1. Thread one end 50 mm into the eye of a large needle.
  2. Push the needle into the hollow braided core of the other end, run it 40 mm inside, and out.
  3. Pull the tail through until the free end disappears into the splice; stitch across it twice.

Route: around the rod one full turn at the cradle gap → down to guide 1 → guide 2 → across the slack loop (weight hanger + pulley riding in it) → up over the drive wheel → guide 3 → vertically back up into the gap to the rod. Splice the loop to length in place so the weight hangs with ~150 mm of travel.

5. Cord path

Screw the spool brackets to the face at the left end (~60 mm apart); the spool rides on the M8 axle resting in the open slots. Screw eye 1 to the face at ~130 mm from the left edge with its flange top flush with the board’s top edge (eye at rod height, guiding the spool run). Screw eye 2 at ~225 mm with its flange top ~30 mm below the edge — from there the cord rises to the bind point at roughly 50°. The tensioner goes between them at (170, 50): cord runs spool → eye 1 → down between the tensioner discs → eye 2 → up onto the rod.

Per the article, the cord must approach the rod from the in-feed side, rising at a steep angle — never straight down, and never from the out-feed side. Eye 2 sitting low and left of the cradle delivers this.

Tensioner stack on the M5 bolt: captive head in base → base → disc → cord → disc → spring → knob (captive nut, pocket facing the spring). The knob compresses the spring for fine, stable drag.

6. Feed supports

Cut two 1" dowels to length: measure H = bench top to the bottom of the cradle trough, then cut dowels to H − 24 mm. Push into base and head sockets, drive the pinch screws. The big 1¾" troughs end up level with the cradle trough bottom — exactly the alignment the article calls for. The base flanges have screw holes; leave them unscrewed if you want to reposition the stands between butt and tip sections.

Tuning

All of the Garrison Binder tuning advice applies. The short version:

  • Weight: start at ~450 g (1 lb). More is not better — if the rod drags in the cradle or the corners chip, remove weight.
  • Cord tension: must be less than the belt weight. Test per the article — tie a loop in the cord and hang the weight on it; the weight should pull cord off the spool easily. Too much cord tension twists the rod on the first pass.
  • Spool take-off drag: cord pulling the spool round adds hidden tension upstream of the tensioner, and it grows as the spool empties — the exact problem the article describes. Its fix works here too: bend the 1/8" brass rod into a loop rising above the spool and take the cord off over the end through it; the springy rod also absorbs tension spikes.
  • Belt clearance: if the belt rubs a cradle block, widen the gap slightly or nudge guide 1 further from the cradle — the belt leaving the rod should angle away, never scrape. With guide 1 at the drilling-plan position the belt departs at ~168° of wrap, inside the article’s ≤170° rule, and the cradle chamfers give it clear air.
  • Bind twice, once in each direction, per standard Garrison practice.

Related

  • Garrison Binder — the reference article: theory, tuning, and troubleshooting
  • Rod Binder Notes — Smithwick binder and a gallery of other designs
  • ‘New’ Smithwick Binder — my first (wooden) binder build

item.title: Garrison Binder
item.description:
I’ve copied this content from http://www.canerod.com/rodmakers/tips/binder.html (Wayback Machine). I’ve reformatted it for reading and placed the images in-line after each paragraph.

Unlocking the Mysteries of the Garrison Binder

by Chris Bogart

Hiding this ramble.

Did you ever wonder why (to quote Andy Rooney) the Garrison binder is for many rodmakers the source of contentious problems while other rodmakers never seem to have problems. One of the primary reasons for the mystery the Garrison binder presents is that rodmakers often built it by following a diagram in a book and then hoped for the best. As a result, some binders worked as desired because of dumb luck and others didn’t because of bad luck. When the binder did not behave and was cantankerous to use, it was assumed that it worked that way for the master himself. I have since learned that when properly constructed and adjusted (tuned) the Garrison binder is a pleasure to operate and does a great job with little problems.

This article will discuss the how and why of constructing the Garrison binder and then how to tune it to perform at it’s best. Like most people, I first blindly followed a diagram in a book and did some things right and did some things wrong. It was initially hard for me to tell what was important and critical to its operation and what wasn’t. I have since looked at numerous other rodmakers’ binders and discussed their operation and their solutions to traditional problems. I have applied the lessons learned to my binder with great success. I have come to the following conclusions on how the Garrison binder should be constructed and why.

The Garrison binder is essentially an incredibly simple but clever device. What makes it mysterious is that there are very subtle things that are sometimes not obvious that have impact upon performance. The heart of the binder is the cradle that holds the rod, the drive belt that wraps around the rod applying pressure and the string that binds the segments together. It is here where we will analyze the binder.

The Cradle

The cradle is the starting point from which to build the rest of the binder. Everything else is aligned relative to the cradle. The point from which all this alignment is done is the bottom of the trough (half circle) that holds the rod. The size of the trough is not important. I find a larger diameter (approximately 1" or larger) trough is easier to use than a small one (5/8"). Too small and it constrains the rod on larger sections. The space left between the two sections determines the spacing of wraps of the binding cord. This space is usually just wide enough (3/16 - 1/4") so the drive belt fits but doesn’t constrain it. This distance needs to be adjusted until you get a good working distance. This is why there are slots so it can be adjusted by sliding the cradle back and forth. I recommend only adjusting the left side since all other alignments and positioning is done from the right side. Once the cradle is in place, then all other parts of the binder will be aligned to it referenced to the trough bottom of the forward side of the cradle. This is where the drive belt comes out.

Feed Supports

The in-feed and out-feed supports can be aligned using a wooden dowel. The out feed supports have troughs that are of a larger diameter (1 and 3/4 inches). The centers of the bottom of the support troughs need to be the same distance from the binder as the cradle trough is. On the parallel plane to the binder face centered on our reference point all guide wheels and the drive wheel.

Drive Wheels

Word about drive wheels. Most wheels are too shallow and the drive belt easily jumps out of it. This is also true concerning the pulley that holds the weight. I have switched from a small one to a larger one that has a good deep wheel. I found a ready source for these at my local hardware store. I disassemble two wheeled pulleys for my guide wheels. These wheels have a standard 5/16 ID holes that fits the bolts I use as an axle.

Now for the placement of the first guide whose position is very important and its misplacement will cause problems. It should be positioned so the drive belt does not drag on the cradle. This means the angle of the drive belt to it should not be equal or greater than 180 degrees. It should be approximately 170 degrees or less, or if you prefer a clock reference, about 25 minutes pass the hour. On most diagrams of binders this point is not clear. I feel that when diagrams of the binder where made the graphic artist did not appreciate this fact and aligned the wheels to make it look neat. Wrong, this neatness has caused many problems. On my binder the angle is the maximum it could be (29 minutes pass the hour) without causing problems (dumb luck). I have seen other rodmakers who have bought binders that where made with this wheel too far left and it causes drag. This drag is one cause of problems that can cause twists in the rod. I know of one modification that uses a rod to push the belt out away from the cradle that some rodmakers use to try and correct this problem. Easiest way to remedy the problem is to move the wheel to the right.

Now for the good news, the placement of the other wheels and drive wheel are not critical. They just guide the belt. On the left side of the cradle the cord usually doesn’t drag and most rodmakers don’t have it close to the cradle.

Binding Cord

The last part of constructing the binder is the components for holding the binding cord, its guide path, and a tensioning device. The binding cord usually comes on a spool or bobbin depending on the rodmaker’s source. I have the large industrial spool. The trick here is to let the cord come off the spool with no drag. I previously let the spool turn as I pulled the cord off. After a lot of use, the spool did not turn easily and caused drag. This increased tension on the cord and would cause the rod to twist. I solved this problem by using a 1/8 brass rod with a loop in the end that is long enough to allow the cord to freely come off the spool upwards. The rod also serves as shock absorber (like the tip of your fly rod with a delicate tippet) even if the cord drags a bit it does not cause excess tension. The cord then flows through the guides and tensioner to the last guide that allows the cord to come from behind into the drive belt and rod at approximately 45 degree angle. You do not want the cord to come directly down to where it is being bound. It must come from the same direction the rod that is being bound.

Drive Belt

How to make a knotless drive belt is easy. I use braided chalk and mason line for my drive belt. It can be found in most hardware stores. Do not choose twisted line for this purpose. To make a make the knotless drive belt you will need a large sewing needle whose eye is big enough for the line. Once you cut the line to approximate length, thread the line through the eye of the needle for about 2 - 3 inches. Because the line is braided, you can take the needle and stick it into the hollow core or the other end of the line for about 1 and 1/2 inches and then out through the line. You can now remove the needle and pull the line back until the end just goes back into the line. I now take a regular needle and thread and make a few stitches to hold the line in place with a few extras where it comes out to keep the braid from unraveling. The is just like a snake eating itself. No glue or knots are needed and you will never know when the spliced area goes around the rod. The splice is very flexible and never binds. Making this knotless belt takes very little time and requires very little effort or skill.

Weight

Now for the last part of tuning your binder, adjusting weights and tension. First, adjust the weight you have on the pulley that rides on the drive belt. This is the mechanism for applying pressure to the glued up rod. More weight is not necessarily better. I feel that the weight should be a little as necessary to give satisfactory results. I use a coffee jar that has old nuts and bolts in it as a weight . I can add and subtract weight easily. The first sign of excess weight is the rod will drag on the cradle. Look carefully at the rod to see if you have rounded or chipped the corners of the rod. Look also at the bottom of the cradle. I used a soft metal (Aluminum) for my binder and the bamboo will actually shave off metal if there is too much weight. So play with the weight so that you are not destroying your rod or binder. I have found that about 1 - 1.5 pounds is more than enough. This weight is based upon the glue (epoxy) I use. You may want to have one weight for butts and one for tips depending on the type of rods you build. I use the same weight for both and have had no ill effects.

Tension

You now need to tension the binding cord. You now need to tension the binding cord. The binding cord does not apply any clamping pressure to the rod. It just holds the pressure that has been applied by thedrive belt. It wraps the rod maintaining the pressure. Too much tension on the drive cord will cause a twist. Normally this will happen on the first pass and cannot be corrected on the second. What happens is the excess tension starts to pull the rod segments and this causes them to rotate them. The tension should be adjusted to allow a firm even pull on the binding cord. A good way to check to see if there is too much tension is to tie a loop in the cord and hang the weight on it. If the binding cord holds the weight, then there is too much tension. The weight should pull the binding cord easily. I know other rodmakers that use a small spring scale to measure and adjust the tension so weight and tension are even. I believe that tension should be slightly less than the weight.

With a properly tuned and adjusted Garrison binder you achieve excellent results. The only problem I have had is when the binding cord has had too much tension on it. That problem is now solved. I now have now had numerous rods that come out of gluing straight and true, requiring little or no straightening. Understanding your Garrison binder and making some subtle changes can allow you to get maximum performance out of it.

item.title: Mitered Picture Frame, 1¼″ × ⅞″ Profile (Proposed)
item.description:
A plain, square-profile mitered picture frame made from stock that is 1¼″ wide and ⅞″ tall, rabbeted on the back to hold glass, a picture and a backing board. The worked example is a picture 11½″ tall × 15⅝″ wide; a formula and a size table at the bottom give the numbers for any other picture.

Provenance of the numbers. (stated) = given by you: the stock profile and the picture size. (chosen) = a design decision I made because the profile alone doesn’t settle it (rabbet size, glass clearance). (derived) = worked out from those so everything closes. Change a (chosen) value and the (derived) ones move with it. The Alternate rabbet section shows how.

What is stated, what is chosen

Item Value
Stock profile 1¼″ wide × ⅞″ tall, square edges (stated)
Picture / glass 11½″ tall × 15⅝″ wide (stated); landscape
Rabbet ⅜″ wide × ½″ deep, cut on the back inside edge (chosen)
Glass-to-rabbet clearance 1/16″ each side (chosen)
Joint Four 45° miters

Why that rabbet: ½″ deep holds ⅛″ glass + the print (≤ 1/16″) + a ⅛″ backing board ≈ 5/16″ and still leaves ≈ 3/16″ for the retaining points. That leaves a ⅜″-thick front lip on the ⅞″ stock. ⅜″ wide gives the lip a 5/16″ overlap on the picture edge (⅜″ − 1/16″ clearance). That is enough to hide a ragged edge and hold the picture, and it leaves a ⅞″ wall behind it.

Drawings (true scale)

Drawn from the dimensions on this page. Click to open full size.

Front elevation

Profile section

Parts and stick layout

The numbers

Derived Working Result
Rabbet opening picture + 2 × 1/16″ 15¾″ × 11⅝″ (derived)
Sight opening (what you see) rabbet opening − 2 × ⅜″ 15″ × 10⅞″ (derived)
Outside size sight + 2 × 1¼″ 17½″ × 13⅜″ (derived)
Visible face width stock width 1¼″ all round
Picture hidden under the lip ⅜″ − 1/16″ 5/16″ per side
Rabbet-opening diagonals (square check) √(15¾² + 11⅝²) 19.58″, both equal

Shortcut for any picture: every piece is cut to the picture dimension + 1⅞″, measured long point to long point. 15⅝″ + 1⅞″ = 17½″; 11½″ + 1⅞″ = 13⅜″.

Cut list

Finished stock is ⅞″ × 1¼″, rabbeted before mitering. Lengths are long point to long point.

Part Qty T × W × L Notes
Rails (top, bottom) 2 ⅞″ × 1¼″ × 17½″ 45° at both ends, long point on the outside edge
Stiles (sides) 2 ⅞″ × 1¼″ × 13⅜″ Same
Glass 1 ⅛″ × 11½″ × 15⅝″ Ask the glass shop for exactly this size; acrylic works and is lighter
Backing board 1 ⅛″ × 11½″ × 15⅝″ Hardboard, thin ply or foam-core
Retainers 6–8 Flexi-points or small turn buttons, about ⅛″ proud of the rabbet floor
Hanger 1 set Two D-rings (screws ≤ ½″ long, since the wall is ⅞″ thick) + picture wire, or one sawtooth hanger for a light frame

Stock to buy: the four pieces total 61¾″ of long-point length. Alternating the miters nests the pieces, so each shared cut saves 1¼″ and the stick only needs about 58½″ with kerfs (61¾″ − 3 × 1¼″ + 3 kerfs). Buy one 6′ length (5/4 stock milled to ⅞″ × 1¼″) so the corners share grain and about 13½″ is left for test cuts. Mill a little extra width for the rabbet setup pieces.

Build sequence

  1. Mill one straight stick to ⅞″ × 1¼″, longer than needed. Pick the best face as the front.
  2. Cut the rabbet first, on the whole stick: ⅜″ wide × ½″ deep on the back inside edge. Table-saw it in two passes, or use a router with a rabbeting bit. Test on an offcut: the leftover front lip should be ⅜″ thick.
  3. Ease the front edges with a light 1/16″ chamfer or sanding if you want. Do it now, while the stick is straight.
  4. Check the saw’s 45° with a square cut-off test: cut two scraps, join them, and measure against a 90° square. Fix it before cutting good stock.
  5. Cut the miters on a miter saw or sled with a stop block. Set the stop for 17½″ and cut both rails with the same setting, then reset to 13⅜″ for the stiles. Measure on the outside (long-point) edge, with the rabbet side up or down, but the same way each time.
  6. Dry-fit the four pieces. Check that the rabbet opening is 15¾″ × 11⅝″ and that its diagonals match at 19.58″. If they don’t, sneak up on the miters with a shooting board.
  7. Glue the miters. End grain drinks glue, so size each miter with a thin coat, wait a minute, then apply glue and clamp with a band or corner clamps. Check the diagonals again before it sets.
  8. Reinforce the corners, because a plain miter is a weak joint: ⅛″ splines (a contrasting wood looks good), loose tenons or at least a pair of 18-ga brads at each corner.
  9. Sand and finish before the glass goes in. Keep finish out of the rabbet where the glass sits.
  10. Assemble: glass, picture, backing, then the points or turn buttons. Fit the D-rings on the back of each stile about a third of the way down (the wall is ⅞″ thick, so use short screws) and run the wire.

Other picture sizes

Picture (H × W) Rabbet opening Sight opening Outside (H × W) Rail / stile long point
5″ × 7″ 5⅛″ × 7⅛″ 4⅜″ × 6⅜″ 6⅞″ × 8⅞″ 8⅞″ / 6⅞″
8″ × 10″ 8⅛″ × 10⅛″ 7⅜″ × 9⅜″ 9⅞″ × 11⅞″ 11⅞″ / 9⅞″
11″ × 14″ 11⅛″ × 14⅛″ 10⅜″ × 13⅜″ 12⅞″ × 15⅞″ 15⅞″ / 12⅞″
11½″ × 15⅝″ (this plan) 11⅝″ × 15¾″ 10⅞″ × 15″ 13⅜″ × 17½″ 17½″ / 13⅜″

Here rails are the long top and bottom pieces, and stiles are the shorter sides. With a mat, use the mat’s outside size as the “picture”.

For any other size, with or without a mat, use the picture-frame calculator: it gives the outside and inside length of every member, a cut list and a mat bill of materials, and prints to PDF.

Alternate rabbet

If a ⅜″-wide rabbet hides too much of the picture, a ¼″ rabbet is fine (the stock is the same size). Everything shifts by +¼″: sight opening 15¼″ × 11⅛″, outside 17¾″ × 13⅝″, so rails become 17¾″ and stiles 13⅝″ (formula: picture + 2⅛″). The lip then overlaps the picture by only 3/16″ per side.

Open questions

  • Rabbet size is my choice, not part of your profile. If the profile you have in mind already includes a rabbet or a decorative bevel on the front, tell me and I’ll redo the numbers.
  • Mat or no mat: if the picture is to be matted, the “picture” in every formula is the mat’s outside size, and the glass is cut to that.
  • Print thickness: a thick print or a stretched canvas needs a deeper rabbet. ½″ allows about 5/16″ of glass + print + backing.
  • Hanging weight: the D-ring setup suits anything up to the 5–10 lb range. A frame this size with glass weighs about 2–3 lb.

item.title: Rod Binder Notes
item.description:
Notes on Rod Binders

Because my brain isn’t the lint catch that it used to be, here are some notes for reference. Preference toward Internet Archive and ensuring they’re cataloged in the Wayback Machine.

Smithwick Rod Binder

From Canerod.com, there’s a PDF referenced.

Fantastic Gallery of Binders on bamboorodmaking.com

Wayback Machine

Pulleys for Belt Drive

I have a couple of questions regarding building a binder. I’ve located some pulleys at the hardware store with ~ 1/4" channel in them, is this too wide or doesn’t it matter? What should I use for a belt? (Mark Pohl)

You can use either a round leather, or round urethane drive belt. The 1/4" wide groove shouldn’t be a problem, and you can get the belting in 1/4", too. (Martin-Darrell)

I used something similar, rollers from a patio door - got them at Lowes, brass with bushings about 1/4 inch groove. I built my binder ALA Garrison design, but have modified it per a suggestion on the list. Make a second main drive pulley and stack them together. Wind one pulley full of 50# braided nylon masons twine - I anchored the twine by drilling a small hole for a screw, sticking the end of the drive belt/string in the hole and screwing the screw in. Do the same think with the end of the belt on the empty drive pulley. Crank the pulleys backwards to rewind all of the belt onto the other pulley. Thread the belt through your pulleys and around a 1/4 test dowel, hang your weight on the belt and away you go. The benefit is NO slipping of the belt, and NO bump as the splice or knot in the belt traverses the rod.
